📌 Chapter 1

What is SQL?

SQL (Structured Query Language) is the standard language for managing and querying relational databases. Whether you're a data analyst, backend developer, or data engineer — SQL is the universal skill that lets you speak to any database.

SQL in plain English

Imagine your company stores millions of customer orders in a spreadsheet. SQL is the language you use to ask questions like: "Show me all orders from Mumbai placed in the last 30 days, sorted by value." SQL translates your business question into a precise instruction that the database engine executes in milliseconds — even across billions of rows.

🗄️

Database

An organized collection of structured information stored electronically. Examples: MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQL Server, Oracle. Think of it as a container that holds multiple related tables.

📊

Table

Data organized in rows (records) and columns (fields) — like a spreadsheet with strict rules. Each table represents one entity: customers, orders, products, employees.

🔑

Primary Key

A unique identifier for each row. No two rows can share a primary key value, and it can never be NULL. Usually an auto-incrementing integer like customer_id.

🔗

Foreign Key

A column that references the primary key of another table — creating a relationship between tables. For example, orders.customer_id references customers.customer_id.

📐

Schema

The blueprint of your database — the collection of all tables, columns, types, constraints, and relationships. Designing a good schema upfront saves you from painful migrations later.

⚡

Query

A statement written in SQL to retrieve or manipulate data. Every query is declarative — you describe what you want, and the database engine figures out how to get it efficiently.

SQL Command Categories

SQL commands are grouped into four categories based on what they do. Understanding which category a command belongs to helps you reason about permissions, transactions, and reversibility.

🏗️

DDL — Data Definition Language

Commands: CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE
Defines or modifies database structure. DDL changes are auto-committed — you can't roll them back. Run these carefully in production.

✏️

DML — Data Manipulation Language

Commands: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, SELECT
Works with the actual data inside tables. DML statements can be wrapped in transactions and rolled back if something goes wrong.

🔒

DCL — Data Control Language

Commands: GRANT, REVOKE
Controls which users can access which tables and perform which operations. Critical for database security in multi-user environments.

💾

TCL — Transaction Control Language

Commands: COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT
Manages grouping of DML statements into atomic units. If any step fails, you can ROLLBACK all changes to maintain data integrity.

SQL Data Types

Every column in a table must have a data type. This tells SQL what kind of data to expect and how to store it efficiently.

Numeric Data Types
TypeRangeUse Case

BIGINT±9.2 quintillionLarge IDs, timestamps

TypeStorageUse Case

VARCHAR(n)Variable-length, up to n charsNames, emails, titles

Choosing the Right Type Matters

  • Use DECIMAL not FLOAT for money — floats have rounding errors
  • Use VARCHAR over CHAR unless length is truly fixed
  • Use TIMESTAMP for audit fields like created_at
🏗️ Chapter 3

DDL — Data Definition Language

DDL commands define and manage the structure of your database — not the data inside. These are the commands you run when setting up a new project or modifying your schema over time.

DDL is Auto-Committed

Unlike DML (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE), DDL commands like DROP TABLE or ALTER TABLE are automatically committed the moment they execute. You cannot roll them back inside a transaction. Always back up data before running destructive DDL in production.

CREATE TABLE

Define a new table with its columns, data types, and constraints.

SQL 
-- Create a customers table
CREATE TABLE customers (
  customer_id  INT          PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,
  name         VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
  email        VARCHAR(255) UNIQUE NOT NULL,
  city         VARCHAR(50),
  age          INT          CHECK (age >= 18),
  created_at   TIMESTAMP    DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);

Common Constraints

🔑

PRIMARY KEY

Uniquely identifies each row. Cannot be NULL.

🔗

FOREIGN KEY

Links to a primary key in another table.

❌

NOT NULL

Column must always have a value.

✨

UNIQUE

No duplicate values allowed in this column.

📋

DEFAULT

Assigns a default value if none is provided.

✅

CHECK

Validates data against a boolean condition.

ALTER TABLE

Modify an existing table structure — add columns, change types, drop columns.

SQL
-- Add a new column
ALTER TABLE customers
  ADD COLUMN phone VARCHAR(20);

-- Change column data type
ALTER TABLE customers
  MODIFY COLUMN phone VARCHAR(15) NOT NULL;

-- Rename a column
ALTER TABLE customers
  RENAME COLUMN phone TO phone_number;

-- Drop a column
ALTER TABLE customers
  DROP COLUMN age;

DROP vs TRUNCATE

SQL
-- TRUNCATE: Remove all rows, keep the table structure
TRUNCATE TABLE customers;

-- DROP: Completely delete the table (structure + data)
DROP TABLE customers;

-- DROP IF EXISTS: Safe version, no error if table doesn't exist
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS customers;
Comparison: DROP vs TRUNCATE vs DELETE
CommandRemoves Rows?Removes Structure?Can Rollback?Speed
DELETEYes (selective)NoYesSlow
TRUNCATEAll rowsNoNoFast
DROPAll rowsYesNoInstant
✏️ Chapter 4

DML — Data Manipulation Language

DML commands work with the actual data in your tables. INSERT adds data, UPDATE modifies it, and DELETE removes it.

INSERT INTO

SQL
-- Insert a single row
INSERT INTO customers (name, email, city)
VALUES ('Alice Johnson', '[email protected]', 'Mumbai');

-- Insert multiple rows at once
INSERT INTO customers (name, email, city)
VALUES
  ('Bob Smith',   '[email protected]',   'Delhi'),
  ('Carol White', '[email protected]', 'Bangalore'),
  ('David Lee',   '[email protected]', 'Chennai');

UPDATE

Always use a WHERE clause with UPDATE! Without it, every single row gets updated.

SQL
-- Update a specific customer's city
UPDATE customers
SET city = 'Pune'
WHERE customer_id = 1;

-- Update multiple columns at once
UPDATE customers
SET 
  city  = 'Hyderabad',
  email = '[email protected]'
WHERE name = 'Alice Johnson';

DELETE

SQL
-- Delete a specific row
DELETE FROM customers
WHERE customer_id = 5;

-- Delete with multiple conditions
DELETE FROM customers
WHERE city = 'Delhi'
  AND created_at < '2023-01-01';
🔍 Chapter 5

SELECT — Querying Data

SELECT is the most-used SQL command — you'll write it hundreds of times a day. It retrieves data from one or more tables and is the foundation of everything from reports to dashboards to ETL pipelines.

The Logical Order of Execution

SQL doesn't execute in the order you write it. The database engine processes clauses in this order: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY → LIMIT. This is why you can't use a SELECT alias in a WHERE clause — WHERE runs before SELECT evaluates the alias.

SELECT columns -- 6. Choose what to return FROM table_name -- 1. Which table(s) WHERE condition -- 2. Filter rows GROUP BY column -- 3. Collapse into groups HAVING agg_condition -- 4. Filter groups ORDER BY column [ASC|DESC] -- 5. Sort output LIMIT count; -- 7. Cap the rows

Basic SELECT Examples

SQL
-- Select all columns
SELECT * FROM customers;

-- Select specific columns
SELECT name, email, city
FROM customers;

-- Remove duplicates with DISTINCT
SELECT DISTINCT city
FROM customers;

-- Use aliases for readable output
SELECT
  name  AS "Customer Name",
  email AS "Email Address"
FROM customers;

-- Order results
SELECT name, city
FROM customers
ORDER BY name ASC;

-- Limit results (pagination)
SELECT * FROM customers
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 10;
Sample Output — SELECT name, city FROM customers
namecity
Alice JohnsonMumbai
Bob SmithDelhi
Carol WhiteBangalore
David LeeChennai

Computed Columns & String Functions

SQL
-- Math expressions in SELECT
SELECT
  product_name,
  price,
  price * 1.18 AS price_with_tax
FROM products;

-- String functions
SELECT
  UPPER(name)              AS upper_name,
  LOWER(email)             AS lower_email,
  LENGTH(name)             AS name_length,
  CONCAT(name, ' - ', city) AS full_info
FROM customers;
🎯 Chapter 6

WHERE & Filtering

The WHERE clause filters rows before any aggregation happens. Think of it as a gate — only rows that pass the condition move forward. Mastering WHERE operators lets you write precise, efficient queries that return exactly what you need.

WHERE vs HAVING

Use WHERE to filter individual rows before grouping. Use HAVING to filter aggregated groups after GROUP BY. A common mistake is trying to use an aggregate like SUM() inside a WHERE clause — that's what HAVING is for.

Comparison Operators

SQL
SELECT * FROM products WHERE price = 100;   -- Equal
SELECT * FROM products WHERE price != 100;  -- Not equal
SELECT * FROM products WHERE price > 500;   -- Greater than
SELECT * FROM products WHERE price <= 200;  -- Less or equal

Logical Operators — AND, OR, NOT

SQL
-- AND: both conditions must be true
SELECT * FROM customers
WHERE city = 'Mumbai' AND age > 25;

-- OR: at least one condition true
SELECT * FROM customers
WHERE city = 'Mumbai' OR city = 'Delhi';

-- NOT: negate a condition
SELECT * FROM customers
WHERE NOT city = 'Chennai';

Special Operators

SQL
-- IN: check if value is in a list
SELECT * FROM customers
WHERE city IN ('Mumbai', 'Delhi', 'Bangalore');

-- BETWEEN: range check (inclusive)
SELECT * FROM products
WHERE price BETWEEN 100 AND 500;

-- LIKE: pattern matching
SELECT * FROM customers
WHERE email LIKE '%@gmail.com';   -- ends with

SELECT * FROM customers
WHERE name LIKE 'A%';              -- starts with A

SELECT * FROM customers
WHERE name LIKE '_ob%';            -- _ matches exactly 1 char

-- IS NULL / IS NOT NULL
SELECT * FROM customers
WHERE phone IS NULL;

LIKE Pattern Wildcards

  • % — matches zero or more characters
  • _ — matches exactly one character
  • Example: 'A_i%' matches "Alice", "Alia", "Arid..."
🔗 Chapter 7

JOINs — Combining Tables

JOINs combine rows from two or more tables based on a related column. In real databases, data is spread across many tables — JOINs are how you bring it back together for analysis. Understanding JOINs is what separates beginners from intermediate SQL users.

The Join Condition

A JOIN needs an ON clause that tells SQL which columns to match. The most common pattern is matching a foreign key in one table to the primary key in another. Example: ON orders.customer_id = customers.customer_id — this links every order back to its customer. Without a proper ON condition, you'd get a Cartesian product (every row × every row), which is almost never what you want.

  • INNER JOIN — only rows with a match in both tables. Missing data on either side is excluded.
  • LEFT JOIN — all rows from the left table, plus matched rows from the right. Unmatched right side returns NULL.
  • RIGHT JOIN — all rows from the right table, plus matched rows from the left. Rarely used (just flip the tables and use LEFT JOIN).
  • FULL OUTER JOIN — all rows from both tables. Unmatched sides get NULL. Not natively supported in MySQL — use UNION of LEFT and RIGHT JOINs.
  • CROSS JOIN — every row from table A × every row from table B. Produces a Cartesian product. Use intentionally for generating combinations.
  • SELF JOIN — a table joined to itself. Useful for hierarchical data like employee → manager relationships.
Visual Comparison of JOIN Types
INNER JOIN
Matching rows only
LEFT JOIN
All left + matched right
RIGHT JOIN
All right + matched left
FULL OUTER JOIN
All rows from both

INNER JOIN — Most Common

Returns only rows where there's a match in both tables. If a customer has no orders, they won't appear in the result. Use this when you only care about records that exist on both sides.

SQL
-- Get all orders with customer names
SELECT
  c.name       AS customer_name,
  o.order_id,
  o.order_date,
  o.total
FROM customers c
INNER JOIN orders o
  ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;
Result
customer_nameorder_idorder_datetotal
Alice Johnson10012024-01-15₹2,500.00
Alice Johnson10042024-02-20₹800.00
Bob Smith10022024-01-17₹1,200.00
David Lee10032024-01-22₹4,100.00

LEFT JOIN — Keep All From Left

SQL
-- All customers, even those with NO orders
SELECT
  c.name,
  o.order_id  -- NULL if no orders
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o
  ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;

-- Find customers who NEVER ordered
SELECT c.name
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o
  ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.order_id IS NULL;

Joining Three Tables

SQL
-- Customers + Orders + Products in one query
SELECT
  c.name         AS customer,
  p.name         AS product,
  oi.quantity,
  oi.quantity * p.price AS line_total
FROM customers     c
JOIN orders        o  ON c.customer_id  = o.customer_id
JOIN order_items   oi ON o.order_id     = oi.order_id
JOIN products      p  ON oi.product_id  = p.product_id;
📊 Chapter 8

Aggregate Functions

Aggregate functions collapse many rows into a single value. They're the backbone of every analytics query — from counting users to summing revenue to finding the highest-performing product. Used alone they summarize the whole table; used with GROUP BY they summarize per category.

All Aggregates Ignore NULL — Except COUNT(*)

COUNT(*) counts every row regardless of NULLs. But COUNT(column), SUM(), AVG(), MIN(), and MAX() all silently skip NULL values. This means AVG(salary) gives you the average of non-NULL salaries only — which can be misleading. Use COALESCE(salary, 0) if you need NULLs treated as zero.

🔢

COUNT()

COUNT(*) counts all rows including NULLs. COUNT(col) counts only non-NULL values in that column. COUNT(DISTINCT col) counts unique values.

➕

SUM()

Adds up all non-NULL values. Perfect for total revenue, total quantity, or any cumulative metric. Returns NULL if all values are NULL.

📐

AVG()

Returns the arithmetic mean of non-NULL values. Equivalent to SUM() / COUNT(col). Watch out — it excludes NULLs from the denominator, which can skew results.

⬇️

MIN()

Returns the smallest value. Works on numbers, dates, and strings (alphabetical). Useful for earliest date, cheapest price, or first alphabetical entry.

⬆️

MAX()

Returns the largest value. Works on numbers, dates, and strings. Useful for latest date, highest price, or last alphabetical entry.

📊

GROUP_CONCAT()

MySQL-specific. Concatenates values from multiple rows into a single comma-separated string. Useful for collecting tags, categories, or IDs per group.

Examples

SQL
-- How many customers do we have?
SELECT COUNT(*) AS total_customers
FROM customers;

-- Total revenue from all orders
SELECT SUM(total) AS total_revenue
FROM orders;

-- Average order value
SELECT AVG(total) AS avg_order_value
FROM orders;

-- Price range of products
SELECT
  MIN(price) AS cheapest,
  MAX(price) AS most_expensive,
  AVG(price) AS average_price
FROM products;
📦 Chapter 9

GROUP BY & HAVING

GROUP BY groups rows that share the same value in a column, then lets you run aggregate functions on each group independently. It's how you answer questions like "total sales per city" or "number of orders per customer per month."

The GROUP BY Contract

In a SELECT with GROUP BY, every column in the SELECT list must either appear in the GROUP BY clause or be wrapped in an aggregate function like COUNT(), SUM(), etc. If you select a column that's not grouped and not aggregated, the result is undefined (MySQL may allow it, but the value returned is arbitrary).

  • Use HAVING to filter groups after aggregation — for example, only show cities with more than 10 customers.
  • Use WHERE to filter rows before grouping — for example, only count orders placed in 2024.
  • You can GROUP BY multiple columns to create more granular groups: GROUP BY city, category.
SQL
-- Count customers per city
SELECT city, COUNT(*) AS customer_count
FROM customers
GROUP BY city
ORDER BY customer_count DESC;
Result
citycustomer_count
Mumbai42
Delhi38
Bangalore27
Chennai19
SQL — HAVING
-- HAVING filters groups (WHERE filters rows)
SELECT
  city,
  COUNT(*) AS count,
  AVG(o.total) AS avg_spend
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
GROUP BY city
HAVING COUNT(*) > 5           -- Only cities with 5+ orders
   AND AVG(o.total) > 1000      -- AND avg spend over 1000
ORDER BY avg_spend DESC;

Key Difference

  • WHERE — filters individual rows before grouping
  • HAVING — filters groups after aggregation
  • You CANNOT use aggregate functions in a WHERE clause
🪆 Chapter 10

Subqueries

A subquery is a query nested inside another query. Subqueries let you break a complex problem into steps — compute something first, then use that result in the outer query. They can appear in SELECT, FROM, WHERE, and HAVING clauses.

Scalar, Row, Table, and Correlated Subqueries

  • Scalar subquery — returns exactly one value (one row, one column). Used in SELECT or WHERE comparisons: WHERE price > (SELECT AVG(price) ...)
  • Row subquery — returns one row with multiple columns. Compared using row constructors.
  • Table subquery — returns multiple rows. Used with IN, NOT IN, EXISTS, or in FROM as a derived table.
  • Correlated subquery — references a column from the outer query. Runs once per outer row — can be very slow on large tables. Usually replaceable with a JOIN or window function for better performance.

Tip: Prefer CTEs or JOINs over deeply nested subqueries when possible — they're easier to read, debug, and often faster.

Subquery in WHERE

SQL
-- Find products more expensive than the average price
SELECT name, price
FROM products
WHERE price > (
  SELECT AVG(price) FROM products
);

Subquery with IN

SQL
-- Find customers who placed orders in January 2024
SELECT name, email
FROM customers
WHERE customer_id IN (
  SELECT customer_id
  FROM orders
  WHERE order_date BETWEEN '2024-01-01' AND '2024-01-31'
);

EXISTS Subquery

SQL
-- Customers who have at least one order (EXISTS is often faster)
SELECT name
FROM customers c
WHERE EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM orders o
  WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id
);

Subquery in FROM (Derived Table)

SQL
-- Find cities where the average order is over 2000
SELECT city, avg_order
FROM (
  SELECT c.city, AVG(o.total) AS avg_order
  FROM customers c
  JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
  GROUP BY c.city
) AS city_stats
WHERE avg_order > 2000;
⚡ Chapter 11 — Deep Dive

Indexes — The Engine of Fast Queries

An index is a separate data structure that the database maintains alongside your table to make data retrieval dramatically faster. Understanding indexes is the single most impactful skill for writing high-performance SQL.

The Problem Indexes Solve

Imagine a library with 10 million books in no particular order. To find a book about "Python", you'd have to check every single book one by one — this is what a database does without an index (called a Full Table Scan, or FTS).

Now imagine an index card catalog sorted alphabetically by topic. You flip to "P", find "Python", and the card tells you exactly which shelf and row the book is on. That card catalog is exactly what a database index is.

Without vs With Index

  • Without index: O(n) full scan — must read every row. On 10M rows: potentially 30+ seconds.
  • With B-tree index: O(log n) — binary search through the tree. On 10M rows: microseconds.
  • With hash index: O(1) — direct lookup by hash. Fastest for exact equality checks.

How B-Tree Indexes Work Internally

The most common index type is a B-Tree (Balanced Tree). Here's what happens when you create one:

The B-Tree organizes index values in a sorted tree with multiple levels:

  • Root node: Top of the tree — contains a few "pivot" values that guide navigation.
  • Branch nodes: Intermediate nodes that continue narrowing down the search.
  • Leaf nodes: Bottom level — contain the actual indexed values + a pointer (row ID) to the physical row location in the table.

When you run WHERE email = '[email protected]', the DB traverses the tree root → branch → leaf in O(log n) steps — typically 3-4 comparisons even for millions of rows. The leaf then gives a direct pointer to Alice's row.

B-Tree Traversal Example — 7 items, find 45
LevelNode ValuesAction
Root3045 > 30 → go right
Branch40 | 5040 < 45 < 50 → go between
Leaf42 | 45 | 48Found 45 → row pointer returned ✅

Types of Indexes

An index on a single column. Most basic and common type. Best for filtering by one column in WHERE, JOIN ON, or ORDER BY.

SQL — Simple Index
-- Create index on email for fast login lookups
CREATE INDEX idx_users_email
  ON users (email);

-- Now this query is O(log n) instead of O(n)
SELECT * FROM users
WHERE email = '[email protected]';

-- Create index on salary for range queries
CREATE INDEX idx_emp_salary
  ON employees (salary);

-- This range scan now uses the index
SELECT name, salary FROM employees
WHERE salary BETWEEN 50000 AND 80000;
EXPLAIN — without vs with index
Scenariotyperows examinedExtra
No index on emailALL1,000,000Using where
Index on emailref1Using index condition

An index on multiple columns. The order of columns matters critically — the index is most useful when your WHERE clause filters on the leftmost column(s) first. This is the leftmost prefix rule.

SQL — Composite Index
-- Index on (customer_id, order_date)
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_cust_date
  ON orders (customer_id, order_date);

-- ✅ USES the index (filters on leftmost column first)
SELECT * FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 42;

-- ✅ USES the index (both columns)
SELECT * FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 42
  AND order_date > '2024-01-01';

-- ❌ CANNOT use the index (skips leftmost column)
SELECT * FROM orders
WHERE order_date > '2024-01-01';
-- Reason: B-Tree is sorted by customer_id first.
-- Without filtering customer_id, entire tree must be scanned.

For an index on (A, B, C): queries filtering on A, A+B, or A+B+C use the index. Queries on B, C, or B+C alone cannot use it. Plan composite indexes around your most common query patterns.

Enforces uniqueness on a column AND creates an index. The PRIMARY KEY is always a unique index. UNIQUE constraints create unique indexes automatically. Useful for natural keys like email, phone, username.

SQL — Unique Index
-- Method 1: CREATE UNIQUE INDEX
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_users_email_uniq
  ON users (email);

-- Method 2: UNIQUE constraint (same effect)
ALTER TABLE users
  ADD CONSTRAINT uq_email UNIQUE (email);

-- Composite unique index (combination must be unique)
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_user_date
  ON attendance (user_id, attendance_date);
-- A user can appear many times, but not twice on the same date

-- Inserting a duplicate now throws an error
INSERT INTO users (email) VALUES ('[email protected]');
-- ERROR 1062: Duplicate entry '[email protected]' for key 'uq_email'

A covering index includes ALL columns needed by a query — so the database answers the query entirely from the index, without ever touching the base table rows. This eliminates the second "row fetch" step, making queries dramatically faster. EXPLAIN shows Using index in Extra column when a covering index is used.

SQL — Covering Index
-- Query: find customer's orders in 2024, show total
SELECT order_date, total
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 42
  AND order_date >= '2024-01-01';

-- Regular index: uses index to find rows, then fetches table for 'total'
CREATE INDEX idx_cust_date
  ON orders (customer_id, order_date);

-- Covering index: query answered 100% from index (no table fetch)
CREATE INDEX idx_cust_date_total
  ON orders (customer_id, order_date, total);
-- The index now contains customer_id, order_date AND total
-- → Database never needs to read actual table rows

-- EXPLAIN confirms: Extra = 'Using index' (not 'Using index condition')
EXPLAIN SELECT order_date, total
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 42
  AND order_date >= '2024-01-01';
EXPLAIN — Regular vs Covering Index
Index TypetyperowsExtraTable fetch?
No indexALL500,000Using whereYes (all rows)
Regular indexref12Using index conditionYes (12 rows)
Covering indexref12Using indexNo ✨

A specialized index for searching natural language text inside VARCHAR or TEXT columns. Supports word-level search, relevance scoring, and Boolean operators. Much better than LIKE '%keyword%' which can't use regular indexes.

SQL — Full-Text Index
-- Create a full-text index on article title and body
CREATE FULLTEXT INDEX idx_articles_ft
  ON articles (title, body);

-- Natural language search (relevance scored)
SELECT
  title,
  MATCH(title, body) AGAINST('machine learning python') AS relevance
FROM articles
WHERE MATCH(title, body) AGAINST('machine learning python')
ORDER BY relevance DESC;

-- Boolean mode: + required, - excluded, * wildcard
SELECT title FROM articles
WHERE MATCH(title, body)
  AGAINST('+python -java machine*' IN BOOLEAN MODE);
-- Must have 'python', must NOT have 'java', optional 'machine...'

Clustered vs Non-Clustered Indexes

🗂️

Clustered Index

Determines the physical storage order of rows. Data rows ARE the leaf nodes. Only one per table (usually the Primary Key). Range scans are fast because consecutive rows are physically adjacent on disk. In MySQL InnoDB, the PK is always clustered.

📋

Non-Clustered Index

A separate structure with (indexed_value → row pointer). Many allowed per table. Requires two I/Os: one to find the pointer in the index, one to fetch the actual row. A covering index eliminates the second step.

SQL — Clustered vs Non-Clustered Behavior
-- InnoDB: PRIMARY KEY = clustered index (physical row order)
CREATE TABLE orders (
  id          INT PRIMARY KEY,       -- CLUSTERED: rows physically sorted by id
  customer_id INT,
  order_date  DATE,
  total       DECIMAL(10,2)
);

-- Non-clustered index — separate B-tree, pointer back to PK
CREATE INDEX idx_customer ON orders(customer_id);

-- Range scan on PK (clustered) → consecutive pages, very fast
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id BETWEEN 1000 AND 2000;

-- Non-clustered lookup → finds pointer in idx_customer, then fetches row by PK
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42;

Index Pitfalls — When Indexes Don't Work

These patterns silently prevent index usage and cause full table scans:

SQL — Index Anti-Patterns and Fixes
-- ❌ Wrapping an indexed column in a function → index unusable
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE YEAR(order_date) = 2024;
-- ✅ Fix: use a range instead
SELECT * FROM orders
WHERE order_date >= '2024-01-01' AND order_date < '2025-01-01';

-- ❌ Leading wildcard in LIKE → index unusable (can't seek start point)
SELECT * FROM users WHERE email LIKE '%@gmail.com';
-- ✅ Fix: trailing wildcard works fine
SELECT * FROM users WHERE email LIKE 'alice%';
-- Or use FULLTEXT index for substring searches

-- ❌ Implicit type conversion (string vs int) → index unusable
SELECT * FROM users WHERE user_id = '42';   -- user_id is INT, '42' is string
-- ✅ Fix: match the data type
SELECT * FROM users WHERE user_id = 42;

-- ❌ OR conditions across different columns → may not use index
SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '[email protected]' OR phone = '999';
-- ✅ Fix: UNION (each branch can use its own index)
SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '[email protected]'
UNION
SELECT * FROM users WHERE phone = '999';

-- ❌ NOT IN / NOT LIKE on non-indexed column → full scan
-- ❌ NULL comparison (IS NULL on non-indexed column) → full scan
-- ✅ Fix: ensure the column has an index and avoid negations where possible

Managing Indexes — Full Command Reference

SQL — Index Management
-- Create basic index
CREATE INDEX idx_name ON table_name (column1);

-- Create composite index
CREATE INDEX idx_name ON table_name (col1, col2, col3);

-- Create unique index
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_name ON table_name (column);

-- Create full-text index
CREATE FULLTEXT INDEX idx_name ON table_name (col1, col2);

-- View all indexes on a table
SHOW INDEX FROM orders;

-- Drop an index
DROP INDEX idx_name ON table_name;

-- Check if a query uses an index (EXPLAIN)
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 42 AND order_date > '2024-01-01';
-- Key columns: type, key, rows, Extra

EXPLAIN Deep Dive — Reading Query Plans

EXPLAIN shows exactly how the query optimizer will execute your query. Learning to read it is one of the most valuable skills for a data engineer or analyst.

SQL — Running EXPLAIN
EXPLAIN SELECT
  o.id, c.name, o.total
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.order_date > '2024-01-01'
ORDER BY o.total DESC;
EXPLAIN Output — Column Meanings
ColumnValueMeaning
typeALLFull table scan — worst case
typeindexFull index scan — better but still slow
typerangeIndex range scan — good for BETWEEN, >, <
typerefNon-unique index lookup — good
typeeq_refUnique index or PK join — very good
typeconst/systemSingle row result — optimal
keyidx_orders_cust_dateWhich index is being used
rows12Estimated rows the engine will examine
ExtraUsing indexCovering index — no table fetch needed ✨
ExtraUsing filesortIn-memory/disk sort — add ORDER BY col to index
ExtraUsing temporaryTemp table for GROUP BY — expensive
ExtraUsing whereWHERE applied after index scan

When to (and Not to) Add Indexes

Index Decision Guide
✅ Add Index When❌ Skip Index When
Column appears in WHERE frequentlyTable has fewer than ~1,000 rows
Column used in JOIN ON clauseColumn has very low cardinality (boolean, status with 2-3 values)
Column used in ORDER BY or GROUP BYTable is insert/update heavy (index maintenance cost high)
Column has high cardinality (email, UUID, phone)Column is rarely used in WHERE/JOIN/ORDER BY
FK columns (for JOIN performance)Column has many NULLs (index less selective)
Columns in range queries (dates, prices)You already have too many indexes (>10 per table)

Indexes are not free. Every INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE must also update all applicable indexes. A table with 15 indexes on it can be 5-10x slower on writes than the same table with 2 indexes. Always measure write performance after adding indexes. In write-heavy systems (like log tables), fewer indexes are better.

👁️ Chapter 12 — Deep Dive

Views & Materialized Views

A view is a named, saved SQL query that behaves like a virtual table. A materialized view goes further — it physically stores the query result for instant retrieval. Together they are essential tools for organizing complex SQL and supercharging dashboard performance.

Regular Views — Virtual Tables

A view stores only the SQL query definition, not the data. Every time you query a view, the underlying query runs fresh. Think of it as a macro or alias for a complex query.

  • Security: Expose only specific columns — hide salary, PII, passwords from certain users.
  • Abstraction: Application code queries vw_active_orders instead of a 10-table JOIN — schema changes only need to be updated in the view.
  • Reusability: Write a complex JOIN once, reference it everywhere without copy-pasting.
  • Simplicity: Give business-friendly names to technical queries.

Creating and Using Views

SQL — View Lifecycle
-- CREATE VIEW: save a complex query as a named view
CREATE VIEW vw_premium_customers AS
  SELECT
    c.id,
    c.name,
    c.email,
    COUNT(o.id)        AS order_count,
    SUM(o.total)       AS lifetime_value,
    MAX(o.order_date)  AS last_order
  FROM customers c
  JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id
  GROUP BY c.id, c.name, c.email
  HAVING SUM(o.total) > 10000;

-- USE VIEW: query it exactly like a table
SELECT * FROM vw_premium_customers
WHERE order_count > 5
ORDER BY lifetime_value DESC;

-- JOIN a view with another table
SELECT
  vpc.name,
  vpc.lifetime_value,
  s.rep_name AS account_manager
FROM vw_premium_customers vpc
JOIN sales_reps s ON vpc.id = s.customer_id;

-- UPDATE a view (modify its definition)
CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW vw_premium_customers AS
  SELECT
    c.id, c.name, c.email,
    SUM(o.total) AS lifetime_value
  FROM customers c
  JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id
  GROUP BY c.id, c.name, c.email
  HAVING SUM(o.total) > 5000;  -- lowered threshold

-- DROP VIEW
DROP VIEW IF EXISTS vw_premium_customers;

-- List all views in the database
SELECT TABLE_NAME, VIEW_DEFINITION
FROM INFORMATION_SCHEMA.VIEWS
WHERE TABLE_SCHEMA = DATABASE();

Updatable Views

Some views allow INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE operations through them — provided the view follows strict rules:

SQL — Updatable Views
-- Simple updatable view (single table, no aggregates, no DISTINCT)
CREATE VIEW vw_active_users AS
  SELECT id, name, email, status
  FROM users
  WHERE status = 'active';

-- INSERT through the view
INSERT INTO vw_active_users (name, email, status)
VALUES ('Alice', '[email protected]', 'active');

-- UPDATE through the view
UPDATE vw_active_users
SET email = '[email protected]'
WHERE id = 42;
Views that CANNOT be updated
Makes View Non-UpdatableWhy
GROUP BY / HAVINGOutput rows don't correspond 1:1 to base table rows
DISTINCTMultiple base rows may map to one view row
Aggregate functions (SUM, COUNT, etc.)Computed columns cannot be reverse-mapped
UNION / UNION ALLMultiple source tables involved
Subquery in SELECTComplex derivation prevents write-back
JOINs (in most cases)Ambiguous which base table to update

Materialized Views — Stored Snapshots

A materialized view (MV) is like a regular view, except it physically stores the query result on disk. It behaves like a cached table. Querying it is instant — no complex JOINs or aggregations run at query time. The trade-off: the data must be periodically refreshed to stay up to date.

⚡

Read Performance

Query a complex 8-table JOIN with aggregations in milliseconds instead of seconds. Pre-computed results sit ready on disk.

📊

Dashboard Power

Perfect for executive dashboards, KPI cards, and reports that millions of users view — compute once, serve to all.

🔄

Controlled Staleness

Data is stale between refreshes (minutes to hours). Acceptable for analytics; not for real-time transactional data.

Materialized View in PostgreSQL (Native Support)

SQL — PostgreSQL Materialized View
-- CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW: computed and stored on disk NOW
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW mv_monthly_sales_summary AS
  SELECT
    DATE_TRUNC('month', o.order_date)    AS month,
    c.country,
    p.category,
    COUNT(DISTINCT o.id)                  AS order_count,
    COUNT(DISTINCT o.customer_id)          AS unique_customers,
    SUM(oi.quantity)                       AS units_sold,
    SUM(oi.unit_price * oi.quantity)       AS gross_revenue,
    AVG(o.total)                            AS avg_order_value
  FROM orders       o
  JOIN customers    c  ON o.customer_id  = c.id
  JOIN order_items  oi ON o.id           = oi.order_id
  JOIN products     p  ON oi.product_id = p.id
  GROUP BY 1, 2, 3
WITH DATA;
-- WITH DATA: compute and store immediately
-- WITH NO DATA: create shell, populate later on first REFRESH

-- QUERY IT: fast as a simple table scan (no joins at runtime)
SELECT month, SUM(gross_revenue) AS total_rev
FROM mv_monthly_sales_summary
WHERE country = 'India'
GROUP BY month
ORDER BY month;

-- REFRESH: update the stored data
REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW mv_monthly_sales_summary;

-- REFRESH CONCURRENTLY: allows reads while refreshing (needs unique index)
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ON mv_monthly_sales_summary (month, country, category);
REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY mv_monthly_sales_summary;

-- INDEX on materialized view (just like a regular table)
CREATE INDEX ON mv_monthly_sales_summary (month);
CREATE INDEX ON mv_monthly_sales_summary (country);

-- DROP
DROP MATERIALIZED VIEW mv_monthly_sales_summary;

Simulating Materialized Views in MySQL

MySQL does not natively support materialized views. The standard approach is to use a summary table and populate it via a scheduled job or stored procedure:

SQL — MySQL Materialized View Pattern
-- Step 1: Create the summary table (this IS your materialized view)
CREATE TABLE mv_daily_revenue (
  report_date   DATE           NOT NULL,
  country       VARCHAR(50),
  category      VARCHAR(50),
  order_count   INT            DEFAULT 0,
  gross_revenue DECIMAL(15,2) DEFAULT 0,
  refreshed_at  DATETIME       DEFAULT NOW(),
  PRIMARY KEY (report_date, country, category)
);

-- Step 2: Stored procedure to refresh data
DELIMITER $$
CREATE PROCEDURE RefreshDailyRevenue()
BEGIN
  -- Clear yesterday's data and recompute
  DELETE FROM mv_daily_revenue
  WHERE report_date = DATE_SUB(CURDATE(), INTERVAL 1 DAY);

  INSERT INTO mv_daily_revenue
    (report_date, country, category, order_count, gross_revenue)
  SELECT
    DATE(o.created_at)         AS report_date,
    c.country,
    p.category,
    COUNT(DISTINCT o.id),
    SUM(oi.unit_price * oi.quantity)
  FROM orders       o
  JOIN customers    c  ON o.customer_id  = c.id
  JOIN order_items  oi ON o.id           = oi.order_id
  JOIN products     p  ON oi.product_id = p.id
  WHERE DATE(o.created_at) = DATE_SUB(CURDATE(), INTERVAL 1 DAY)
  GROUP BY 1, 2, 3;
END$$
DELIMITER ;

-- Step 3: Schedule using MySQL EVENT SCHEDULER (runs daily at 2 AM)
CREATE EVENT evt_refresh_daily_revenue
ON SCHEDULE EVERY 1 DAY
STARTS TIMESTAMP(CURDATE(), '02:00:00')
DO CALL RefreshDailyRevenue();

-- Step 4: Query is now instant!
SELECT country, SUM(gross_revenue) AS revenue
FROM mv_daily_revenue
WHERE report_date = DATE_SUB(CURDATE(), INTERVAL 1 DAY)
GROUP BY country
ORDER BY revenue DESC;

Views vs Materialized Views — Decision Guide

Comparison Table
FeatureRegular ViewMaterialized View
Data storageNone — just a queryYes — physically stored on disk
Query speedDepends on underlying queryVery fast — simple table scan
Data freshnessAlways current (real-time)Stale until refreshed
Can be indexed?NoYes — like a regular table
MySQL supportYes (native)No — must simulate with summary tables
PostgreSQL supportYesYes (native MATERIALIZED VIEW)
Best forSecurity, abstraction, reuseDashboards, heavy aggregations, reports
MaintenanceNoneMust schedule REFRESH
  • Use a regular view when: you need always-fresh data, the underlying query is fast enough, or you want to restrict which columns users see.
  • Use a materialized view when: the query involves many JOINs or aggregations, the data is queried far more often than it changes (e.g., monthly sales reports), or query latency is causing problems.
🪟 Chapter 13

Window Functions

Window functions are the most powerful tool in SQL analytics. They let you compute values across a set of related rows — without collapsing the result set like GROUP BY does. Every row stays in the output, but gets a new computed column that "looks across" a window of rows.

The Problem GROUP BY Can't Solve

Imagine you want to show each employee's salary alongside their department's average salary in the same row. With GROUP BY, you'd lose individual rows — you'd only get one row per department. Window functions solve this: they compute the department average but attach it to every row, so you can compare individual and group values side-by-side. This is what makes them indispensable for cohort analysis, running totals, rankings, and time-series calculations.

  • PARTITION BY — divides rows into independent groups (like GROUP BY, but rows are kept). The function restarts for each partition.
  • ORDER BY — defines the sequence within each partition. Required for LAG, LEAD, and running calculations.
  • ROWS / RANGE BETWEEN — the frame clause narrows the window further (e.g., only the last 3 rows, or everything up to current row).
FUNCTION() OVER ( [PARTITION BY column] -- restart per group (optional) [ORDER BY column] -- ordering within group [ROWS BETWEEN start AND end] -- frame clause (optional) )

All Window Functions at a Glance

  • ROW_NUMBER() — sequential integer per row within partition. Always unique, even for ties.
  • RANK() — rank with gaps. Tied rows get the same rank, next rank skips (1,2,2,4).
  • DENSE_RANK() — rank without gaps. Tied rows get the same rank, next rank is consecutive (1,2,2,3).
  • NTILE(n) — divides rows into n equal buckets. Useful for quartiles, deciles, percentiles.
  • LAG(col, n) — value of col from n rows before the current row. NULL if no prior row exists.
  • LEAD(col, n) — value of col from n rows after the current row. NULL if no next row exists.
  • FIRST_VALUE(col) — value of col from the first row in the window frame.
  • LAST_VALUE(col) — value from the last row in the frame (watch out — default frame stops at current row).
  • SUM() OVER (ORDER BY...) — running total when ordered. Cumulative sum up to current row.
  • AVG() OVER (PARTITION BY...) — moving/group average without collapsing rows.

Ranking Functions — ROW_NUMBER vs RANK vs DENSE_RANK

All three assign a rank to each row within a partition ordered by a column. The difference is how they handle ties. Choose based on whether you want unique rankings (ROW_NUMBER), gap-producing rankings (RANK), or sequential rankings with no gaps (DENSE_RANK).

SQL
SELECT
  name,
  city,
  salary,
  ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC)             AS row_num,
  RANK()       OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC)             AS rank,
  DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC)             AS dense_rank,
  RANK()       OVER (PARTITION BY city ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rank_in_city
FROM employees;
Difference: RANK vs DENSE_RANK vs ROW_NUMBER
namesalaryROW_NUMBERRANKDENSE_RANK
Alice90,000111
Bob85,000222
Carol85,000322
David80,00044 (skips 3)3 (no skip)

LAG & LEAD — Compare to Previous/Next Row

LAG() looks back N rows; LEAD() looks forward N rows. They're essential for calculating growth rates, detecting gaps, identifying trends, and building month-over-month comparisons — all without a self-join. Both return NULL when there is no prior/next row (the first and last rows in a partition). You can provide a default value as the third argument: LAG(revenue, 1, 0).

SQL
-- Month-over-month sales comparison
SELECT
  month,
  revenue,
  LAG(revenue, 1) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS prev_month,
  revenue - LAG(revenue, 1) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS growth
FROM monthly_sales;

Running Total with SUM OVER

SQL
SELECT
  order_date,
  total,
  SUM(total) OVER (
    ORDER BY order_date
    ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
  ) AS running_total
FROM orders;
🔄 Chapter 14

CTEs — Common Table Expressions

A CTE (written with the WITH keyword) creates a named, temporary result set you can reference later in the same query. Think of it as a named subquery that lives at the top — making complex multi-step logic readable, testable, and maintainable.

Why CTEs Beat Nested Subqueries

You could write the same logic as a deeply nested subquery, but CTEs give you several advantages:

  • Readability — each step is named and defined at the top. You read top-to-bottom instead of inside-out.
  • Reusability — a CTE defined once can be referenced multiple times in the same query. A subquery would need to be repeated.
  • Debuggability — you can test each CTE independently by running just that SELECT block.
  • Recursive queries — WITH RECURSIVE is the only clean way to traverse hierarchical data (org charts, folder structures, bill of materials) in SQL.

Limitation: CTEs are not materialized by default in MySQL — each reference re-executes the query. For heavy CTEs referenced multiple times, a temporary table may perform better.

Basic CTE

SQL
-- Find the top 5 customers by lifetime value
WITH customer_lifetime AS (
  SELECT
    c.customer_id,
    c.name,
    SUM(o.total) AS total_spent
  FROM customers c
  JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
  GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.name
)
SELECT * FROM customer_lifetime
ORDER BY total_spent DESC
LIMIT 5;

Multiple CTEs

SQL
WITH
  top_customers AS (
    SELECT customer_id, SUM(total) AS ltv
    FROM orders
    GROUP BY customer_id
    HAVING SUM(total) > 5000
  ),
  city_stats AS (
    SELECT city, COUNT(*) AS city_count
    FROM customers
    GROUP BY city
  )
SELECT c.name, c.city, tc.ltv, cs.city_count
FROM customers c
JOIN top_customers tc ON c.customer_id = tc.customer_id
JOIN city_stats    cs ON c.city        = cs.city;

Recursive CTE — Hierarchy / Tree

SQL
-- Org chart: find all subordinates of an employee
WITH RECURSIVE org_hierarchy AS (
  -- Base case: start with the root employee
  SELECT emp_id, name, manager_id, 0 AS level
  FROM employees
  WHERE emp_id = 1

  UNION ALL

  -- Recursive case: join subordinates
  SELECT e.emp_id, e.name, e.manager_id, h.level + 1
  FROM employees e
  JOIN org_hierarchy h ON e.manager_id = h.emp_id
)
SELECT * FROM org_hierarchy
ORDER BY level;
💾 Chapter 15

Transactions & ACID

A transaction is a group of SQL operations treated as a single atomic unit — either ALL operations succeed and are committed, or ALL are rolled back as if nothing happened. Transactions protect your data from partial failures due to crashes, network errors, or application bugs.

Why Transactions Matter

Consider a bank transfer: you debit ₹5,000 from Account A and credit ₹5,000 to Account B. Without transactions, if the system crashes after the debit but before the credit, ₹5,000 simply disappears. A transaction ensures that both operations happen together — or neither happens at all.

⚛️

Atomicity

All operations in the transaction succeed, or all are rolled back. There is no "partial" commit — it's all or nothing. This is the core guarantee that prevents data corruption.

✅

Consistency

The database moves from one valid state to another. Every constraint (PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, CHECK) must remain satisfied before and after the transaction completes.

🔒

Isolation

Concurrent transactions don't see each other's in-progress changes. The degree of isolation is controlled by isolation levels: READ UNCOMMITTED, READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ, SERIALIZABLE.

💎

Durability

Once a transaction is committed, it permanently survives system crashes, power failures, and restarts. Achieved via write-ahead logging (WAL / redo log) in MySQL InnoDB.

SQL — Bank Transfer Example
-- Transfer ₹5000 from Account A to Account B
BEGIN TRANSACTION;

  UPDATE accounts
  SET balance = balance - 5000
  WHERE account_id = 'A001';

  UPDATE accounts
  SET balance = balance + 5000
  WHERE account_id = 'B001';

  -- If both succeeded:
COMMIT;

-- OR if something went wrong:
-- ROLLBACK;

-- SAVEPOINT: partial rollback
SAVEPOINT before_debit;
  -- some operations...
ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT before_debit;
⚙️ Chapter 16 — Deep Dive

Stored Procedures, Functions & Triggers

Stored procedures are named, reusable SQL programs stored inside the database itself. They encapsulate business logic, reduce network round-trips, improve security, and can contain full procedural logic — variables, loops, conditionals, and error handling.

What Is a Stored Procedure?

A stored procedure is a precompiled set of SQL statements saved under a name. Instead of sending 10 queries from your application, you send one CALL ProcedureName(). The database executes everything server-side. Benefits:

⚡

Performance

Precompiled and cached by the query optimizer. Executes faster than ad-hoc queries. Reduces network round-trips between app and DB.

🔒

Security

Grant users EXECUTE permission on a procedure without exposing the underlying tables. Prevents SQL injection via parameterization.

♻️

Reusability

Write once, call from any application — Java, Python, PHP, Power BI. Business logic lives in one place.

🧩

Modularity

Break complex operations into discrete, testable units. Procedures can call other procedures.

Procedure Parameters: IN, OUT, INOUT

SQL — Parameter Types
-- IN: caller passes value IN, procedure reads it (cannot modify)
DELIMITER $$
CREATE PROCEDURE GetCustomerSummary(IN p_customer_id INT)
BEGIN
  SELECT
    c.name,
    COUNT(o.id)   AS total_orders,
    SUM(o.total) AS total_spent,
    MAX(o.order_date) AS last_order
  FROM customers c
  LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id
  WHERE c.id = p_customer_id
  GROUP BY c.name;
END$$
DELIMITER ;
CALL GetCustomerSummary(42);

-- OUT: procedure writes a value OUT to caller
DELIMITER $$
CREATE PROCEDURE GetOrderTotal(
  IN  p_order_id INT,
  OUT p_total    DECIMAL(10,2),
  OUT p_items    INT
)
BEGIN
  SELECT
    SUM(unit_price * quantity),
    COUNT(*)
  INTO p_total, p_items
  FROM order_items
  WHERE order_id = p_order_id;
END$$
DELIMITER ;

CALL GetOrderTotal(101, @total, @items);
SELECT @total AS order_total, @items AS line_items;

-- INOUT: caller passes value, procedure can modify and return it
DELIMITER $$
CREATE PROCEDURE ApplyDiscount(INOUT p_price DECIMAL(10,2), IN p_pct INT)
BEGIN
  SET p_price = p_price * (1 - p_pct / 100.0);
END$$
DELIMITER ;

SET @price = 1000.00;
CALL ApplyDiscount(@price, 15);   -- apply 15% discount
SELECT @price;                       -- 850.00

Variables, Conditionals & Loops

SQL — Control Flow
DELIMITER $$
CREATE PROCEDURE ProcessMonthlyBonus(IN p_dept VARCHAR(50))
BEGIN
  -- Declare local variables
  DECLARE v_avg_salary  DECIMAL(10,2);
  DECLARE v_emp_count   INT;
  DECLARE v_bonus_rate  DECIMAL(4,2);

  -- Fetch stats into variables
  SELECT AVG(salary), COUNT(*)
  INTO   v_avg_salary, v_emp_count
  FROM   employees
  WHERE  department = p_dept;

  -- IF / ELSEIF / ELSE conditional
  IF v_avg_salary > 80000 THEN
    SET v_bonus_rate = 0.10;
  ELSEIF v_avg_salary > 50000 THEN
    SET v_bonus_rate = 0.07;
  ELSE
    SET v_bonus_rate = 0.05;
  END IF;

  -- Apply the bonus
  UPDATE employees
  SET    bonus = salary * v_bonus_rate
  WHERE  department = p_dept;

  -- Return a summary
  SELECT
    p_dept              AS department,
    v_emp_count         AS employees,
    v_avg_salary        AS avg_salary,
    v_bonus_rate * 100  AS bonus_pct;
END$$
DELIMITER ;

CALL ProcessMonthlyBonus('Engineering');
SQL — WHILE & REPEAT Loops
DELIMITER $$
CREATE PROCEDURE BatchInsertSampleData(IN p_rows INT)
BEGIN
  DECLARE v_counter INT DEFAULT 1;

  -- WHILE loop
  WHILE v_counter <= p_rows DO
    INSERT INTO test_data (value, created_at)
    VALUES (RAND() * 1000, NOW());
    SET v_counter = v_counter + 1;
  END WHILE;

  SELECT CONCAT('Inserted ', p_rows, ' rows') AS result;
END$$
DELIMITER ;

-- REPEAT ... UNTIL (do-while equivalent)
DELIMITER $$
CREATE PROCEDURE ArchiveOldOrders()
BEGIN
  DECLARE v_rows_deleted INT DEFAULT 1;

  REPEAT
    DELETE FROM orders
    WHERE  order_date < DATE_SUB(NOW(), INTERVAL 2 YEAR)
    LIMIT 500;                            -- batch delete: avoids lock
    SET v_rows_deleted = ROW_COUNT();
  UNTIL v_rows_deleted = 0              -- stop when nothing left to delete
  END REPEAT;
END$$
DELIMITER ;

Error Handling with DECLARE ... HANDLER

SQL — Error Handling
DELIMITER $$
CREATE PROCEDURE SafeTransfer(
  IN p_from_id  INT,
  IN p_to_id    INT,
  IN p_amount   DECIMAL(12,2)
)
BEGIN
  -- Declare error flag
  DECLARE v_error   BOOLEAN DEFAULT FALSE;
  DECLARE v_message VARCHAR(200);

  -- Handler fires on ANY SQL exception
  DECLARE CONTINUE HANDLER FOR SQLEXCEPTION
  BEGIN
    SET v_error   = TRUE;
    GET DIAGNOSTICS CONDITION 1
      v_message = MESSAGE_TEXT;
  END;

  START TRANSACTION;

    UPDATE accounts
    SET    balance = balance - p_amount
    WHERE  id = p_from_id;

    UPDATE accounts
    SET    balance = balance + p_amount
    WHERE  id = p_to_id;

    IF v_error THEN
      ROLLBACK;
      SELECT CONCAT('Transfer failed: ', v_message) AS status;
    ELSE
      COMMIT;
      SELECT 'Transfer successful' AS status;
    END IF;
END$$
DELIMITER ;

CALL SafeTransfer(1, 2, 500.00);

Stored Functions vs Stored Procedures

Key Differences
FeatureStored ProcedureStored Function
Called withCALL ProcName()SELECT FuncName() or inside SQL
Returns0 or more result sets via OUT paramsExactly ONE scalar value
Use in SELECT?NoYes — SELECT CalcTax(price)
TransactionsCan START / COMMIT / ROLLBACKCannot use transactions
DML inside?Yes (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE)Restricted (read-only by default)
Best forComplex operations, batch jobs, ETLCalculations reused inside queries
SQL — Stored Function Example
DELIMITER $$
CREATE FUNCTION CalculateTax(p_amount DECIMAL(10,2), p_rate DECIMAL(4,2))
RETURNS DECIMAL(10,2)
DETERMINISTIC
BEGIN
  RETURN ROUND(p_amount * p_rate / 100, 2);
END$$
DELIMITER ;

-- Use the function directly inside a SELECT
SELECT
  product_name,
  price,
  CalculateTax(price, 18)          AS gst,
  price + CalculateTax(price, 18) AS price_with_tax
FROM products;

-- Another function: get customer tier based on LTV
DELIMITER $$
CREATE FUNCTION GetCustomerTier(p_ltv DECIMAL(12,2))
RETURNS VARCHAR(20)
DETERMINISTIC
BEGIN
  DECLARE v_tier VARCHAR(20);
  IF     p_ltv >= 50000 THEN SET v_tier = 'Platinum';
  ELSEIF p_ltv >= 10000 THEN SET v_tier = 'Gold';
  ELSEIF p_ltv >=  1000 THEN SET v_tier = 'Silver';
  ELSE                       SET v_tier = 'Bronze';
  END IF;
  RETURN v_tier;
END$$
DELIMITER ;

SELECT
  name,
  SUM(total) AS ltv,
  GetCustomerTier(SUM(total)) AS tier
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id
GROUP BY c.id, c.name;

Cursors — Row-by-Row Processing

A cursor lets you iterate over a result set row by row inside a procedure — useful when each row needs custom processing that can't be expressed as a set-based operation.

SQL — Cursor Example
DELIMITER $$
CREATE PROCEDURE SendRenewalAlerts()
BEGIN
  -- Variables to hold each cursor row
  DECLARE v_done       BOOLEAN DEFAULT FALSE;
  DECLARE v_cust_id    INT;
  DECLARE v_cust_name  VARCHAR(100);
  DECLARE v_expires    DATE;

  -- Declare the cursor
  DECLARE cur_expiring CURSOR FOR
    SELECT c.id, c.name, s.expires_at
    FROM customers c
    JOIN subscriptions s ON c.id = s.customer_id
    WHERE s.expires_at BETWEEN CURDATE()
      AND DATE_ADD(CURDATE(), INTERVAL 7 DAY);

  -- Handler: sets v_done = TRUE when no more rows
  DECLARE CONTINUE HANDLER FOR NOT FOUND
    SET v_done = TRUE;

  OPEN cur_expiring;

  read_loop: LOOP
    FETCH cur_expiring INTO v_cust_id, v_cust_name, v_expires;
    IF v_done THEN LEAVE read_loop; END IF;

    -- Insert an alert record for each expiring customer
    INSERT INTO alerts (customer_id, type, message, created_at)
    VALUES (
      v_cust_id,
      'renewal',
      CONCAT('Hi ', v_cust_name, ', your plan expires on ', v_expires),
      NOW()
    );
  END LOOP;

  CLOSE cur_expiring;
  SELECT ROW_COUNT() AS alerts_created;
END$$
DELIMITER ;

Cursors process one row at a time — they are significantly slower than set-based SQL for large datasets. Use them only when row-by-row processing is truly unavoidable. For most operations, a single UPDATE or INSERT...SELECT is orders of magnitude faster.

Triggers — Deep Dive

A trigger is a stored program that automatically fires in response to a DML event on a table. Triggers are invisible to the application — they run transparently inside the database.

Trigger Timing Matrix
TimingEventAccessUse Case
BEFORE INSERTINSERTNEW.*Validate/transform data before writing
AFTER INSERTINSERTNEW.*Audit log, update summary tables
BEFORE UPDATEUPDATEOLD.*, NEW.*Validate changes, compute derived values
AFTER UPDATEUPDATEOLD.*, NEW.*Audit log, propagate changes
BEFORE DELETEDELETEOLD.*Archive before deleting
AFTER DELETEDELETEOLD.*Cascade cleanup, audit log
SQL — 4 Real Trigger Examples
-- TRIGGER 1: Auto-reduce stock after order placed
CREATE TRIGGER trg_reduce_stock
AFTER INSERT ON order_items
FOR EACH ROW
BEGIN
  UPDATE products
  SET    stock_qty = stock_qty - NEW.quantity
  WHERE  id = NEW.product_id;
END;

-- TRIGGER 2: Audit log for salary changes
CREATE TRIGGER trg_salary_audit
AFTER UPDATE ON employees
FOR EACH ROW
BEGIN
  IF OLD.salary <> NEW.salary THEN
    INSERT INTO salary_audit
      (employee_id, old_salary, new_salary, change_pct, changed_at, changed_by)
    VALUES (
      NEW.id,
      OLD.salary,
      NEW.salary,
      ROUND((NEW.salary - OLD.salary) / OLD.salary * 100, 2),
      NOW(),
      USER()
    );
  END IF;
END;

-- TRIGGER 3: BEFORE INSERT — auto-set slug and validate email
CREATE TRIGGER trg_before_user_insert
BEFORE INSERT ON users
FOR EACH ROW
BEGIN
  -- Normalise email to lowercase
  SET NEW.email      = LOWER(TRIM(NEW.email));
  -- Auto-build username slug from name
  SET NEW.username   = LOWER(REPLACE(TRIM(NEW.name), ' ', '_'));
  -- Set created_at if not provided
  IF NEW.created_at IS NULL THEN
    SET NEW.created_at = NOW();
  END IF;
END;

-- TRIGGER 4: Archive row before deletion
CREATE TRIGGER trg_archive_before_delete
BEFORE DELETE ON orders
FOR EACH ROW
BEGIN
  INSERT INTO orders_archive
  SELECT OLD.*, NOW() AS archived_at, USER() AS archived_by;
END;

Managing Stored Objects

SQL — Administration Commands
-- List all stored procedures in current DB
SHOW PROCEDURE STATUS WHERE Db = DATABASE();

-- View the definition of a procedure
SHOW CREATE PROCEDURE GetCustomerSummary;

-- Drop procedures and functions
DROP PROCEDURE IF EXISTS GetCustomerSummary;
DROP FUNCTION  IF EXISTS CalculateTax;

-- List all triggers on a table
SHOW TRIGGERS WHERE `Table` = 'employees';

-- Drop a trigger
DROP TRIGGER IF EXISTS trg_salary_audit;

-- Disable / Enable trigger (MySQL 8.0.26+)
ALTER TABLE employees DISABLE TRIGGER trg_salary_audit;
ALTER TABLE employees ENABLE  TRIGGER trg_salary_audit;

Stored Procedure — Real-World ETL Example

One of the most powerful uses of stored procedures is automating ETL (Extract, Transform, Load) pipelines entirely inside the database. Here's a production-style example that loads daily sales data into a data mart:

SQL — Daily Sales ETL Procedure
DELIMITER $$
CREATE PROCEDURE LoadDailySales(IN p_load_date DATE)
BEGIN
  DECLARE v_rows_loaded  INT DEFAULT 0;
  DECLARE v_rows_skipped INT DEFAULT 0;
  DECLARE v_error_msg    VARCHAR(500);
  DECLARE EXIT HANDLER FOR SQLEXCEPTION
  BEGIN
    GET DIAGNOSTICS CONDITION 1
      v_error_msg = MESSAGE_TEXT;
    ROLLBACK;
    INSERT INTO etl_log (procedure_name, load_date, status, message, logged_at)
    VALUES ('LoadDailySales', p_load_date, 'FAILED', v_error_msg, NOW());
  END;

  START TRANSACTION;

  -- Delete existing data for this date (idempotent reload)
  DELETE FROM fact_daily_sales
  WHERE  sale_date = p_load_date;

  -- Load aggregated sales from staging area
  INSERT INTO fact_daily_sales
    (sale_date, customer_id, product_id, quantity, revenue, cost, profit)
  SELECT
    DATE(s.created_at)             AS sale_date,
    s.customer_id,
    si.product_id,
    SUM(si.quantity)               AS quantity,
    SUM(si.quantity * si.unit_price) AS revenue,
    SUM(si.quantity * p.cost_price)  AS cost,
    SUM(si.quantity * (si.unit_price - p.cost_price)) AS profit
  FROM stg_orders       s
  JOIN stg_order_items  si ON s.id         = si.order_id
  JOIN products         p  ON si.product_id = p.id
  WHERE DATE(s.created_at) = p_load_date
  GROUP BY 1, 2, 3;

  SET v_rows_loaded = ROW_COUNT();

  COMMIT;

  -- Log success
  INSERT INTO etl_log (procedure_name, load_date, status, rows_loaded, logged_at)
  VALUES ('LoadDailySales', p_load_date, 'SUCCESS', v_rows_loaded, NOW());

  SELECT
    p_load_date     AS loaded_date,
    v_rows_loaded   AS rows_loaded,
    'SUCCESS'       AS status;
END$$
DELIMITER ;

-- Call it for yesterday's data
CALL LoadDailySales(DATE_SUB(CURDATE(), INTERVAL 1 DAY));

Stored Procedure — Pagination Helper

A common utility procedure that handles server-side pagination — used to power "load more" and page navigation features:

SQL — Pagination Procedure
DELIMITER $$
CREATE PROCEDURE GetProductsPaged(
  IN  p_category    VARCHAR(50),
  IN  p_page        INT,       -- 1-based page number
  IN  p_page_size   INT,       -- rows per page
  IN  p_sort_col    VARCHAR(30),-- sort column
  IN  p_sort_dir    VARCHAR(4), -- 'ASC' or 'DESC'
  OUT p_total_rows  INT
)
BEGIN
  DECLARE v_offset INT;
  DECLARE v_sql    TEXT;

  SET v_offset = (p_page - 1) * p_page_size;

  -- Get total count for pagination controls
  SELECT COUNT(*) INTO p_total_rows
  FROM products
  WHERE (p_category IS NULL OR category = p_category);

  -- Dynamic SQL for flexible sort column
  SET v_sql = CONCAT(
    'SELECT id, name, price, category FROM products ',
    'WHERE (? IS NULL OR category = ?) ',
    'ORDER BY ', p_sort_col, ' ', p_sort_dir, ' ',
    'LIMIT ? OFFSET ?'
  );

  PREPARE stmt FROM v_sql;
  EXECUTE stmt USING p_category, p_category, p_page_size, v_offset;
  DEALLOCATE PREPARE stmt;
END$$
DELIMITER ;

-- Page 2 of Electronics, 10 items per page, sorted by price DESC
CALL GetProductsPaged('Electronics', 2, 10, 'price', 'DESC', @total);
SELECT @total AS total_products;
