Control Flow — IF, CASE, LOOP, WHILE, REPEAT

Stored procedures support full procedural logic, letting you write programs that make decisions, iterate, and handle complex workflows entirely within the database.

SQL — IF / ELSEIF / ELSE
DELIMITER $$
CREATE PROCEDURE CategorizeCustomer(IN p_customer_id INT)
BEGIN
  DECLARE v_total_spent DECIMAL(12,2);
  DECLARE v_tier        VARCHAR(20);

  -- Fetch customer lifetime spend
  SELECT COALESCE(SUM(total), 0)
  INTO   v_total_spent
  FROM   orders
  WHERE  customer_id = p_customer_id;

  -- Conditional branching
  IF v_total_spent >= 50000 THEN
    SET v_tier = 'Platinum';
  ELSEIF v_total_spent >= 10000 THEN
    SET v_tier = 'Gold';
  ELSEIF v_total_spent >= 1000 THEN
    SET v_tier = 'Silver';
  ELSE
    SET v_tier = 'Bronze';
  END IF;

  -- Update the customer record
  UPDATE customers
  SET    tier        = v_tier,
         updated_at  = NOW()
  WHERE  id          = p_customer_id;

  -- Return the result
  SELECT p_customer_id AS customer_id,
         v_total_spent AS total_spent,
         v_tier        AS assigned_tier;
END$$
DELIMITER ;

CALL CategorizeCustomer(42);
SQL — CASE Statement in Procedure
DELIMITER $$
CREATE PROCEDURE ApplyDiscount(
  IN  p_order_id      INT,
  IN  p_promo_code    VARCHAR(20),
  OUT p_discount_pct  DECIMAL(5,2)
)
BEGIN
  -- CASE statement (matches first true condition)
  CASE p_promo_code
    WHEN 'WELCOME10'  THEN SET p_discount_pct = 10.00;
    WHEN 'SAVE20'     THEN SET p_discount_pct = 20.00;
    WHEN 'FLASH50'    THEN SET p_discount_pct = 50.00;
    ELSE                   SET p_discount_pct = 0.00;
  END CASE;

  -- Apply the discount to the order
  UPDATE orders
  SET   discount_pct   = p_discount_pct,
        total_after_disc = subtotal * ((100 - p_discount_pct) / 100)
  WHERE id            = p_order_id;
END$$
DELIMITER ;

CALL ApplyDiscount(1001, 'SAVE20', @disc);
SELECT @disc;  -- 20.00
SQL — WHILE Loop (Batch Processing)
DELIMITER $$
CREATE PROCEDURE BatchDeleteOldLogs(IN p_batch_size INT)
BEGIN
  DECLARE v_deleted  INT DEFAULT 1;
  DECLARE v_total    INT DEFAULT 0;

  -- Keep deleting in batches until no rows remain
  WHILE v_deleted > 0 DO
    DELETE FROM activity_logs
    WHERE  created_at < DATE_SUB(NOW(), INTERVAL 90 DAY)
    LIMIT  p_batch_size;

    SET v_deleted = ROW_COUNT();
    SET v_total   = v_total + v_deleted;

    -- Small sleep between batches to reduce lock pressure
    DO SLEEP(0.05);
  END WHILE;

  SELECT v_total AS total_rows_deleted;
END$$
DELIMITER ;

CALL BatchDeleteOldLogs(1000);

Deleting millions of rows at once acquires a massive table lock that blocks all reads and writes. Batch deletes (1,000 rows at a time with small sleeps) reduce lock duration, keep the system responsive, and give the InnoDB undo log time to breathe.

A cursor lets you iterate through a result set one row at a time, applying logic to each. Cursors are slower than set-based operations but necessary when each row requires unique, stateful processing.

SQL — Cursor to Process Each Employee
DELIMITER $$
CREATE PROCEDURE ProcessAnnualBonuses()
BEGIN
  DECLARE v_done      INT     DEFAULT FALSE;
  DECLARE v_emp_id    INT;
  DECLARE v_salary    DECIMAL(10,2);
  DECLARE v_rating    VARCHAR(10);
  DECLARE v_bonus     DECIMAL(10,2);

  -- 1. Declare cursor
  DECLARE emp_cursor CURSOR FOR
    SELECT id, salary, performance_rating
    FROM   employees
    WHERE  is_active = TRUE;

  -- 2. Handler: set v_done=TRUE when no more rows
  DECLARE CONTINUE HANDLER FOR NOT FOUND SET v_done = TRUE;

  -- 3. Open cursor
  OPEN emp_cursor;

  -- 4. Loop through rows
  bonus_loop: LOOP
    FETCH emp_cursor INTO v_emp_id, v_salary, v_rating;
    IF v_done THEN
      LEAVE bonus_loop;
    END IF;

    -- Per-employee bonus logic
    SET v_bonus = CASE v_rating
      WHEN 'Exceeds'  THEN v_salary * 0.15
      WHEN 'Meets'    THEN v_salary * 0.08
      WHEN 'Below'    THEN 0
      ELSE                v_salary * 0.05
    END;

    INSERT INTO bonus_payments (employee_id, amount, paid_date)
    VALUES (v_emp_id, v_bonus, CURDATE());
  END LOOP;

  -- 5. Close cursor
  CLOSE emp_cursor;
  SELECT ROW_COUNT() AS bonuses_issued;
END$$
DELIMITER ;

Without error handling, a failed statement inside a procedure rolls back only that statement and continues. Using DECLARE HANDLER you can catch exceptions, roll back entire transactions, and return meaningful error messages.

SQL — Error Handling in Stored Procedures
DELIMITER $$
CREATE PROCEDURE TransferFunds(
  IN  p_from_account  INT,
  IN  p_to_account    INT,
  IN  p_amount        DECIMAL(12,2),
  OUT p_status        VARCHAR(100)
)
BEGIN
  DECLARE v_balance  DECIMAL(12,2);
  DECLARE v_error    TINYINT DEFAULT FALSE;

  -- Catch any SQL exception → set flag + roll back
  DECLARE CONTINUE HANDLER FOR SQLEXCEPTION
  BEGIN
    SET v_error = TRUE;
    ROLLBACK;
    SET p_status = 'ERROR: Transaction rolled back';
  END;

  START TRANSACTION;

    -- Check sufficient balance
    SELECT balance INTO v_balance
    FROM   accounts
    WHERE  id = p_from_account
    FOR UPDATE;  -- lock row during transaction

    IF v_balance < p_amount THEN
      SET p_status = 'ERROR: Insufficient funds';
      SET v_error  = TRUE;
      ROLLBACK;
    ELSE
      UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - p_amount WHERE id = p_from_account;
      UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + p_amount WHERE id = p_to_account;
      INSERT INTO transfer_log (from_id, to_id, amount, txn_time)
      VALUES (p_from_account, p_to_account, p_amount, NOW());
    END IF;

  IF NOT v_error THEN
    COMMIT;
    SET p_status = CONCAT('SUCCESS: Transferred ', p_amount);
  END IF;
END$$
DELIMITER ;

CALL TransferFunds(101, 202, 500.00, @status);
SELECT @status;

Stored Functions vs Stored Procedures

Procedure vs Function — Key Differences
FeatureStored ProcedureStored Function
Called withCALL ProcName()SELECT FuncName() or inside SQL
Returns0 or more result sets, OUT paramsExactly ONE scalar value
Can DML (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE)?YesNot recommended (can cause issues)
Can use in SELECT clause?NoYes — like a built-in function
Transaction control (COMMIT/ROLLBACK)?YesNo
Best forBusiness workflows, batch jobs, ETLCalculations reused in queries
SQL — Stored Function Example
DELIMITER $$
CREATE FUNCTION GetCustomerTier(p_customer_id INT)
RETURNS VARCHAR(20)
DETERMINISTIC READS SQL DATA
BEGIN
  DECLARE v_spend DECIMAL(12,2);

  SELECT COALESCE(SUM(total), 0)
  INTO   v_spend
  FROM   orders
  WHERE  customer_id = p_customer_id;

  RETURN CASE
    WHEN v_spend >= 50000 THEN 'Platinum'
    WHEN v_spend >= 10000 THEN 'Gold'
    WHEN v_spend >= 1000  THEN 'Silver'
    ELSE                        'Bronze'
  END;
END$$
DELIMITER ;

-- USE IT inside any SELECT — like a built-in function
SELECT
  name,
  email,
  GetCustomerTier(id) AS tier
FROM customers
ORDER BY GetCustomerTier(id);

Real-World Procedure: Monthly Report Generator

This procedure ties together multiple concepts: variables, conditionals, CTEs, and multiple result sets — a pattern common in production reporting systems.

SQL — Monthly Sales Report Procedure
DELIMITER $$
CREATE PROCEDURE GenerateMonthlySalesReport(
  IN  p_year      INT,
  IN  p_month     INT,
  OUT p_total_rev DECIMAL(15,2)
)
BEGIN
  DECLARE v_start_date DATE;
  DECLARE v_end_date   DATE;
  DECLARE v_prev_rev   DECIMAL(15,2);

  -- Calculate date range
  SET v_start_date = DATE(CONCAT(p_year, '-', p_month, '-01'));
  SET v_end_date   = LAST_DAY(v_start_date);

  -- Result Set 1: Summary KPIs
  SELECT
    COUNT(DISTINCT id)          AS total_orders,
    COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) AS unique_customers,
    SUM(total)                   AS gross_revenue,
    AVG(total)                   AS avg_order_value,
    MAX(total)                   AS largest_order
  INTO @o, @c, p_total_rev, @aov, @max
  FROM  orders
  WHERE order_date BETWEEN v_start_date AND v_end_date;

  SELECT @o AS orders, @c AS customers,
         p_total_rev AS revenue, @aov AS avg_order;

  -- Result Set 2: Top 5 products this month
  SELECT
    p.product_name,
    SUM(oi.quantity)   AS units_sold,
    SUM(oi.unit_price * oi.quantity) AS revenue
  FROM  order_items  oi
  JOIN  orders       o  ON oi.order_id   = o.id
  JOIN  products     p  ON oi.product_id = p.id
  WHERE o.order_date BETWEEN v_start_date AND v_end_date
  GROUP BY p.product_name
  ORDER BY revenue DESC
  LIMIT 5;

  -- Result Set 3: MoM growth vs last month
  SELECT COALESCE(SUM(total),0)
  INTO   v_prev_rev
  FROM   orders
  WHERE  order_date BETWEEN
         DATE_SUB(v_start_date, INTERVAL 1 MONTH)
     AND DATE_SUB(v_end_date, INTERVAL 1 MONTH);

  SELECT
    v_prev_rev                                     AS last_month_rev,
    p_total_rev                                    AS this_month_rev,
    ROUND((p_total_rev - v_prev_rev) * 100.0
           / NULLIF(v_prev_rev,0), 1)            AS mom_growth_pct;
END$$
DELIMITER ;

CALL GenerateMonthlySalesReport(2024, 11, @rev);
SELECT @rev AS nov_2024_revenue;

Triggers — Deep Dive

Triggers fire automatically in response to data changes. They are invisible to the application — no code change needed to activate them. Use them for audit logging, enforcing business rules, auto-calculating columns, and cascading changes.

SQL — Trigger Types and Examples
-- BEFORE INSERT: validate or modify data before it's saved
CREATE TRIGGER trg_before_order_insert
BEFORE INSERT ON orders
FOR EACH ROW
BEGIN
  -- Auto-set created_at if not provided
  IF NEW.created_at IS NULL THEN
    SET NEW.created_at = NOW();
  END IF;
  -- Enforce minimum order value
  IF NEW.total < 1 THEN
    SIGNAL SQLSTATE '45000'
      SET MESSAGE_TEXT = 'Order total must be at least 1';
  END IF;
END;

-- AFTER INSERT: update stock when an order item is added
CREATE TRIGGER trg_after_order_item_insert
AFTER INSERT ON order_items
FOR EACH ROW
BEGIN
  UPDATE products
  SET   stock_qty = stock_qty - NEW.quantity
  WHERE id        = NEW.product_id;
END;

-- AFTER UPDATE: full salary change audit log
CREATE TRIGGER trg_salary_audit
AFTER UPDATE ON employees
FOR EACH ROW
BEGIN
  IF OLD.salary <> NEW.salary THEN
    INSERT INTO salary_audit (
      employee_id, old_salary, new_salary,
      pct_change,  changed_at,  changed_by
    ) VALUES (
      NEW.id,
      OLD.salary,
      NEW.salary,
      ROUND((NEW.salary-OLD.salary)*100.0/OLD.salary,2),
      NOW(),
      USER()
    );
  END IF;
END;

-- BEFORE DELETE: soft-delete pattern (archive instead of delete)
CREATE TRIGGER trg_soft_delete_customer
BEFORE DELETE ON customers
FOR EACH ROW
BEGIN
  INSERT INTO customers_deleted
  SELECT *, NOW(), USER() FROM customers
  WHERE id = OLD.id;
END;

-- View all triggers in the database
SHOW TRIGGERS LIKE 'orders';
SELECT TRIGGER_NAME, EVENT_MANIPULATION, ACTION_TIMING
FROM   INFORMATION_SCHEMA.TRIGGERS
WHERE  TRIGGER_SCHEMA = DATABASE();

-- Drop a trigger
DROP TRIGGER IF EXISTS trg_salary_audit;
📦 New — Data Warehousing

Slowly Changing Dimensions (SCD)

In data warehouses, dimension tables (customers, products, employees) change slowly over time — a customer moves cities, a product gets re-priced, an employee switches departments. Slowly Changing Dimensions are the patterns used to track, store, and query these historical changes.

Why SCDs Matter

📜

Historical Accuracy

When a customer order was placed, they lived in Mumbai. Even if they later moved to Delhi, reports for that order should still show Mumbai.

📊

Accurate Analytics

Sales by region should reflect the region at the time of sale — not the customer's current region. Wrong SCD handling = wrong numbers.

🔍

Audit & Compliance

Who was the account manager when a contract was signed? What was the product price at purchase time? SCDs answer these questions.

SCDs apply to dimension tables in a star/snowflake schema. The fact table stores measurements (sales, events); dimension tables provide context (who, what, where, when). When dimension attributes change, you must decide: overwrite? track history? add a new row?

SCD Type 0 — Fixed / Ignore Changes

Once a dimension attribute is written, it never changes. Any updates to the source are simply ignored. Use when data should remain fixed for historical accuracy — like a customer's original sign-up date, date of birth, or original lead source.

SCD Type 0 — Example
-- dim_customer: original_signup_source is SCD Type 0
-- Even if customer was re-acquired via a different channel, we keep the original
CREATE TABLE dim_customer (
  customer_id           INT PRIMARY KEY,
  name                  VARCHAR(100),
  original_signup_source VARCHAR(50),  -- Type 0: never updated
  signup_date           DATE          -- Type 0: never updated
);

-- ETL logic: ignore updates to Type 0 columns
UPDATE dim_customer
SET   name = 'Alice Johnson'           -- only update non-Type-0 columns
-- original_signup_source is intentionally NOT updated here
WHERE customer_id = 42;

SCD Type 1 — Overwrite (No History)

When an attribute changes, simply overwrite the old value with the new one. No history is kept. Use when the old value was an error or when historical accuracy for that attribute doesn't matter (e.g., a corrected spelling of a name, updated phone number).

Before & After — Customer Changes City
Statecustomer_idnamecity
BEFORE42AliceMumbai
AFTER (Type 1)42AliceDelhi ← overwritten
SCD Type 1 — Overwrite Pattern
-- Type 1: simple UPDATE overwrites the old value
UPDATE dim_customer
SET
  city        = 'Delhi',
  updated_at  = NOW()
WHERE customer_id = 42;

-- ETL MERGE / UPSERT pattern (common in warehouse loads)
INSERT INTO dim_customer (customer_id, name, city, updated_at)
VALUES (42, 'Alice', 'Delhi', NOW())
ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE
  name       = VALUES(name),
  city       = VALUES(city),
  updated_at = NOW();

-- ⚠ Historical reports now reflect NEW city for ALL orders
-- even orders placed when customer lived in Mumbai

Pros: Simple to implement, small table size. Cons: You permanently lose history. Any report querying historical data will now show the updated attribute — orders placed when Alice was in Mumbai will now appear as Delhi orders.

SCD Type 2 — Add New Row (Full History) ⭐ Most Important

When an attribute changes, insert a new row with the new values and mark the old row as expired. The table keeps the complete history. You can now query the state of a dimension at any point in time. This is the most widely used SCD type in production data warehouses.

Type 2 — Full History Preserved
surrogate_keycustomer_idnamecityis_currenteff_starteff_end
100142AliceMumbai02022-01-012024-03-15
100242AliceDelhi12024-03-169999-12-31
SCD Type 2 — Table Design
-- Type 2 dimension table design
CREATE TABLE dim_customer (
  surrogate_key  INT          AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,  -- synthetic PK
  customer_id    INT          NOT NULL,                    -- natural/business key
  name           VARCHAR(100),
  city           VARCHAR(100),
  country        VARCHAR(50),
  is_current     TINYINT      DEFAULT 1,                    -- 1=active, 0=expired
  eff_start_date DATE         NOT NULL,                    -- when this row became valid
  eff_end_date   DATE         DEFAULT '9999-12-31'          -- 9999 means "currently active"
);
SCD Type 2 — ETL Update Procedure
-- Step 1: Expire the current active row
UPDATE dim_customer
SET
  is_current   = 0,
  eff_end_date = DATE_SUB(CURDATE(), INTERVAL 1 DAY)
WHERE customer_id = 42
  AND   is_current  = 1;

-- Step 2: Insert new row with updated attributes
INSERT INTO dim_customer
  (customer_id, name, city, country, is_current, eff_start_date, eff_end_date)
VALUES
  (42, 'Alice', 'Delhi', 'India', 1, CURDATE(), '9999-12-31');

-- Query: current state of all customers
SELECT * FROM dim_customer
WHERE is_current = 1;

-- Query: what city was customer 42 in on 2023-06-01?
SELECT city, country
FROM dim_customer
WHERE customer_id = 42
  AND '2023-06-01' BETWEEN eff_start_date AND eff_end_date;

-- Join fact table with Type 2 dimension (point-in-time accuracy)
SELECT
  f.order_date,
  f.amount,
  d.city    AS city_at_time_of_sale,
  d.country AS country_at_sale
FROM fact_sales f
JOIN dim_customer d
  ON  f.customer_id  = d.customer_id
  AND f.order_date   BETWEEN d.eff_start_date
                           AND d.eff_end_date;

SCD Type 3 — Add Column (Limited History)

Instead of a new row, add a new column to store the previous value. The table keeps the current and one prior value. Simple to query, but limited — you can only track one level of history, and you need a schema change for every new tracked attribute.

Type 3 Table Design — current + previous city
customer_idnamecurrent_cityprevious_citycity_changed_at
42AliceDelhiMumbai2024-03-16
43BobChennaiNULLNULL
SCD Type 3 — Table & Update
-- Table design: current + previous value
CREATE TABLE dim_customer (
  customer_id    INT PRIMARY KEY,
  name           VARCHAR(100),
  current_city   VARCHAR(100),
  previous_city  VARCHAR(100),     -- one step of history
  city_changed_at DATE
);

-- Update: shift current → previous, then set new current
UPDATE dim_customer
SET
  previous_city  = current_city,   -- move current to previous
  current_city   = 'Delhi',          -- set new current
  city_changed_at= CURDATE()
WHERE customer_id = 42;

-- Query: compare current vs previous region performance
SELECT
  d.name,
  d.current_city,
  d.previous_city,
  SUM(f.amount) AS total_sales
FROM fact_sales f
JOIN dim_customer d ON f.customer_id = d.customer_id
GROUP BY d.name, d.current_city, d.previous_city;

If Alice moves a third time (Delhi → Bangalore), you lose the Mumbai record entirely. Type 3 can only track one change. For more depth, you'd need to add more columns (city_2, city_3...) which gets messy fast. Use Type 3 only when exactly one historical value is sufficient.

SCD Type 4 — History Table (Mini-Dimension)

Keep a "current" dimension table for fast lookups, and a separate history table that records every change as a new row with timestamps. The main table stays lean; the history table provides the full audit trail. Useful when history is needed but the main dimension table must stay simple.

SCD Type 4 — Two-Table Pattern
-- Main table: always has current state only
CREATE TABLE dim_customer (
  customer_id  INT PRIMARY KEY,
  name         VARCHAR(100),
  city         VARCHAR(100),
  updated_at   DATETIME
);

-- History table: append-only log of every change
CREATE TABLE dim_customer_history (
  history_id   INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id  INT,
  name         VARCHAR(100),
  city         VARCHAR(100),
  valid_from   DATETIME,
  valid_to     DATETIME
);

-- Trigger to auto-archive before update
CREATE TRIGGER trg_archive_customer
BEFORE UPDATE ON dim_customer
FOR EACH ROW
BEGIN
  INSERT INTO dim_customer_history
    (customer_id, name, city, valid_from, valid_to)
  VALUES
    (OLD.customer_id, OLD.name, OLD.city, OLD.updated_at, NOW());
END;

-- Now update the main table — trigger auto-logs old record
UPDATE dim_customer
SET city = 'Delhi', updated_at = NOW()
WHERE customer_id = 42;

-- Query full history from history table
SELECT * FROM dim_customer_history
WHERE customer_id = 42
ORDER BY valid_from;

SCD Type 6 — Hybrid (Type 1 + 2 + 3 Combined)

Type 6 (named as 1+2+3=6) combines all three approaches in a single row: it adds new rows like Type 2 (full history), keeps the current value as a separate column like Type 3, and updates all rows with the current value like Type 1. This allows both point-in-time queries AND easy "current state" filtering without needing a join.

SCD Type 6 — All History Rows Also Know the Current Value
skcust_idcity (historical)current_cityis_currenteff_starteff_end
100142MumbaiDelhi02022-01-012024-03-15
100242DelhiDelhi12024-03-169999-12-31
SCD Type 6 — Table & ETL
CREATE TABLE dim_customer (
  surrogate_key  INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id    INT NOT NULL,
  name           VARCHAR(100),
  city           VARCHAR(100),      -- Type 2: historical value at this row
  current_city   VARCHAR(100),      -- Type 1/3: always reflects current city
  is_current     TINYINT DEFAULT 1, -- Type 2: current row flag
  eff_start_date DATE NOT NULL,
  eff_end_date   DATE DEFAULT '9999-12-31'
);

-- ETL: customer 42 moves from Mumbai to Delhi

-- Step 1: Expire old row (Type 2)
UPDATE dim_customer
SET   is_current   = 0,
      eff_end_date = DATE_SUB(CURDATE(), INTERVAL 1 DAY),
      current_city = 'Delhi'  -- also update current_city on OLD row (Type 1)
WHERE customer_id = 42 AND is_current = 1;

-- Step 2: Insert new current row
INSERT INTO dim_customer
  (customer_id, name, city, current_city, is_current, eff_start_date)
VALUES
  (42, 'Alice', 'Delhi', 'Delhi', 1, CURDATE());

-- Query: sales by historical city (Type 2 accuracy)
SELECT d.city AS city_at_sale, SUM(f.amount)
FROM fact_sales f
JOIN dim_customer d
  ON f.customer_id = d.customer_id
  AND f.order_date BETWEEN d.eff_start_date AND d.eff_end_date
GROUP BY d.city;

-- Query: current city for all customers — no date join needed!
SELECT DISTINCT customer_id, name, current_city
FROM dim_customer;

SCD Type Comparison — Quick Reference

All SCD Types at a Glance
TypeMechanismHistory?Table SizeComplexityBest For
Type 0Never updateNoneSmallNoneFixed attributes (DOB, signup source)
Type 1OverwriteNoneSmallVery LowError corrections, non-critical changes
Type 2 ⭐New row + flagsFullGrows with changesMediumAny attribute needing point-in-time accuracy
Type 3Add prev_colOne stepSmallLowWhen only 1 prior value matters
Type 4Separate history tableFullTwo tablesMediumHigh-churn dimensions needing clean main table
Type 6Type 1+2+3 combinedFull + currentGrows with changesHighWhen you need history AND easy current-state queries
🚀 Chapter 17

Query Optimization

Writing correct SQL is one thing. Writing fast SQL that scales to millions of rows is another. Query optimization is about understanding how the database engine executes your query — and removing the bottlenecks before they become production incidents.

The MySQL Query Optimizer

When you run a query, MySQL doesn't execute it literally. The optimizer first analyzes multiple possible execution plans, estimates the cost of each (based on statistics like row counts and index cardinality), and picks the cheapest one. You can inspect its chosen plan with EXPLAIN. Key things the optimizer decides:

  • Which index to use — or whether to do a full table scan (type=ALL in EXPLAIN is a red flag)
  • Join order — which table to scan first and which to use as the "probe" table
  • Whether to use a temporary table or filesort — both appear in the Extra column of EXPLAIN and are expensive

Run ANALYZE TABLE tablename after large data loads to refresh the optimizer's statistics so it makes better decisions.

EXPLAIN — Read Your Query's Execution Plan

The single most important optimization tool. EXPLAIN shows you how MySQL executes a query without actually running it. Look for: type=ALL (full table scan — usually bad), high rows estimates, and Using filesort or Using temporary in the Extra column.

SQL
-- See the execution plan
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 42;

-- Detailed analysis (MySQL 8+)
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 42;

Best Practices — The Optimization Checklist

Most slow queries share the same root causes. Here are the most common performance killers and their fixes:

Optimization Checklist
❌ Slow (Avoid)✅ Fast (Do This)Why
SELECT *SELECT only needed columnsReduces data transferred; enables covering indexes
WHERE YEAR(date) = 2024WHERE date BETWEEN '2024-01-01' AND '2024-12-31'Function on column breaks index usage
WHERE email LIKE '%gmail%'WHERE email LIKE 'gmail%'Leading wildcard forces full scan; prefix search uses index
Correlated subquery per rowUse JOINs or CTEs insteadSubquery runs N times; JOIN is a single pass
No indexes on JOIN columnsIndex all FK and WHERE columnsUnindexed JOINs cause full scans on every join
SELECT DISTINCT as a workaroundFix the JOIN producing duplicatesDISTINCT adds a sort step; fixing the root cause is always better
NOT IN with possible NULLsUse NOT EXISTS insteadNOT IN with NULLs returns empty set — a silent bug
OR on indexed columnUse UNION insteadOR can prevent index use; UNION allows one index scan per branch

Five Immediate Improvements for Any Slow Query

  1. Run EXPLAIN and check for type=ALL — add an index on the WHERE/JOIN column to fix it.
  2. Replace SELECT * with only the columns you actually need.
  3. Add LIMIT if you're exploring data — don't scan 10 million rows when you only need 100.
  4. Move expensive subqueries into a CTE and check if the optimizer can cache them.
  5. Run ANALYZE TABLE tablename — stale statistics cause the optimizer to pick bad plans.

5 Real-World SQL Projects

PROJECT 01

🛒 E-Commerce Analytics Dashboard

Build a complete analytics layer for an online store — top products, customer LTV, monthly trends.

SELECTJOINsGROUP BYAggregatesWindow Functions
1

Schema Setup

SQL — Schema
CREATE TABLE customers (
  id INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,
  name VARCHAR(100), city VARCHAR(50),
  created_at DATE
);
CREATE TABLE products (
  id INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,
  name VARCHAR(100), category VARCHAR(50),
  price DECIMAL(10,2)
);
CREATE TABLE orders (
  id INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,
  customer_id INT, order_date DATE,
  FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES customers(id)
);
CREATE TABLE order_items (
  id INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,
  order_id INT, product_id INT, qty INT,
  FOREIGN KEY (order_id) REFERENCES orders(id),
  FOREIGN KEY (product_id) REFERENCES products(id)
);
2

Query 1: Top 10 Products by Revenue

SQL — Solution
SELECT
  p.name                          AS product,
  p.category,
  SUM(oi.qty * p.price)            AS revenue,
  SUM(oi.qty)                      AS units_sold,
  RANK() OVER (
    ORDER BY SUM(oi.qty * p.price) DESC
  )                                 AS revenue_rank
FROM products p
JOIN order_items oi ON p.id = oi.product_id
GROUP BY p.id, p.name, p.category
ORDER BY revenue DESC
LIMIT 10;
3

Query 2: Month-over-Month Revenue Growth

SQL — Solution
WITH monthly AS (
  SELECT
    DATE_FORMAT(o.order_date, '%Y-%m') AS month,
    SUM(oi.qty * p.price)             AS revenue
  FROM orders o
  JOIN order_items oi ON o.id = oi.order_id
  JOIN products     p  ON oi.product_id = p.id
  GROUP BY month
)
SELECT
  month,
  revenue,
  LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS prev_revenue,
  ROUND(
    (revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month))
    / LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) * 100, 2
  ) AS growth_pct
FROM monthly
ORDER BY month;

We first aggregate revenue by month in a CTE, then use LAG() to look back at the previous month's revenue and compute the % change. This is a classic analytics pattern.

PROJECT 02

👥 HR Payroll System

Employee management — departments, salaries, performance tiers, reporting chains.

Recursive CTEWindow FunctionsCASE WHENSubqueries
1

Schema

SQL
CREATE TABLE departments (
  id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(100), budget DECIMAL(15,2)
);
CREATE TABLE employees (
  id         INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,
  name       VARCHAR(100),
  dept_id    INT,
  manager_id INT,        -- self-reference for hierarchy
  salary     DECIMAL(10,2),
  hire_date  DATE,
  FOREIGN KEY (dept_id) REFERENCES departments(id)
);
2

Query: Salary Percentile & Performance Tier

SQL — Solution
SELECT
  e.name,
  d.name                                   AS department,
  e.salary,
  PERCENT_RANK() OVER (
    PARTITION BY e.dept_id
    ORDER BY e.salary
  ) * 100                                  AS salary_percentile,
  CASE
    WHEN e.salary >= AVG(e.salary) OVER (PARTITION BY e.dept_id) * 1.2
      THEN 'Top Earner'
    WHEN e.salary >= AVG(e.salary) OVER (PARTITION BY e.dept_id)
      THEN 'Above Average'
    ELSE 'Below Average'
  END                                      AS tier
FROM employees e
JOIN departments d ON e.dept_id = d.id
ORDER BY d.name, salary_percentile DESC;

PERCENT_RANK() calculates each employee's position within their department (0–100%). The CASE WHEN uses window-averaged salary to assign a tier — all computed in one elegant query without subqueries.

3

Query: Org Chart — All Reports Under a Manager

SQL — Recursive CTE
WITH RECURSIVE reports AS (
  SELECT id, name, manager_id, 1 AS level
  FROM employees WHERE id = 10  -- root manager
  UNION ALL
  SELECT e.id, e.name, e.manager_id, r.level+1
  FROM employees e
  INNER JOIN reports r ON e.manager_id = r.id
)
SELECT
  REPEAT('  ', level - 1) || name AS org_tree,
  level
FROM reports
ORDER BY level;
PROJECT 03

🏨 Hotel Booking System

Room availability, booking conflicts, occupancy rates, and revenue per room type.

BETWEENNOT EXISTSCASE WHENDate Functions
1

Schema

SQL
CREATE TABLE rooms (
  id INT PRIMARY KEY, room_number VARCHAR(10),
  type ENUM('Standard','Deluxe','Suite'),
  price_per_night DECIMAL(8,2)
);
CREATE TABLE bookings (
  id         INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,
  room_id    INT,
  guest_name VARCHAR(100),
  check_in   DATE,
  check_out  DATE,
  status     ENUM('confirmed', 'cancelled'),
  FOREIGN KEY (room_id) REFERENCES rooms(id)
);
2

Query: Find Available Rooms for a Date Range

SQL — Solution
SELECT r.room_number, r.type, r.price_per_night
FROM rooms r
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM bookings b
  WHERE b.room_id = r.id
    AND b.status = 'confirmed'
    AND b.check_in  < '2025-03-20'
    AND b.check_out > '2025-03-15'
)
ORDER BY r.type, r.price_per_night;

The overlap condition is: booking starts before our checkout AND booking ends after our check-in. NOT EXISTS excludes rooms with any overlapping confirmed booking.

3

Query: Occupancy Report by Room Type

SQL — Solution
SELECT
  r.type,
  COUNT(b.id)                  AS total_bookings,
  SUM(DATEDIFF(b.check_out, b.check_in)) AS total_nights,
  SUM(DATEDIFF(b.check_out, b.check_in)
    * r.price_per_night)        AS total_revenue,
  ROUND(
    SUM(DATEDIFF(b.check_out, b.check_in))
    / (COUNT(DISTINCT r.id) * 365) * 100, 1
  )                              AS occupancy_pct
FROM rooms r
JOIN bookings b ON r.id = b.room_id
WHERE b.status = 'confirmed'
GROUP BY r.type
ORDER BY total_revenue DESC;
PROJECT 04

📚 Library Management System

Track books, members, loans, overdue fines, and popular titles.

Multiple JOINsCASE WHENDate FunctionsStored Procedure
1

Schema

SQL
CREATE TABLE books (
  id INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,
  title VARCHAR(200), author VARCHAR(100),
  isbn VARCHAR(20) UNIQUE, genre VARCHAR(50),
  copies_total INT, copies_available INT
);
CREATE TABLE members (
  id INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,
  name VARCHAR(100), email VARCHAR(255),
  membership_type ENUM('Regular','Premium'),
  joined_date DATE
);
CREATE TABLE loans (
  id          INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,
  book_id     INT,
  member_id   INT,
  loan_date   DATE,
  due_date    DATE,
  return_date DATE,    -- NULL if not yet returned
  FOREIGN KEY (book_id)   REFERENCES books(id),
  FOREIGN KEY (member_id) REFERENCES members(id)
);
2

Query: Overdue Books & Calculate Fines

SQL — Solution
SELECT
  m.name                             AS member,
  b.title                            AS book,
  l.due_date,
  DATEDIFF(CURDATE(), l.due_date)   AS days_overdue,
  CASE
    WHEN m.membership_type = 'Premium'
      THEN DATEDIFF(CURDATE(), l.due_date) * 0   -- Premium waived
    ELSE
      DATEDIFF(CURDATE(), l.due_date) * 5.00    -- ₹5/day fine
  END                                AS fine_amount
FROM loans     l
JOIN members   m ON l.member_id = m.id
JOIN books     b ON l.book_id   = b.id
WHERE l.return_date IS NULL
  AND l.due_date < CURDATE()
ORDER BY days_overdue DESC;

We filter for unreturned books past their due date. DATEDIFF() gives days overdue. CASE WHEN applies different fine logic for Premium vs Regular members.

3

Query: Most Popular Books This Year

SQL — Solution
SELECT
  b.title,
  b.author,
  b.genre,
  COUNT(l.id)                         AS times_borrowed,
  RANK() OVER (
    PARTITION BY b.genre
    ORDER BY COUNT(l.id) DESC
  )                                     AS rank_in_genre
FROM books b
JOIN loans l ON b.id = l.book_id
WHERE YEAR(l.loan_date) = YEAR(CURDATE())
GROUP BY b.id, b.title, b.author, b.genre
HAVING COUNT(l.id) >= 3
ORDER BY b.genre, rank_in_genre;
PROJECT 05

📈 Social Media Analytics

User growth, engagement rates, viral posts, influencer identification, and cohort analysis.

CTE ChainsWindow FunctionsCohort AnalysisSelf JOIN
1

Schema

SQL
CREATE TABLE users (
  id INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,
  username VARCHAR(50), joined_date DATE
);
CREATE TABLE posts (
  id INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,
  user_id INT, content TEXT,
  posted_at TIMESTAMP
);
CREATE TABLE interactions (
  id INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,
  post_id INT, user_id INT,
  type ENUM('like', 'comment', 'share'),
  created_at TIMESTAMP
);
CREATE TABLE follows (
  follower_id INT, following_id INT,
  PRIMARY KEY (follower_id, following_id)
);
2

Query: Top Influencers by Weighted Engagement

SQL — Solution
WITH
  post_engagement AS (
    SELECT
      p.user_id,
      p.id                                              AS post_id,
      SUM(CASE WHEN i.type='like'    THEN 1
               WHEN i.type='comment' THEN 3
               WHEN i.type='share'   THEN 5
               ELSE 0 END)                               AS score
    FROM posts p
    LEFT JOIN interactions i ON p.id = i.post_id
    WHERE p.posted_at >= DATE_SUB(NOW(), INTERVAL 30 DAY)
    GROUP BY p.user_id, p.id
  ),
  user_totals AS (
    SELECT
      user_id,
      SUM(score)   AS total_score,
      COUNT(*)      AS posts_count,
      AVG(score)   AS avg_score
    FROM post_engagement
    GROUP BY user_id
  )
SELECT
  u.username,
  COUNT(f.follower_id)             AS followers,
  ut.total_score,
  ROUND(ut.avg_score, 1)           AS avg_engagement,
  DENSE_RANK() OVER (
    ORDER BY ut.total_score DESC
  )                                  AS influencer_rank
FROM users      u
JOIN user_totals ut ON u.id = ut.user_id
LEFT JOIN follows   f  ON u.id = f.following_id
GROUP BY u.id, u.username, ut.total_score, ut.avg_score
ORDER BY influencer_rank
LIMIT 20;

We use a weighted scoring system (shares worth 5x likes) inside a CASE WHEN. Two CTEs build up incrementally: first per-post scores, then per-user totals. Finally, we JOIN follower counts and use DENSE_RANK for the leaderboard.

3

Query: Cohort Retention Analysis

SQL — Advanced
-- Which month's signups are most engaged 30 days later?
WITH
  cohorts AS (
    SELECT
      id,
      DATE_FORMAT(joined_date, '%Y-%m') AS cohort_month
    FROM users
  ),
  activity AS (
    SELECT
      p.user_id,
      DATE_FORMAT(p.posted_at, '%Y-%m') AS active_month
    FROM posts p
  )
SELECT
  c.cohort_month,
  COUNT(DISTINCT c.id)                AS cohort_size,
  COUNT(DISTINCT a.user_id)           AS still_active,
  ROUND(
    COUNT(DISTINCT a.user_id) * 100.0
    / COUNT(DISTINCT c.id), 1
  )                                    AS retention_pct
FROM cohorts c
LEFT JOIN activity a
  ON c.id = a.user_id
  AND a.active_month = DATE_FORMAT(
    DATE_ADD(STR_TO_DATE(CONCAT(c.cohort_month, '-01'), '%Y-%m-%d'),
    INTERVAL 1 MONTH), '%Y-%m')
GROUP BY c.cohort_month
ORDER BY c.cohort_month;

This is a cohort retention query — a crucial metric for product analytics. We group users by the month they joined (cohort), then check if they were still active the following month. The retention % tells you product stickiness.

📐 New Deep Dive

Database Normalization

Normalization reduces redundancy and improves data integrity by organizing tables into progressively stricter "Normal Forms." Each form builds on the last.

Why Normalize?

🔁

Eliminate Redundancy

Same data in multiple places causes update anomalies — change it once, it's stale everywhere else.

🛡️

Data Integrity

Constraints and FK relationships prevent invalid data from entering the system.

🔍

Easier Queries

Well-structured data is intuitive to query and less prone to incorrect results.

First Normal Form (1NF)

1NF: Every column must hold atomic (indivisible) values. No repeating groups or arrays in a cell.

Orders table — multiple values in one cell
order_idcustomerproducts
1AliceLaptop, Mouse, Keyboard
2BobPhone

The products column contains multiple values — non-atomic, violates 1NF.

Orders table — atomic values (one product per row)
order_idcustomerproduct
1AliceLaptop
1AliceMouse
1AliceKeyboard
2BobPhone

Second Normal Form (2NF)

2NF: In 1NF + every non-key column depends on the entire composite primary key (no partial dependencies).

order_items — composite PK (order_id + product_id)
order_idproduct_idquantityproduct_nameproduct_price
1102Laptop999.99
1111Mouse25.00

product_name and product_price depend only on product_id — partial dependency.

order_items (only order-specific data)
order_idproduct_idquantity
1102
1111
products (product data lives here)
product_idproduct_nameproduct_price
10Laptop999.99
11Mouse25.00

Third Normal Form (3NF)

3NF: In 2NF + no transitive dependencies — non-key columns must depend only on the PK, not on other non-key columns.

student_idstudent_namezip_codecitystate
1Alice10001New YorkNY
2Bob90210Beverly HillsCA

city and state depend on zip_code, not directly on student_id — transitive dependency.

student_idstudent_namezip_code
1Alice10001
zip_codecitystate
10001New YorkNY

Controlled Denormalization

Normalization is ideal for writes. For heavy read/analytics workloads (data warehouses), intentional denormalization reduces JOINs and speeds up queries. Normalize first, denormalize only with measurements.
