String Functions

SQL's string functions let you search, format, and transform text. Here's a complete reference with real-world use cases.

Core Functions Reference

SQL — String Functions
LENGTH('Hello')                           -- 5
UPPER('hello')                            -- 'HELLO'
LOWER('WORLD')                            -- 'world'
TRIM('  hello  ')                        -- 'hello'
SUBSTRING('Hello World', 7, 5)          -- 'World'
CONCAT('John', ' ', 'Doe')             -- 'John Doe'
CONCAT_WS(', ', 'Alice', 'Bob')        -- 'Alice, Bob'
REPLACE('I love cats', 'cats', 'dogs')  -- 'I love dogs'
INSTR('Hello World', 'World')           -- 7 (position)
LEFT('Hello World', 5)                  -- 'Hello'
RIGHT('Hello World', 5)                 -- 'World'
LPAD('42', 5, '0')                     -- '00042'
RPAD('Hi', 6, '.')                     -- 'Hi....'
REVERSE('SQL')                           -- 'LQS'
REPEAT('ab', 3)                          -- 'ababab'
FORMAT(1234567.89, 2)                   -- '1,234,567.89'
CHAR_LENGTH('héllo')                     -- 5 characters (vs bytes)

Pattern Matching: LIKE & REGEXP

SQL — Pattern Matching
-- LIKE: % = any chars, _ = single char
SELECT * FROM users WHERE email LIKE '%@gmail.com';
SELECT * FROM users WHERE name  LIKE 'A%';
SELECT * FROM products WHERE code LIKE 'P_-2024';

-- REGEXP: full regex power
SELECT * FROM users
WHERE phone REGEXP '^[0-9]{10}$';       -- exactly 10 digits
SELECT * FROM products
WHERE name REGEXP '(laptop|notebook)';  -- either word

Real-World Examples

SQL — Practical String Scenarios
-- Properly capitalize a name
SELECT CONCAT(
  UPPER(LEFT(TRIM(first_name),1)),
  LOWER(SUBSTRING(TRIM(first_name),2))
) AS clean_name FROM users;

-- Extract domain from email
SELECT email,
  SUBSTRING(email, INSTR(email,'@')+1) AS domain
FROM users;

-- Mask credit card (show last 4 only)
SELECT CONCAT(REPEAT('*',12), RIGHT(card_number,4)) AS masked
FROM payments;

-- Count words in a column
SELECT description,
  LENGTH(description) - LENGTH(REPLACE(description,' ',''))+1 AS word_count
FROM articles;

-- Build a URL slug: 'My Blog Post' → 'my-blog-post'
SELECT LOWER(REPLACE(TRIM(title),' ','-')) AS slug
FROM blog_posts;
📅 Deep Dive

Date & Time Functions

Dates appear in almost every real-world database. These functions handle everything from simple formatting to complex time-series calculations.

Current Date & Time

SQL — Current DateTime Functions
NOW()            -- '2024-11-15 14:32:55' (date + time)
CURDATE()        -- '2024-11-15' (date only)
CURTIME()        -- '14:32:55' (time only)
UTC_TIMESTAMP()  -- UTC datetime (essential for global apps)
UNIX_TIMESTAMP() -- seconds since epoch: 1731677575

Extracting Parts

SQL — Date Part Extraction
SELECT
  YEAR(order_date)       AS yr,        -- 2024
  MONTH(order_date)      AS mo,        -- 11
  DAY(order_date)        AS dy,        -- 15
  DAYNAME(order_date)    AS day_name,  -- 'Friday'
  MONTHNAME(order_date)  AS mth_name,  -- 'November'
  WEEK(order_date)       AS week_num,  -- 46
  QUARTER(order_date)    AS qtr,       -- 4
  DAYOFWEEK(order_date)  AS dow        -- 1=Sun...7=Sat
FROM orders;

Date Arithmetic

SQL — Date Arithmetic
DATE_ADD(NOW(), INTERVAL 7 DAY)           -- 7 days from now
DATE_SUB(NOW(), INTERVAL 1 MONTH)         -- 1 month ago
DATEDIFF('2024-12-31', '2024-01-01')      -- 365 (days between)
TIMESTAMPDIFF(MONTH, hire_date, NOW())    -- months employed
DATE_FORMAT(NOW(), '%d %M %Y')            -- '15 November 2024'
DATE_FORMAT(NOW(), '%Y-%m')               -- '2024-11' (for grouping)
STR_TO_DATE('15-Nov-2024', '%d-%b-%Y')   -- parse string → date

Real-World Date Patterns

SQL — Practical Date Queries
-- Last 30 days of orders
SELECT * FROM orders
WHERE created_at >= DATE_SUB(CURDATE(), INTERVAL 30 DAY);

-- Revenue by month (for line charts)
SELECT
  DATE_FORMAT(created_at,'%Y-%m') AS month,
  SUM(amount) AS revenue
FROM orders GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;

-- Users with birthdays this month
SELECT name FROM users
WHERE MONTH(birthdate) = MONTH(NOW());

-- Calculate age
SELECT name,
  TIMESTAMPDIFF(YEAR, birthdate, CURDATE()) AS age
FROM users;

-- Subscriptions expiring in next 7 days
SELECT user_id, expires_at FROM subscriptions
WHERE expires_at BETWEEN NOW()
  AND DATE_ADD(NOW(), INTERVAL 7 DAY);

-- Busiest day of the week
SELECT DAYNAME(created_at) AS day, COUNT(*) AS orders
FROM orders
GROUP BY DAYOFWEEK(created_at), DAYNAME(created_at)
ORDER BY orders DESC;
⛔ Deep Dive

NULL Handling

NULL represents absence of value — not zero, not empty string. It has unique behavior that trips up many developers. Master it here.

The Golden Rule

NULL ≠ NULL

Any comparison with NULL returns UNKNOWN — not TRUE or FALSE. You must use IS NULL or IS NOT NULL, never = NULL.

SQL — NULL Comparisons
-- WRONG: returns no rows
SELECT * FROM users WHERE phone = NULL;    -- ❌
-- CORRECT
SELECT * FROM users WHERE phone IS NULL;     -- ✅
SELECT * FROM users WHERE phone IS NOT NULL; -- ✅

NULL-Safe Functions

SQL — Handling NULLs
-- COALESCE: first non-NULL value
SELECT COALESCE(phone, mobile, 'No Contact') AS contact
FROM users;

-- IFNULL: two-argument shorthand
SELECT IFNULL(discount, 0) AS discount
FROM products;

-- NULLIF: returns NULL when values match (safe division)
SELECT revenue / NULLIF(units_sold, 0) AS rev_per_unit
FROM sales;

-- COUNT behavior with NULLs
SELECT
  COUNT(*)         AS all_rows,      -- includes NULLs
  COUNT(phone)    AS with_phone,   -- excludes NULL phones
  AVG(score)      AS avg_non_null  -- NULLs excluded from avg
FROM users;

-- Anti-join: customers with NO orders (LEFT JOIN + IS NULL)
SELECT c.name
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.id IS NULL;
🟢 Practice & Interview Prep

Q&A — Beginner (30 Questions)

Core SQL fundamentals. Try to answer each question before expanding the answer.

Theoretical (Q1–Q10)

Q1. What is SQL and what is it used for? ▼

SQL (Structured Query Language) is a domain-specific language for managing relational databases. Uses: creating structures (DDL), manipulating data (DML), querying with SELECT, access control (DCL), and transaction management (TCL). Each RDBMS (MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQL Server, Oracle) has slight dialect differences on top of the ANSI/ISO standard.

Q2. What is the difference between a Database and a DBMS? ▼

A database is an organized collection of structured data. A DBMS (Database Management System) is the software that manages it — providing tools to create, read, update, delete, secure, and back up data. MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server are all DBMS software. The database is the data; the DBMS is the engine powering it.

Q3. What are the five SQL command categories? ▼
  • DDL (Data Definition Language): CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE — define structure
  • DML (Data Manipulation Language): INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE — manipulate rows
  • DQL (Data Query Language): SELECT — retrieve data
  • DCL (Data Control Language): GRANT, REVOKE — permissions
  • TCL (Transaction Control Language): COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT — transactions
Q4. What is a Primary Key? ▼

A column (or combination) that uniquely identifies each row. Rules: must be UNIQUE, must be NOT NULL, one per table. Can be a single column (simple PK) or multiple columns (composite PK). Creates a clustered index automatically.

Q5. What is a Foreign Key? ▼

A column that references the Primary Key of another table, enforcing referential integrity. You cannot insert an FK value that doesn't exist in the referenced table. ON DELETE CASCADE/SET NULL/RESTRICT controls behavior when the referenced row is deleted.

Q6. What is the difference between DELETE, TRUNCATE, and DROP? ▼
  • DELETE: DML. Removes specific rows (WHERE clause). Can be rolled back. Fires triggers. Slow on large tables.
  • TRUNCATE: DDL. Removes ALL rows instantly. No WHERE clause. Cannot roll back in most DBs. Very fast (deallocates pages). Does not fire row-level triggers.
  • DROP: DDL. Removes the entire table structure and all data permanently.
Q7. What is the difference between CHAR and VARCHAR? ▼

CHAR(n): fixed-length, always stores n bytes (padded with spaces if shorter). Best for consistent-length values (country codes, hashes). VARCHAR(n): variable-length, stores only used bytes + 1-2 byte length prefix. Best for names, emails, descriptions. VARCHAR saves space but has a tiny overhead to read the length prefix.

Q8. What does NULL mean in SQL? ▼

NULL means absence of a value — not zero, not empty string, not false. It means "unknown" or "not applicable." Key behaviors: arithmetic with NULL = NULL; comparison with NULL = UNKNOWN; COUNT(*) includes NULLs but COUNT(col) excludes them; SUM/AVG/MIN/MAX ignore NULLs. Always use IS NULL / IS NOT NULL.

Q9. What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING? ▼

WHERE filters rows BEFORE aggregation — works on individual row values, cannot reference aggregate functions. HAVING filters groups AFTER GROUP BY — can reference COUNT(), SUM(), etc. Memory trick: WHERE = filter rows; HAVING = filter groups.

Q10. What is the logical execution order of a SELECT statement? ▼
  1. FROM / JOINs — identify source tables
  2. WHERE — filter individual rows
  3. GROUP BY — group rows
  4. HAVING — filter groups
  5. SELECT — compute output columns
  6. DISTINCT — remove duplicates
  7. ORDER BY — sort results
  8. LIMIT / OFFSET — paginate

Important: aliases defined in SELECT cannot be used in WHERE (WHERE executes before SELECT).

Query Practice (Q11–Q30)

Q11. Find all employees with salary above 50,000. ▼
SQL
SELECT employee_id, name, salary
FROM employees
WHERE salary > 50000
ORDER BY salary DESC;
Q12. Count employees per department. ▼
SQL
SELECT department, COUNT(*) AS headcount
FROM employees
GROUP BY department
ORDER BY headcount DESC;
Q13. Get top 5 most expensive products. ▼
SQL
SELECT product_name, price
FROM products
ORDER BY price DESC
LIMIT 5;
Q14. Insert a new customer record. ▼
SQL
INSERT INTO customers (name, email, phone, created_at)
VALUES ('Alice Johnson', '[email protected]', '9876543210', NOW());
Q15. Update a user's email address. ▼
SQL
UPDATE users
SET email = '[email protected]'
WHERE user_id = 42;

Never run UPDATE without WHERE unless you intend to update every row.

Q16. Find duplicate records by email. ▼
SQL
SELECT email, COUNT(*) AS occurrences
FROM users
GROUP BY email
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
ORDER BY occurrences DESC;
Q17. Find products containing 'phone' in the name. ▼
SQL
SELECT product_id, product_name, price
FROM products
WHERE LOWER(product_name) LIKE '%phone%';
Q18. Get the second highest salary (two methods). ▼
SQL — Two Approaches
-- Method 1: subquery
SELECT MAX(salary) AS second_highest
FROM employees
WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employees);

-- Method 2: LIMIT OFFSET
SELECT DISTINCT salary
FROM employees
ORDER BY salary DESC
LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1;
Q19. Find customers with no orders (three methods). ▼
SQL — Three Methods
-- Method 1: LEFT JOIN anti-join
SELECT c.id, c.name
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.id IS NULL;

-- Method 2: NOT EXISTS (often fastest)
SELECT id, name FROM customers c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM orders WHERE customer_id = c.id
);

-- Method 3: NOT IN (beware NULLs in subquery)
SELECT id, name FROM customers
WHERE id NOT IN (
  SELECT DISTINCT customer_id FROM orders
  WHERE customer_id IS NOT NULL
);
Q20. What is the difference between UNION and UNION ALL? ▼

UNION removes duplicate rows (implicit DISTINCT). UNION ALL keeps all rows including duplicates and is faster. Use UNION ALL unless you need deduplication. Both require same column count and compatible types.

SQL
SELECT email FROM customers
UNION ALL
SELECT email FROM suppliers;
Q21. Get avg, min, max salary per department. ▼
SQL
SELECT department,
  ROUND(AVG(salary),2) AS avg_salary,
  MIN(salary) AS min_salary,
  MAX(salary) AS max_salary
FROM employees
GROUP BY department
ORDER BY avg_salary DESC;
Q22. Retrieve only unique country values. ▼
SQL
SELECT DISTINCT country FROM customers ORDER BY country;
Q23. Sort employees by department (A–Z) then salary (high to low). ▼
SQL
SELECT name, department, salary
FROM employees
ORDER BY department ASC, salary DESC;
Q24. Find products priced between 100 and 500. ▼
SQL
SELECT * FROM products
WHERE price BETWEEN 100 AND 500;

BETWEEN is inclusive on both ends — equivalent to >= 100 AND <= 500.

Q25. Find employees in Engineering, Design, or Product. ▼
SQL
SELECT * FROM employees
WHERE department IN ('Engineering', 'Design', 'Product');
Q26. CREATE TABLE with all major constraint types. ▼
SQL
CREATE TABLE employees (
  id         INT          AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  name       VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
  email      VARCHAR(150) NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  salary     DECIMAL(10,2) CHECK (salary > 0),
  hire_date  DATE         DEFAULT (CURDATE()),
  is_active  BOOLEAN      DEFAULT TRUE
);
Q27. What is an alias? Show column and table aliases. ▼

An alias is a temporary name given to a column or table using AS. Table aliases shorten long names; column aliases rename output columns.

SQL
SELECT
  e.name          AS employee_name,
  salary * 12     AS annual_salary
FROM employees e  -- table alias
WHERE e.salary > 50000;
Q28. Find departments with more than 10 employees. ▼
SQL
SELECT department, COUNT(*) AS headcount
FROM employees
GROUP BY department
HAVING COUNT(*) > 10
ORDER BY headcount DESC;
Q29. Retrieve rows 3 through 7 from a table. ▼
SQL
SELECT * FROM products
ORDER BY id
LIMIT 5 OFFSET 2;  -- skip 2, take 5 = rows 3-7
Q30. Add a new column to an existing table. ▼
SQL
ALTER TABLE users
ADD COLUMN last_login DATETIME DEFAULT NULL;

-- Add multiple columns at once
ALTER TABLE products
  ADD COLUMN weight_kg   DECIMAL(6,2),
  ADD COLUMN is_featured BOOLEAN DEFAULT FALSE;

Additional Practice (Q31–Q45)

Q31. What is a constraint? List the main types in SQL. ▼

A constraint is a rule enforced on a column or table to ensure data integrity. Main types:

  • NOT NULL: Column cannot contain NULL values.
  • UNIQUE: All values in the column must be distinct.
  • PRIMARY KEY: Combination of NOT NULL + UNIQUE. One per table.
  • FOREIGN KEY: Links to another table's PK, enforcing referential integrity.
  • CHECK: Validates values against an expression (salary > 0).
  • DEFAULT: Provides a value when none is specified on INSERT.
Q32. Write a query to display the current date and time. ▼
SQL
SELECT
  NOW()       AS datetime_now,
  CURDATE()   AS today,
  CURTIME()   AS current_time,
  DAYNAME(NOW()) AS day_name;
Q33. What is the difference between a table and a view? ▼

A table physically stores data on disk — rows are persisted and occupy storage. A view stores only a SQL query definition — it has no data of its own. When you query a view, it executes its underlying query and returns results dynamically. Views cannot be indexed (unlike tables), and querying complex views re-runs the full join/aggregation each time. Use tables for raw data; use views for simplified or secured access to that data.

Q34. How do you calculate the number of days between two dates? ▼
SQL
-- DATEDIFF: returns whole days
SELECT DATEDIFF('2024-12-31', '2024-01-01') AS days;   -- 365

-- Real example: days since each customer's last order
SELECT
  customer_id,
  MAX(order_date)                            AS last_order,
  DATEDIFF(CURDATE(), MAX(order_date))       AS days_since
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id
ORDER BY days_since DESC;
Q35. What is the difference between IS NULL and = NULL? ▼

= NULL never works. NULL represents an unknown value, and comparing an unknown to anything — even another unknown — always returns UNKNOWN (not TRUE or FALSE). SQL's WHERE clause only returns rows where the condition is TRUE, so WHERE column = NULL always returns zero rows. You must always use IS NULL or IS NOT NULL to check for NULL values.

SQL
SELECT * FROM users WHERE phone = NULL;     -- ❌ 0 rows always
SELECT * FROM users WHERE phone IS NULL;    -- ✅ finds NULLs
Q36. Write a query to concatenate first and last name columns. ▼
SQL
SELECT
  first_name,
  last_name,
  CONCAT(first_name, ' ', last_name)      AS full_name,
  CONCAT_WS(' ', first_name, last_name)   AS full_name_safe
  -- CONCAT_WS ignores NULLs: safer if middle name might be NULL
FROM employees;
Q37. What is COALESCE and when would you use it? ▼

COALESCE(val1, val2, ..., valN) returns the first non-NULL value in its argument list. It's the standard SQL way to substitute a default when a column might be NULL. Common uses: replace NULL numbers with 0, replace NULL strings with a fallback label, choose the first available contact method from multiple columns.

SQL
SELECT
  name,
  COALESCE(phone, mobile, 'No contact')   AS best_contact,
  COALESCE(discount, 0)                     AS discount,
  price * (1 - COALESCE(discount, 0) / 100) AS final_price
FROM products;
Q38. How do you delete all rows from a table but keep the table structure? ▼
SQL — Two Ways
-- TRUNCATE: fast, resets AUTO_INCREMENT, cannot rollback
TRUNCATE TABLE temp_log;

-- DELETE without WHERE: slow, can rollback, fires triggers
DELETE FROM temp_log;

-- Choose TRUNCATE when: bulk clear, no rollback needed, reset counter
-- Choose DELETE when: you need rollback or triggers must fire
Q39. Write a query to find the length of each product name. ▼
SQL
SELECT
  product_name,
  LENGTH(product_name)      AS char_length,
  CHAR_LENGTH(product_name) AS unicode_length
FROM products
ORDER BY LENGTH(product_name) DESC;

Note: for multi-byte character sets (UTF-8 with emojis or regional scripts), CHAR_LENGTH() counts characters while LENGTH() counts bytes — they differ for non-ASCII text.

Q40. What is a subquery? Show an example of a subquery in WHERE. ▼

A subquery (or inner query) is a SELECT statement nested inside another SQL statement. The outer query uses the result of the inner query as a condition, value, or derived table.

SQL — Subquery Types
-- Subquery in WHERE (scalar)
SELECT name, salary
FROM employees
WHERE salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees);

-- Subquery in FROM (derived table)
SELECT dept, ROUND(avg_sal, 0)
FROM (
  SELECT department dept, AVG(salary) avg_sal
  FROM employees GROUP BY department
) t
WHERE avg_sal > 60000;

-- Subquery in SELECT (scalar per row)
SELECT
  name,
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders
   WHERE customer_id = c.id) AS order_count
FROM customers c;
Q41. Write a query to find the total revenue per year. ▼
SQL
SELECT
  YEAR(order_date)       AS year,
  COUNT(DISTINCT id)    AS orders,
  SUM(total)            AS gross_revenue,
  ROUND(AVG(total), 2)  AS avg_order_value
FROM orders
GROUP BY YEAR(order_date)
ORDER BY year;
Q42. What is a CASE WHEN expression? Show an example. ▼

CASE WHEN is SQL's conditional expression — like an if/else inside a SELECT. It evaluates conditions top to bottom and returns the value of the first matching WHEN clause. The ELSE clause handles all non-matching cases.

SQL — CASE WHEN
SELECT
  product_name, stock_qty,
  CASE
    WHEN stock_qty = 0    THEN 'Out of Stock'
    WHEN stock_qty < 10  THEN 'Low Stock'
    WHEN stock_qty < 50  THEN 'Medium Stock'
    ELSE                      'Well Stocked'
  END AS stock_status
FROM products;
Q43. What does LIMIT OFFSET do? Show pagination. ▼

LIMIT restricts the number of rows returned. OFFSET skips a specified number of rows before starting to return results. Together they implement pagination.

SQL — Pagination
SELECT id, name, price
FROM products
ORDER BY id
LIMIT 10 OFFSET  0;   -- Page 1: rows 1-10

LIMIT 10 OFFSET 10;    -- Page 2: rows 11-20
LIMIT 10 OFFSET 20;    -- Page 3: rows 21-30

-- Formula: OFFSET = (page_number - 1) * page_size
Q44. How do you rename a table and rename a column? ▼
SQL — Rename
-- Rename a table
RENAME TABLE old_table_name TO new_table_name;
-- Or equivalently:
ALTER TABLE old_name RENAME TO new_name;

-- Rename a column (MySQL 8+ shorthand)
ALTER TABLE employees
RENAME COLUMN emp_name TO full_name;

-- Rename + change type in one step (older MySQL)
ALTER TABLE employees
CHANGE emp_name full_name VARCHAR(120) NOT NULL;
Q45. What is the difference between INNER JOIN and CROSS JOIN? ▼

An INNER JOIN returns rows where there is a matching value in both tables based on the ON condition — it filters. A CROSS JOIN returns the Cartesian product — every row from table A paired with every row from table B, with no filtering condition. If A has 10 rows and B has 5 rows, CROSS JOIN returns 50 rows. Cross joins are used for generating combinations (size × color), building test data, or comparing every row against every other row.

SQL
-- INNER JOIN: only matching rows (1:1 link)
SELECT o.id, c.name
FROM orders o
INNER JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id;

-- CROSS JOIN: all size × color combos
SELECT s.size, c.color
FROM sizes s
CROSS JOIN colors c;

Additional Theory Questions (Q31–Q45)

Q31. What are constraints in SQL? List all types. ▼

Constraints enforce data integrity rules at the database level. Types:

  • PRIMARY KEY: Unique + Not Null identifier for each row.
  • FOREIGN KEY: Enforces referential integrity between tables.
  • UNIQUE: All values in the column must be distinct (NULLs are allowed).
  • NOT NULL: The column cannot have NULL values.
  • CHECK: Values must satisfy a boolean expression (e.g., salary > 0).
  • DEFAULT: Provides a default value when none is specified.
SQL — All Constraints
CREATE TABLE employees (
  id          INT           PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,
  name        VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
  email       VARCHAR(150) UNIQUE NOT NULL,
  salary      DECIMAL(10,2) CHECK (salary > 0),
  dept_id     INT           REFERENCES departments(id),
  status      VARCHAR(10)  DEFAULT 'active'
);
Q32. What is the difference between a subquery and a JOIN? ▼

A JOIN combines rows from multiple tables into a single result set — ideal when you need columns from both tables. A subquery is a nested query that returns a value, a list, or a table used by the outer query. JOINs are generally faster because the optimizer can use indexes on both sides. Subqueries are often clearer to read and are necessary for correlated logic. For most aggregate comparisons (e.g., "above average"), a subquery is cleaner; for combining data from two tables, a JOIN is preferred.

Q33. What is a composite primary key? ▼

A composite (compound) primary key uses two or more columns together to uniquely identify a row. Neither column alone is unique, but the combination is. Common in junction/bridge tables for many-to-many relationships.

SQL
-- student_courses: one student can enroll in many courses, one course has many students
CREATE TABLE student_courses (
  student_id  INT,
  course_id   INT,
  enrolled_at DATE,
  PRIMARY KEY (student_id, course_id)  -- composite PK
);
Q34. What are aggregate functions? List them all. ▼

Aggregate functions compute a single value from a set of rows. They ignore NULLs (except COUNT(*)).

  • COUNT(*): Total row count (including NULLs)
  • COUNT(col): Count of non-NULL values
  • COUNT(DISTINCT col): Count of unique non-NULL values
  • SUM(col): Total of numeric values
  • AVG(col): Average of non-NULL numeric values
  • MIN(col): Smallest value
  • MAX(col): Largest value
  • GROUP_CONCAT(col): Concatenated string of values (MySQL)
Q35. What is the difference between a natural key and a surrogate key? ▼

A natural key is a real-world identifier that already exists in the data — like email address, PAN number, ISBN, or phone number. A surrogate key is an artificial identifier generated by the database (typically an auto-incremented integer or UUID) with no business meaning. Surrogate keys are preferred because natural keys can change (a person changes their email), can be long (degrading index performance), and may not always be available for every entity. Surrogate keys are stable, short, and fast to join on.

Q36. What is a schema? ▼

In SQL, a schema is a logical namespace that groups database objects — tables, views, indexes, stored procedures, and functions. In MySQL, "schema" and "database" are synonymous (CREATE SCHEMA = CREATE DATABASE). In PostgreSQL and SQL Server, a schema is a container within a database, allowing multiple schemas per database (e.g., sales.orders, hr.employees). Schemas help with organization, security (grant access to a schema), and avoiding name collisions.

Q37. What is ACID and why is it important? ▼
  • Atomicity: A transaction is all-or-nothing. If it fails midway, all changes are rolled back.
  • Consistency: Every transaction moves the DB from one valid state to another — all constraints remain satisfied.
  • Isolation: Concurrent transactions don't interfere. Each sees a consistent snapshot.
  • Durability: Once committed, changes survive crashes and power failures — they are written to durable storage.

ACID is critical in financial systems (bank transfers), e-commerce (order + inventory must update together), and any scenario where partial writes cause data corruption.

Q38. What is the difference between ROLLBACK and COMMIT? ▼
SQL — COMMIT vs ROLLBACK
START TRANSACTION;
  UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 1000 WHERE id = 1;
  UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 1000 WHERE id = 2;

COMMIT;    -- Makes all changes permanent. Visible to other sessions.
-- or --
ROLLBACK; -- Undoes ALL changes since START TRANSACTION. DB returns to prior state.

COMMIT permanently saves the transaction. ROLLBACK cancels everything. Autocommit mode (ON by default in MySQL) automatically commits each statement unless inside an explicit transaction block.

Q39. What is a stored procedure and when would you use one? ▼

A stored procedure is a named, precompiled SQL program stored in the database. Use one when: (1) the same multi-step SQL operation runs frequently — compile once, call many times; (2) you want to restrict direct table access for security — grant EXECUTE only; (3) you need procedural logic (loops, conditionals, error handling) inside the DB; (4) you're building ETL pipelines or batch jobs that run inside the database; (5) you want to reduce network round-trips by executing multiple statements server-side in one call.

Q40. What are the different types of SQL relationships? ▼
  • One-to-One (1:1): Each row in Table A corresponds to at most one row in Table B. Example: users ↔ user_profiles. Implemented with a unique FK.
  • One-to-Many (1:N): One row in Table A corresponds to many rows in Table B. Example: customers → orders. Most common relationship. Implemented with a FK in the "many" table.
  • Many-to-Many (M:N): Many rows in A relate to many rows in B. Example: students ↔ courses. Implemented through a junction/bridge table (student_courses) with two FKs.
Q41. What is the difference between INNER JOIN and OUTER JOIN? ▼

An INNER JOIN returns only rows where there is a matching value in both tables — unmatched rows from either table are excluded. An OUTER JOIN preserves rows from one or both tables even when there's no match: LEFT OUTER keeps all rows from the left table (unmatched right rows become NULL), RIGHT OUTER keeps all from the right, and FULL OUTER keeps all from both sides.

Q42. What is SQL injection and how does parameterized queries prevent it? ▼

SQL injection is an attack where malicious SQL code is inserted into an input to manipulate queries. Example: if a login form concatenates input directly, an attacker can enter ' OR '1'='1 to bypass authentication. Parameterized queries (prepared statements) prevent this by treating user input as data, never as SQL code — the DB separates the query structure from the user-supplied values, so injected SQL syntax cannot alter the query logic.

SQL — Safe Parameterized Query
-- ❌ VULNERABLE: string concatenation
-- "SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '" + userInput + "'"
-- Input: [email protected]' OR '1'='1 → bypasses login

-- ✅ SAFE: prepared statement (PHP PDO example)
-- $stmt = $pdo->prepare("SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = ?");
-- $stmt->execute([$userInput]);
-- Input is bound as a literal string value — cannot alter query structure

-- In stored procedures: always use parameters, never CONCAT into SQL
PREPARE safe_stmt FROM 'SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = ?';
EXECUTE safe_stmt USING @user_input;
Q43. What is a transaction? Give a real-world example. ▼

A transaction is a sequence of SQL operations treated as a single unit of work — either all succeed or all fail together. Real-world example: bank transfer. Transferring ₹1000 from account A to B requires two steps: deduct from A, add to B. If step 2 fails after step 1 succeeds, money disappears. A transaction wraps both in an atomic unit — if step 2 fails, step 1 is automatically rolled back, leaving both accounts unchanged.

Q44. What are DDL, DML, DCL, and TCL? Give one SQL command for each. ▼
  • DDL (Data Definition Language): Defines structure. Example: CREATE TABLE employees (...)
  • DML (Data Manipulation Language): Manipulates data. Example: INSERT INTO employees VALUES (...)
  • DCL (Data Control Language): Controls access. Example: GRANT SELECT ON employees TO 'analyst'@'%'
  • TCL (Transaction Control Language): Manages transactions. Example: COMMIT
Q45. What is normalization vs denormalization? ▼

Normalization organizes data into multiple related tables to eliminate redundancy and protect integrity. Better for OLTP (frequent writes, transactions). Denormalization intentionally combines data (some redundancy) to reduce JOIN complexity and improve read performance. Better for OLAP/analytics (dashboards, reports, data warehouses). The trade-off: normalized = data integrity, fewer anomalies; denormalized = faster queries, simpler analytics. Star and snowflake schemas in data warehouses are controlled forms of denormalization.

Q46. What is the execution order of SQL clauses? (Detailed) ▼
SQL Logical Execution Order
StepClauseWhat It Does
1FROMIdentifies the source tables
2ONApplies JOIN conditions
3JOINCombines tables per join type
4WHEREFilters rows before grouping
5GROUP BYGroups filtered rows
6HAVINGFilters groups
7SELECTComputes output columns & aliases
8DISTINCTRemoves duplicate rows
9ORDER BYSorts the result (can use aliases from step 7)
10LIMIT/OFFSETPaginates final result

Because SELECT runs after WHERE, you cannot use a column alias defined in SELECT inside a WHERE clause. However, you CAN use aliases in ORDER BY and HAVING (in MySQL) since those run after SELECT.

Additional Query Practice (Q31–Q50)

Q31. Find the total revenue and order count per month in 2024. ▼
SQL
SELECT
  MONTHNAME(order_date) AS month,
  MONTH(order_date)     AS month_num,
  COUNT(*)               AS order_count,
  SUM(total)             AS revenue,
  ROUND(AVG(total), 2)   AS avg_order_value
FROM orders
WHERE YEAR(order_date) = 2024
GROUP BY MONTH(order_date), MONTHNAME(order_date)
ORDER BY month_num;
Q32. Find employees who joined in the last 90 days. ▼
SQL
SELECT
  name,
  department,
  hire_date,
  DATEDIFF(CURDATE(), hire_date) AS days_since_hired
FROM employees
WHERE hire_date >= DATE_SUB(CURDATE(), INTERVAL 90 DAY)
ORDER BY hire_date DESC;
Q33. Get the top customer by revenue in each country. ▼
SQL
SELECT t.country, t.name, t.revenue
FROM (
  SELECT
    c.country,
    c.name,
    SUM(o.total) AS revenue,
    RANK() OVER (
      PARTITION BY c.country
      ORDER BY SUM(o.total) DESC
    ) AS rnk
  FROM customers c
  JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id
  GROUP BY c.country, c.id, c.name
) t
WHERE rnk = 1
ORDER BY revenue DESC;
Q34. List products that have never been ordered along with their price. ▼
SQL
SELECT p.product_name, p.price, p.category
FROM products p
LEFT JOIN order_items oi ON p.id = oi.product_id
WHERE oi.product_id IS NULL
ORDER BY p.price DESC;
Q35. Calculate the cumulative (running) percentage of total revenue by product. ▼
SQL — Running % (Pareto / 80-20)
SELECT
  product_name,
  revenue,
  ROUND(revenue * 100.0 / SUM(revenue) OVER(), 2) AS pct,
  ROUND(SUM(revenue) OVER (
    ORDER BY revenue DESC
    ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
  ) * 100.0 / SUM(revenue) OVER(), 2) AS cumulative_pct
FROM (
  SELECT
    p.product_name,
    SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS revenue
  FROM order_items oi
  JOIN products p ON oi.product_id = p.id
  GROUP BY p.product_name
) t
ORDER BY revenue DESC;
Q36–40. Multi-column GROUP BY | COALESCE in reports | IFNULL display | Rank per category | Self-join manager chain ▼
Q36 — Sales by Year and Region
SELECT
  YEAR(order_date) AS yr,
  c.country,
  COUNT(*) AS orders,
  SUM(o.total) AS revenue
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY YEAR(order_date), c.country
ORDER BY yr, revenue DESC;
Q37 — COALESCE for clean reports
SELECT
  name,
  COALESCE(phone, mobile, 'No Number') AS contact,
  COALESCE(discount, 0) AS discount_pct,
  COALESCE(loyalty_tier, 'Standard') AS tier
FROM customers;
Q38 — Rank products within each category
SELECT
  category,
  product_name,
  price,
  RANK() OVER (
    PARTITION BY category
    ORDER BY price DESC
  ) AS price_rank_in_category
FROM products;
Q39 — Manager chain with self-join
SELECT
  e.name  AS employee,
  m.name  AS manager,
  gm.name AS grand_manager
FROM      employees e
LEFT JOIN employees m  ON e.manager_id  = m.id
LEFT JOIN employees gm ON m.manager_id  = gm.id;
Q40 — Employees with salary above company AND department average
SELECT e.name, e.department, e.salary
FROM employees e
WHERE
  e.salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees)           -- above company avg
  AND
  e.salary > (                                               -- above dept avg
    SELECT AVG(e2.salary)
    FROM employees e2
    WHERE e2.department = e.department
  )
ORDER BY e.salary DESC;
Q41–50. Date gaps | Multi-table UPDATE | Conditional aggregation | String ops | Nested GROUP BY ▼
Q41 — Orders with their item count and total
SELECT
  o.id       AS order_id,
  o.order_date,
  COUNT(oi.id)                          AS item_count,
  SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price)     AS subtotal,
  SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) * 0.18 AS tax_18pct
FROM orders o
JOIN order_items oi ON o.id = oi.order_id
GROUP BY o.id, o.order_date
ORDER BY subtotal DESC;
Q42 — Conditional aggregation: orders by status
SELECT
  COUNT(*) AS total_orders,
  SUM(CASE WHEN status='pending'   THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS pending,
  SUM(CASE WHEN status='shipped'   THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS shipped,
  SUM(CASE WHEN status='delivered' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS delivered,
  SUM(CASE WHEN status='cancelled' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS cancelled
FROM orders
WHERE YEAR(order_date) = YEAR(CURDATE());
Q43 — Find users whose email domain is gmail.com
SELECT
  name,
  email,
  SUBSTRING(email, INSTR(email, '@') + 1) AS domain
FROM users
WHERE email LIKE '%@gmail.com';
Q44 — Revenue comparison: current vs previous year
SELECT
  MONTH(order_date) AS mo,
  SUM(CASE WHEN YEAR(order_date)=YEAR(NOW())   THEN total ELSE 0 END) AS this_year,
  SUM(CASE WHEN YEAR(order_date)=YEAR(NOW())-1 THEN total ELSE 0 END) AS last_year
FROM orders
WHERE YEAR(order_date) IN (YEAR(NOW()), YEAR(NOW()) - 1)
GROUP BY MONTH(order_date)
ORDER BY mo;
Q45 — Find the 3 most recent orders per customer
SELECT customer_id, id AS order_id, order_date, total
FROM (
  SELECT *,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
      PARTITION BY customer_id
      ORDER BY order_date DESC
    ) AS rn
  FROM orders
) t
WHERE rn <= 3
ORDER BY customer_id, order_date DESC;

More Beginner Questions (Q31–Q50)

Q31. What is a constraint? Name all constraint types. ▼

A constraint is a rule enforced on table columns to ensure data validity and integrity. The main constraint types:

  • PRIMARY KEY: Uniquely identifies each row. No NULLs allowed. One per table.
  • FOREIGN KEY: References PK of another table. Enforces referential integrity.
  • UNIQUE: All values in column must be distinct. NULLs are allowed (and not counted as duplicates).
  • NOT NULL: Column cannot contain NULL values.
  • CHECK: Validates column values against a boolean expression.
  • DEFAULT: Provides a value when none is supplied.
SQL
CREATE TABLE products (
  id       INT           PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,
  name     VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  price    DECIMAL(10,2) CHECK (price > 0),
  category VARCHAR(50)  NOT NULL DEFAULT 'General',
  stock    INT           DEFAULT 0 CHECK (stock >= 0)
);
Q32. What is AUTO_INCREMENT? How does it work? ▼

AUTO_INCREMENT automatically generates a unique integer for a column each time a row is inserted. The DB tracks the last used value and increments it. Key facts: only one AUTO_INCREMENT column per table; it must be an integer type; must be a key (PRIMARY KEY or UNIQUE); gaps occur when rows are deleted or INSERTs are rolled back — this is normal. Use LAST_INSERT_ID() to retrieve the ID just inserted.

SQL
CREATE TABLE users (
  id   INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  name VARCHAR(100)
);
INSERT INTO users (name) VALUES ('Alice'), ('Bob');
SELECT LAST_INSERT_ID();  -- returns 2 (last auto id)

-- Reset auto_increment counter
ALTER TABLE users AUTO_INCREMENT = 1000;
Q33. What is the difference between TRUNCATE and DELETE with no WHERE? ▼

Both remove all rows from a table but work very differently. DELETE without WHERE: DML command, logs each row deletion individually (slow on large tables), can be rolled back within a transaction, fires row-level triggers, resets nothing — AUTO_INCREMENT counter stays where it was. TRUNCATE: DDL command, deallocates entire data pages (extremely fast), cannot be rolled back in MySQL (in most contexts), does NOT fire row-level triggers, and resets the AUTO_INCREMENT counter to 1.

Q34. What is a composite primary key? Give an example. ▼

A composite primary key uses two or more columns together as the unique identifier. Neither column alone is necessarily unique — but the combination must be. Commonly used in junction/bridge tables representing many-to-many relationships.

SQL
-- student_id + course_id together = unique enrollment
CREATE TABLE enrollments (
  student_id INT NOT NULL,
  course_id  INT NOT NULL,
  grade      CHAR(2),
  PRIMARY KEY (student_id, course_id),
  FOREIGN KEY (student_id) REFERENCES students(id),
  FOREIGN KEY (course_id)  REFERENCES courses(id)
);
Q35. What does COALESCE do? How is it different from IFNULL? ▼

COALESCE(a, b, c, ...) returns the first non-NULL value from a list of any number of arguments. It is ANSI SQL standard and works in all databases. IFNULL(a, b) is MySQL-specific and takes exactly two arguments. COALESCE is preferred because it is more portable and flexible — you can chain fallbacks. Example: COALESCE(cell, landline, email, 'Unknown') tries four columns in order.

Q36. How do you copy data from one table into another? ▼
SQL
-- Copy all rows into existing table
INSERT INTO customers_backup
SELECT * FROM customers;

-- Copy filtered rows
INSERT INTO premium_customers (id, name, email)
SELECT id, name, email
FROM customers
WHERE lifetime_value > 10000;

-- Create new table AND copy data in one shot (MySQL)
CREATE TABLE customers_backup
AS SELECT * FROM customers;
-- Note: this copies data and column types but NOT constraints/indexes
Q37. What is the difference between IS NULL and = NULL? ▼

= NULL uses equality comparison, but NULL is not a value — it is the absence of a value. Any comparison with NULL returns UNKNOWN (not TRUE or FALSE), so WHERE phone = NULL will never return any rows. IS NULL is the correct SQL operator specifically designed to test for absence of value. Similarly, IS NOT NULL correctly finds non-NULL rows while != NULL returns zero rows.

Q38. How do you retrieve the current date and time in SQL? ▼
SQL
NOW()      -- '2024-11-15 14:32:55' — datetime
CURDATE()  -- '2024-11-15'          — date only
CURTIME()  -- '14:32:55'           — time only
SYSDATE()  -- similar to NOW() but evaluated at execution time

-- Common usage: auto-timestamp on insert
INSERT INTO orders (customer_id, total, created_at)
VALUES (42, 150.00, NOW());
Q39. What is a CASE expression? How does it differ from a CASE statement? ▼

A CASE expression is used inside SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY — it returns a value. A CASE statement is used inside stored procedures — it controls program flow. Both use the same WHEN/THEN/ELSE/END syntax. CASE expressions are evaluated for every row; CASE statements execute a block of code once.

SQL — CASE Expression
-- Simple CASE (equality test)
SELECT name,
  CASE status
    WHEN 1 THEN 'Active'
    WHEN 0 THEN 'Inactive'
    ELSE 'Unknown'
  END AS status_label
FROM users;

-- Searched CASE (boolean conditions)
SELECT name, score,
  CASE
    WHEN score >= 90 THEN 'A'
    WHEN score >= 80 THEN 'B'
    WHEN score >= 70 THEN 'C'
    ELSE 'F'
  END AS grade
FROM students;
Q40. What is the difference between a natural join and an inner join? ▼

An INNER JOIN requires you to explicitly specify the join condition with ON. A NATURAL JOIN automatically joins on all columns with the same name in both tables — no ON clause needed. NATURAL JOIN is convenient but dangerous: if you later add a column with the same name to both tables, the join condition changes silently. Best practice is to always use explicit INNER JOIN with ON for clarity and safety.

Q41. How do you rename a column or table? ▼
SQL
-- Rename a table
RENAME TABLE old_name TO new_name;
-- or
ALTER TABLE old_name RENAME TO new_name;

-- Rename a column (MySQL CHANGE or RENAME COLUMN)
ALTER TABLE users
  CHANGE phone_no phone_number VARCHAR(20); -- must repeat data type

-- MySQL 8.0+ cleaner syntax
ALTER TABLE users
  RENAME COLUMN phone_no TO phone_number;
Q42. What is the LIMIT clause and how does OFFSET work with it? ▼

LIMIT n restricts the number of rows returned. OFFSET m skips the first m rows before returning results. Together they implement basic pagination. Warning: OFFSET is inefficient on large tables because the database must still read and discard all rows before the offset position. For large datasets, use keyset pagination (WHERE id > last_seen_id) instead.

SQL
-- Page 1: rows 1–10
SELECT * FROM products ORDER BY id LIMIT 10 OFFSET 0;
-- Page 2: rows 11–20
SELECT * FROM products ORDER BY id LIMIT 10 OFFSET 10;
-- Formula: OFFSET = (page_number - 1) * page_size
Q43. What is a CROSS JOIN? When would you actually use it? ▼

A CROSS JOIN produces the Cartesian product — every row from table A combined with every row from table B. If A has 10 rows and B has 5, the result has 50 rows. Common legitimate uses: generating all combinations for inventory (sizes × colors × materials), creating a test dataset with all date × product combinations, or building combination pricing matrices. Accidentally using CROSS JOIN on large tables is a classic performance disaster.

SQL
-- Generate all size-color combinations for a product catalog
SELECT
  s.size_name,
  c.color_name,
  CONCAT(s.size_name, '-', c.color_name) AS sku_variant
FROM sizes  s
CROSS JOIN colors c
ORDER BY s.size_name, c.color_name;
Q44. What is referential integrity and how do foreign keys enforce it? ▼

Referential integrity ensures that relationships between tables remain consistent — you cannot have a "child" row that references a non-existent "parent." Foreign keys enforce this in three ways: ON INSERT/UPDATE: the FK value must exist in the referenced table. ON DELETE: RESTRICT (default — block the delete), CASCADE (auto-delete child rows), SET NULL (set FK to NULL), SET DEFAULT (set FK to its default value). Example: deleting a customer with ON DELETE CASCADE automatically deletes all their orders too.

Q45. How do you check if a value exists in a subquery? ▼
SQL
-- EXISTS: returns TRUE if subquery returns any row (fast, short-circuits)
SELECT name FROM customers c
WHERE EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM orders WHERE customer_id = c.id
);

-- IN: value must be in the subquery result list
SELECT name FROM customers
WHERE id IN (SELECT DISTINCT customer_id FROM orders);

-- ANY/SOME: value matches at least one in the subquery
SELECT product_name, price FROM products
WHERE price > ANY (
  SELECT avg_price FROM category_averages
);

-- ALL: value must exceed all values in the subquery
SELECT product_name, price FROM products
WHERE price > ALL (
  SELECT avg_price FROM category_averages
);
Q46. Write a query to count NULL and non-NULL values in a column. ▼
SQL
SELECT
  COUNT(*)                     AS total_rows,
  COUNT(phone)               AS non_null_phones,
  COUNT(*) - COUNT(phone)  AS null_phones,
  ROUND(COUNT(phone) * 100.0 / COUNT(*), 1) AS completeness_pct
FROM users;
Q47. What are scalar, row, table, and correlated subqueries? ▼
  • Scalar subquery: Returns exactly one row, one column. Can be used anywhere a single value is expected. Example: SELECT name, (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees) FROM employees.
  • Row subquery: Returns one row with multiple columns. Used with row comparison operators.
  • Table subquery: Returns multiple rows and columns. Used in FROM clause (derived table) or with IN/EXISTS.
  • Correlated subquery: References a column from the outer query — re-runs for every outer row. Powerful but potentially slow.
Q48. How do you handle multiple INSERT rows in one statement? ▼
SQL
-- Multi-row INSERT: much faster than individual INSERTs
INSERT INTO products (name, price, category)
VALUES
  ('Laptop Pro',   999.99,  'Electronics'),
  ('Wireless Mouse',25.00,  'Electronics'),
  ('Desk Chair',   299.00, 'Furniture'),
  ('Notebook',     5.99,   'Stationery');
-- One network round-trip, one transaction — much more efficient
Q49. What does the DISTINCT keyword do and when should you avoid it? ▼

DISTINCT removes duplicate rows from the result set. It applies to all selected columns together — a row is a duplicate only if ALL column values match. When to avoid it: if you're using DISTINCT to "fix" unexpected duplicates from a JOIN, the real problem is the JOIN logic (wrong join key, missing filter, or data quality issue). Fixing the root cause is always better than papering over it with DISTINCT. DISTINCT also has a performance cost as it requires sorting/hashing the result.

Q50. Write a query that shows a sales summary with percentage share per region. ▼
SQL
SELECT
  c.region,
  COUNT(o.id)                            AS order_count,
  SUM(o.total)                          AS revenue,
  ROUND(SUM(o.total) * 100.0
    / SUM(SUM(o.total)) OVER()           , 1) AS pct_of_total
FROM orders    o
JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.region
ORDER BY revenue DESC;
🟡 Practice & Interview Prep

Q&A — Intermediate (35 Questions)

JOINs, subqueries, aggregates, indexes, views, stored procedures. These appear in most SQL technical interviews.

Theoretical (Q1–Q10)

Q1. Explain all types of JOINs. ▼
  • INNER JOIN: rows matching in BOTH tables. Non-matches excluded.
  • LEFT JOIN: ALL rows from left + matching right. Unmatched right = NULL.
  • RIGHT JOIN: ALL rows from right + matching left. Unmatched left = NULL.
  • FULL OUTER JOIN: All rows from both tables. Unmatched = NULL on either side. (MySQL: use LEFT UNION RIGHT.)
  • CROSS JOIN: Cartesian product — every row of A × every row of B.
  • SELF JOIN: A table joined to itself (hierarchies, comparisons within same table).
Q2. Correlated vs non-correlated subquery? ▼

A non-correlated subquery runs once independently and its result is used by the outer query. A correlated subquery references a column from the outer query, so it re-runs for each row the outer query processes. Correlated subqueries are powerful but can be slow on large tables — often replaceable with a JOIN or window function.

Q3. What is a VIEW? Advantages and limitations? ▼

A VIEW is a saved query acting as a virtual table. It stores the query definition, not the data. Advantages: simplifies complex queries, security (hide sensitive columns), reusability. Limitations: no performance benefit (query reruns each time unless materialized), some views are not updatable (those with GROUP BY, DISTINCT, aggregates, certain JOINs).

Q4. What is an index and how does it work? ▼

An index is a B-tree data structure that enables fast row lookup without a full table scan. Without index: O(n) full scan. With index: O(log n) B-tree traversal. Improves SELECT, WHERE, JOIN, ORDER BY. Slows INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE (index must be maintained). Create indexes on: WHERE columns, JOIN columns, ORDER BY columns, high-cardinality columns.

Q5. Clustered vs non-clustered index? ▼

A clustered index determines physical row order in the table (one per table — typically the PK). Data rows ARE the leaf nodes. Fast for range queries. A non-clustered index is a separate structure storing (indexed_value → row_pointer). Multiple allowed per table. Requires two lookups unless it's a covering index.

Q6. Explain 1NF, 2NF, 3NF. ▼
  • 1NF: Atomic values — no arrays or multi-values in a cell.
  • 2NF: In 1NF + no partial dependencies — every non-key column depends on the full composite PK.
  • 3NF: In 2NF + no transitive dependencies — non-key columns depend only on the PK, not on other non-key columns.
Q7. What is ACID? ▼
  • Atomicity: All operations succeed or all fail — no partial results.
  • Consistency: DB moves from one valid state to another.
  • Isolation: Concurrent transactions don't interfere.
  • Durability: Committed changes survive system failures (written to disk).
Q8. IN vs EXISTS — when to use which? ▼

IN loads all subquery results into memory. Good for small result sets. EXISTS stops at the first match (short-circuits). Better for large subquery results. Critical: NOT IN returns zero rows if the subquery returns any NULL values — use NOT EXISTS instead.

Q9. What is a self-join? Give an example. ▼
SQL — Self-Join
-- Find each employee and their manager
SELECT
  e.name AS employee,
  m.name AS manager
FROM employees e
LEFT JOIN employees m
  ON e.manager_id = m.id;
Q10. How do aggregate functions treat NULLs? ▼

COUNT(*) counts all rows including NULLs. COUNT(col) counts only non-NULL values. SUM/AVG/MIN/MAX all ignore NULLs. Important: AVG(col) ≠ SUM(col)/COUNT(*) when NULLs exist because COUNT(*) includes the NULL rows in the denominator.

Query Practice (Q11–Q35)

Q11. Show each department's salary total as % of company total. ▼
SQL
SELECT department,
  SUM(salary) AS dept_total,
  ROUND(SUM(salary)*100.0/(SELECT SUM(salary) FROM employees),2) AS pct
FROM employees
GROUP BY department
ORDER BY dept_total DESC;
Q12. Find employees earning above their department average (correlated subquery). ▼
SQL — Correlated Subquery
SELECT e1.name, e1.department, e1.salary
FROM employees e1
WHERE e1.salary > (
  SELECT AVG(e2.salary)
  FROM employees e2
  WHERE e2.department = e1.department
)
ORDER BY e1.department, e1.salary DESC;
Q13. INNER JOIN vs LEFT JOIN on orders and customers. ▼
SQL
-- INNER: only orders with a valid customer
SELECT o.id, o.total, c.name
FROM orders o
INNER JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id;

-- LEFT: ALL orders, even orphaned (deleted customer)
SELECT o.id, o.total,
  COALESCE(c.name, 'Deleted Customer') AS customer
FROM orders o
LEFT JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id;
Q14. Find products more expensive than the average price. ▼
SQL
SELECT product_name, price
FROM products
WHERE price > (SELECT AVG(price) FROM products)
ORDER BY price DESC;
Q15. Running total of sales by date. ▼
SQL — Running Total
SELECT
  s1.sale_date, s1.amount,
  (SELECT SUM(s2.amount)
   FROM daily_sales s2
   WHERE s2.sale_date <= s1.sale_date) AS running_total
FROM daily_sales s1
ORDER BY s1.sale_date;
Q16. Delete duplicate rows keeping the lowest id. ▼
SQL
DELETE e1 FROM employees e1
INNER JOIN employees e2
  ON e1.email = e2.email
  AND e1.id > e2.id;
-- Keeps lowest id, deletes higher id duplicates
Q17. Pivot sales data using CASE WHEN. ▼
SQL — Manual Pivot
SELECT
  YEAR(sale_date) AS yr,
  SUM(CASE WHEN MONTH(sale_date)=1  THEN amount ELSE 0 END) AS jan,
  SUM(CASE WHEN MONTH(sale_date)=2  THEN amount ELSE 0 END) AS feb,
  SUM(CASE WHEN MONTH(sale_date)=12 THEN amount ELSE 0 END) AS dec_
FROM sales
GROUP BY YEAR(sale_date);
Q18. Create, use, and drop a VIEW. ▼
SQL — Views
CREATE VIEW public_employees AS
  SELECT id, name, department, hire_date
  FROM employees; -- hides salary column

SELECT * FROM public_employees
WHERE department = 'Engineering';

DROP VIEW public_employees;
Q19. Get most recent order per customer (two methods). ▼
SQL
-- Method 1: Correlated subquery
SELECT o.* FROM orders o
WHERE o.order_date = (
  SELECT MAX(order_date) FROM orders
  WHERE customer_id = o.customer_id
);

-- Method 2: JOIN with grouped subquery (faster)
SELECT o.* FROM orders o
INNER JOIN (
  SELECT customer_id, MAX(order_date) last_order
  FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id
) latest
  ON o.customer_id = latest.customer_id
  AND o.order_date = latest.last_order;
Q20. List all products per category as comma-separated string. ▼
SQL — GROUP_CONCAT
SELECT
  category,
  GROUP_CONCAT(product_name ORDER BY product_name SEPARATOR ', ') AS products
FROM products
GROUP BY category;
Q21–25. CASE WHEN salary bands | Three-table JOIN | Derived table | CREATE INDEX | EXPLAIN ▼
Q21 — CASE WHEN salary bands
SELECT name, salary,
  CASE
    WHEN salary <  30000  THEN 'Entry Level'
    WHEN salary <  60000  THEN 'Mid Level'
    WHEN salary <  100000 THEN 'Senior'
    ELSE 'Executive'
  END AS band
FROM employees;
Q22 — Three-table JOIN
SELECT o.id, c.name, p.product_name, oi.quantity
FROM orders o
JOIN customers   c  ON o.customer_id  = c.id
JOIN order_items oi ON o.id           = oi.order_id
JOIN products    p  ON oi.product_id = p.id;
Q23 — Derived table (subquery in FROM)
SELECT department, ROUND(avg_sal,0) AS avg_salary
FROM (
  SELECT department, AVG(salary) AS avg_sal
  FROM employees GROUP BY department
) dept_avgs
WHERE avg_sal > 60000;
Q24 — CREATE INDEX
CREATE INDEX idx_users_email ON users(email);
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_uq_email ON users(email);
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_cust_date ON orders(customer_id, order_date);
Q25 — EXPLAIN
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 42 AND order_date > '2024-01-01';
-- type=ALL = bad (full scan); type=ref/range = good (index used)
-- rows = estimated scanned rows; lower is better
Q26–30. Subquery in SELECT | Multi-column UPDATE | ROLLBACK | Stored Proc | Trigger ▼
Q26 — Subquery in SELECT
SELECT name, salary,
  (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees) AS co_avg,
  salary - (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees) AS diff
FROM employees;
Q27 — Multi-column UPDATE
UPDATE employees
SET
  salary     = salary * 1.10,
  updated_at = NOW()
WHERE department = 'Engineering'
  AND hire_date < '2023-01-01';
Q28 — Transaction with ROLLBACK
START TRANSACTION;
  UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 1000 WHERE id = 1;
  UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 1000 WHERE id = 2;
COMMIT; -- or ROLLBACK if anything fails
Q29 — Stored Procedure
DELIMITER $$
CREATE PROCEDURE GetDeptEmployees(IN dept VARCHAR(50))
BEGIN
  SELECT name, salary FROM employees
  WHERE department = dept ORDER BY salary DESC;
END$$
DELIMITER ;
CALL GetDeptEmployees('Engineering');

A TRIGGER automatically executes SQL in response to INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE. Runs BEFORE or AFTER the event. Use cases: audit logs, auto-calculated fields, business rule enforcement, cascading updates. Example: after INSERT on orders, auto-decrement stock in products table.

Q31–35. FULL OUTER JOIN | CROSS JOIN | UPSERT | Partitioning | Top 5 Performance Tips ▼
Q31 — FULL OUTER JOIN (MySQL)
SELECT c.name, s.name AS supplier
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN suppliers s ON c.id = s.id
UNION
SELECT c.name, s.name
FROM customers c
RIGHT JOIN suppliers s ON c.id = s.id;
Q32 — CROSS JOIN
-- All size-color combinations
SELECT s.size_name, c.color_name
FROM sizes s CROSS JOIN colors c;
Q33 — UPSERT
INSERT INTO product_stats (product_id, view_count)
VALUES (101, 1)
ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE
  view_count = view_count + 1;

Table partitioning splits a large table into smaller physical pieces while keeping a single logical view. Types: RANGE (by date), LIST (by discrete value), HASH (distributed). Queries touching only one partition skip the rest — huge speedup on 100M+ row time-series tables.

  • Index columns in WHERE, JOIN, ORDER BY clauses
  • Use EXPLAIN to spot full table scans (type=ALL)
  • Specify columns in SELECT instead of SELECT *
  • Avoid wrapping indexed columns in functions in WHERE
  • Use LIMIT to cap result sizes; use keyset pagination for deep pages

Additional Practice (Q36–Q50)

Q36. What is a TRANSACTION? Explain with a real example. ▼

A transaction is a sequence of SQL operations that are treated as a single unit of work — all must succeed, or all must be rolled back. The classic example is a bank transfer: debit one account AND credit another. If the credit step fails after the debit, you'd lose money. Wrapping both in a transaction ensures atomicity.

SQL — Bank Transfer Transaction
START TRANSACTION;
  -- Debit sender
  UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 5000
  WHERE id = 101 AND balance >= 5000;

  -- Credit receiver
  UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 5000
  WHERE id = 202;

COMMIT;   -- both succeed: persist
-- ROLLBACK;  -- if anything fails: undo everything
Q37. Write a stored procedure with conditional logic and return a result. ▼
SQL — Stored Procedure
DELIMITER $$
CREATE PROCEDURE ClassifyEmployee(IN p_id INT)
BEGIN
  DECLARE v_salary DECIMAL(10,2);
  DECLARE v_grade  VARCHAR(10);

  SELECT salary INTO v_salary
  FROM   employees WHERE id = p_id;

  IF     v_salary >= 100000 THEN SET v_grade = 'A';
  ELSEIF v_salary >=  60000 THEN SET v_grade = 'B';
  ELSE                           SET v_grade = 'C';
  END IF;

  SELECT v_salary AS salary, v_grade AS grade;
END$$
DELIMITER ;
CALL ClassifyEmployee(42);
Q38. What is a composite key? When would you use one? ▼

A composite key is a primary key made up of two or more columns. No single column uniquely identifies a row, but the combination does. Used for junction/bridge tables (many-to-many relationships) and tables where the natural unique identifier is multi-column (e.g., attendance per student per date, scores per player per game per round).

SQL
-- A student can attend many courses; a course has many students
CREATE TABLE enrollments (
  student_id  INT,
  course_id   INT,
  enrolled_on DATE,
  grade       CHAR(1),
  PRIMARY KEY (student_id, course_id)   -- composite PK
);
Q39. What is query execution order and why does it matter for aliases? ▼

SQL executes logically in this order: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY → LIMIT. Column aliases defined in SELECT are not available in WHERE because WHERE runs before SELECT. However, aliases ARE available in ORDER BY. This trips up many developers who write WHERE alias_name = value and get an error.

SQL
-- ❌ FAILS: WHERE runs before SELECT, alias unknown
SELECT salary * 12 AS annual
FROM employees
WHERE annual > 600000;

-- ✅ WORKS: use HAVING after GROUP BY, or repeat the expression
SELECT salary * 12 AS annual
FROM employees
WHERE salary * 12 > 600000;

-- ✅ WORKS with ORDER BY (runs after SELECT)
SELECT salary * 12 AS annual
FROM employees
ORDER BY annual DESC;
Q40. Write a query for a many-to-many relationship — show all tags per article. ▼
SQL — Many-to-Many JOIN
-- Schema: articles ←→ article_tags ←→ tags
SELECT
  a.title,
  GROUP_CONCAT(t.name ORDER BY t.name SEPARATOR ', ') AS tags,
  COUNT(t.id) AS tag_count
FROM articles     a
JOIN article_tags  at ON a.id  = at.article_id
JOIN tags          t  ON at.tag_id = t.id
GROUP BY a.id, a.title
ORDER BY tag_count DESC;
Q41. What is ROLLUP? Show a totals/subtotals query. ▼

GROUP BY WITH ROLLUP adds extra summary rows to the result — subtotals for each grouping level plus a grand total. The grand total row has NULL in the grouping columns.

SQL — ROLLUP
SELECT
  COALESCE(category, 'ALL CATEGORIES') AS category,
  COALESCE(sub_cat,  'All Sub-Cats')    AS sub_category,
  SUM(revenue)                           AS total_revenue
FROM sales
GROUP BY category, sub_cat WITH ROLLUP;
-- Produces: rows per (category, sub_cat), then per category, then grand total
Q42. What is the difference between CHAR, VARCHAR, and TEXT? ▼
  • CHAR(n): Fixed-length, n bytes always stored (padded with spaces). Fast for exact-length strings like country codes, status flags. Max 255.
  • VARCHAR(n): Variable-length, stores only used bytes + 1-2 byte overhead. Best for emails, names, URLs. Up to 65,535 bytes (limited by row size).
  • TEXT: Variable-length for large text (up to 65,535 bytes). Stored outside the main row. Cannot have a DEFAULT value. Cannot be fully indexed without a prefix. Use for article bodies, descriptions, JSON strings. Subtypes: TINYTEXT (255), TEXT, MEDIUMTEXT (16MB), LONGTEXT (4GB).
Q43. Write a query to calculate a percentage distribution. ▼
SQL — Percentage Distribution
SELECT
  status,
  COUNT(*) AS count,
  ROUND(COUNT(*) * 100.0 / SUM(COUNT(*)) OVER(), 1) AS pct
FROM orders
GROUP BY status
ORDER BY count DESC;
Q44. What is a NATURAL JOIN and why is it risky? ▼

A NATURAL JOIN automatically joins tables on all columns with the same name — you don't specify an ON condition. It seems convenient but is dangerous in production: if someone adds a column with the same name to both tables (like updated_at), the join condition silently changes and you get wrong results. Always prefer explicit JOIN ON conditions for predictability and maintainability.

SQL
-- NATURAL JOIN (implicit, risky)
SELECT * FROM orders NATURAL JOIN customers;

-- Explicit INNER JOIN (safe, always preferred)
SELECT o.*, c.name
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id;
Q45. Explain window functions LEAD and LAG with an example. ▼

LAG(col, n) returns the value of col from n rows before the current row in the window. LEAD(col, n) returns the value n rows ahead. Both are commonly used for period-over-period comparisons without a self-join.

SQL — LEAD & LAG
SELECT
  sale_date, revenue,
  LAG(revenue, 1) OVER (ORDER BY sale_date) AS prev_day,
  LEAD(revenue, 1) OVER (ORDER BY sale_date) AS next_day,
  revenue - LAG(revenue,1) OVER (ORDER BY sale_date) AS day_over_day_change
FROM daily_sales
ORDER BY sale_date;
