Q46 — Batch INSERT
-- Insert multiple rows in one statement (much faster than individual INSERTs)
INSERT INTO products (name, price, category)
VALUES
  ('Laptop Pro',  89999, 'Electronics'),
  ('USB Hub',      1299,  'Accessories'),
  ('Webcam HD',    3499,  'Electronics'),
  ('Desk Lamp',    799,   'Furniture');
Q47 — EXPLAIN ANALYZE (MySQL 8+ / PostgreSQL)
-- EXPLAIN shows the plan; EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually executes and shows real timings
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT c.name, COUNT(o.id) AS orders
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id
GROUP BY c.id;
-- Shows: estimated rows vs actual rows, execution time per step
Q48 — EXCEPT / MINUS (rows in A but not B)
-- EXCEPT (PostgreSQL/SQL Server) — MySQL equivalent uses LEFT JOIN anti-join
-- "Customers who placed orders in 2023 but NOT in 2024"

-- PostgreSQL EXCEPT:
SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE YEAR(order_date)=2023
EXCEPT
SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE YEAR(order_date)=2024;

-- MySQL equivalent (LEFT JOIN anti-join):
SELECT DISTINCT a.customer_id
FROM orders a
LEFT JOIN orders b
  ON a.customer_id = b.customer_id
  AND YEAR(b.order_date) = 2024
WHERE YEAR(a.order_date) = 2023
  AND b.customer_id IS NULL;
Q49 — Simple Recursive CTE (number series)
-- Generate numbers 1 to 10 using recursive CTE
WITH RECURSIVE nums AS (
  SELECT 1 AS n                              -- anchor
  UNION ALL
  SELECT n + 1 FROM nums WHERE n < 10      -- recursive
)
SELECT * FROM nums;
Q50 — Stored Function in SELECT
DELIMITER $$
CREATE FUNCTION FormatINR(amount DECIMAL(15,2))
RETURNS VARCHAR(30)
DETERMINISTIC
BEGIN
  RETURN CONCAT('₹ ', FORMAT(amount, 2));
END$$
DELIMITER ;

SELECT
  product_name,
  FormatINR(price)  AS formatted_price
FROM products;

Additional Theory (Q36–Q50)

Q36. What is query execution plan and how do you read it? ▼

A query execution plan (QEP) is the database engine's step-by-step strategy for executing a query. You access it via EXPLAIN (MySQL) or EXPLAIN ANALYZE (PostgreSQL). Key columns to read:

  • type: Access method — ALL (full scan, bad) → index → range → ref → eq_ref → const (optimal)
  • key: Which index is being used (NULL = no index)
  • rows: Estimated rows the engine will examine
  • Extra: "Using index" (covering index, excellent), "Using filesort" (extra sort step, add index), "Using temporary" (temp table, expensive)
Q37. What is a database transaction? Explain with a real scenario. ▼

A transaction groups multiple SQL statements into one atomic unit. Real scenario: e-commerce checkout. When a customer places an order, three things must happen together: (1) insert into orders table, (2) insert order items, (3) decrement stock. If stock update fails after the order was inserted, you'd have a ghost order. Wrapping all three in a transaction ensures either everything succeeds (COMMIT) or nothing persists (ROLLBACK). This is the Atomicity part of ACID.

Q38. What is the difference between CHAR, VARCHAR, and TEXT? ▼
TypeStorageMax SizeIndexed?Best For
CHAR(n)Fixed n bytes255 charsYesFixed-length: country codes, hashes, flags
VARCHAR(n)Variable + 1-2 bytes65,535 charsYesVariable: names, emails, titles
TEXTVariable, off-row65,535 charsPartial onlyLong content: descriptions, comments, HTML
LONGTEXTVariable, off-row4 GBPartial onlyArticles, JSON blobs, logs
Q39. What is the difference between TRUNCATE and DELETE? When to use each? ▼

Use DELETE when: you need to remove specific rows (with WHERE), need the operation logged row-by-row for recovery, need triggers to fire, or need to be able to rollback. Use TRUNCATE when: you need to clear the entire table as fast as possible, don't need row-by-row logging, don't need triggers, and auto-increment should reset to 1. TRUNCATE is 10-100x faster on large tables because it deallocates entire data pages rather than deleting rows individually.

Q40. Explain the concept of cardinality in SQL. ▼

Cardinality refers to the uniqueness of values in a column. High cardinality = many unique values (e.g., user_id, email — good candidates for indexing). Low cardinality = few unique values (e.g., boolean is_active, status with 3 values — poor index candidates). In JOINs, cardinality also describes the relationship: 1:1, 1:N, M:N. The query optimizer uses column cardinality statistics to choose the best execution plan — it prefers high-cardinality index lookups over low-cardinality full-scan patterns.

Q41. What is a covering index? How does it speed up queries? ▼

A covering index includes all columns needed by a query, so the database engine can answer the query entirely from the index without touching the base table rows. This eliminates the "row fetch" step — instead of two I/O operations (index lookup → row fetch), only one is needed. EXPLAIN shows "Using index" in the Extra column when a covering index is active. Example: if a query SELECTs order_date, total and WHERE filters on customer_id, an index on (customer_id, order_date, total) is fully covering.

Q42. What is a deadlock? How does MySQL resolve it? ▼

A deadlock is a circular wait condition where transaction A holds a lock on row 1 and waits for row 2, while transaction B holds row 2 and waits for row 1. Neither can proceed. MySQL's InnoDB engine detects deadlocks automatically by looking for wait cycles in its lock graph. When detected, it automatically selects the "cheaper" transaction to roll back (based on undo log size) and returns error 1213 to that session. The other transaction then completes. You prevent deadlocks by: accessing tables/rows in a consistent order across all transactions, keeping transactions short, and using row-level locks instead of table locks where possible.

Q43. What is the difference between a function and a stored procedure? ▼
AspectStored ProcedureStored Function
InvocationCALL ProcName()SELECT FuncName() or inline in SQL
Return value0 or many (via OUT params)Exactly one scalar value
Used in SELECT?NoYes
DML (write)?Yes — full INSERT/UPDATE/DELETERestricted (read-only default)
TransactionsSTART/COMMIT/ROLLBACK supportedNot supported
Q44. What is partitioning? What are its types? ▼

Table partitioning divides a large table into smaller physical pieces (partitions) while maintaining a single logical view. The DB can skip entire partitions that don't satisfy a query's WHERE clause (partition pruning). Types: RANGE — partitions based on column value ranges (e.g., by year); LIST — partitions based on discrete values (e.g., by country); HASH — distributes rows evenly using a hash function (e.g., HASH(customer_id)); KEY — like HASH but uses MySQL's internal hash algorithm. Best for tables with 100M+ rows queried by date ranges or region.

Q45. What is the N+1 problem and how do you fix it? ▼

N+1 occurs when code runs 1 query to fetch N parent rows, then N separate queries for each child. Example: fetch 100 customers (1 query), then for each customer fetch their orders (100 queries) = 101 queries total. The fix is eager loading — use a JOIN to fetch parents and children in one query, or use an IN clause to batch-fetch children for all parents at once. In ORMs: use includes (Rails), select_related/prefetch_related (Django), or JOIN FETCH (JPA) to prevent lazy-loading loops.

Q46. What is a schema migration? Best practices? ▼

A schema migration is a versioned, scripted change to a database structure (adding columns, changing types, creating tables). Best practices: (1) Always add nullable columns first, backfill data in batches, then add NOT NULL constraint — never add NOT NULL without DEFAULT to a large live table (locks entire table). (2) Use migration tools (Flyway, Liquibase, Alembic) for version control. (3) Make migrations idempotent — safe to re-run. (4) Test on a production clone first. (5) For large tables (>10M rows), use online schema change tools (gh-ost, pt-online-schema-change) that swap shadow tables atomically without locking.

Q47–50. Window function theory, CTE best practices, locking types, isolation levels ▼

Q47 — Window functions: They compute a result across a "window" of rows related to the current row without collapsing those rows. PARTITION BY divides rows into groups (like GROUP BY but without collapsing). ORDER BY within OVER() defines the row order for running calculations. The ROWS/RANGE BETWEEN clause defines the window frame for aggregations like moving averages.

Q48 — CTE best practices: Name CTEs descriptively (revenue_by_month, not cte1). Use multiple CTEs in sequence for complex multi-step transformations. Avoid CTEs for single-use expressions — a subquery is simpler. In PostgreSQL, use WITH ... AS MATERIALIZED only when the CTE is referenced many times and you want to force a single execution.

Q49 — Lock types: Row-level locks (most granular, least conflict), page-level locks (medium), table-level locks (coarsest, most conflict). Shared lock (S-lock): multiple readers allowed, no writes. Exclusive lock (X-lock): one writer, no readers. Intent locks: signal at table/page level what lock is held at row level.

Q50 — Isolation levels recap: READ UNCOMMITTED (dirty reads possible), READ COMMITTED (no dirty reads, default in PostgreSQL), REPEATABLE READ (no non-repeatable reads, default in MySQL InnoDB), SERIALIZABLE (no phantom reads, full isolation, slowest). Higher isolation = fewer anomalies but more lock contention and reduced throughput.

Additional Query Practice (Q36–Q55)

Q36. Write a query to identify orders placed during business hours (9 AM – 6 PM). ▼
SQL
SELECT
  id, customer_id, created_at, total,
  HOUR(created_at) AS hour_of_day
FROM orders
WHERE HOUR(created_at) BETWEEN 9 AND 17  -- 9 AM to 5:59 PM
ORDER BY created_at;
Q37. Find customers who placed orders in every month of 2024. ▼
SQL
SELECT
  customer_id,
  COUNT(DISTINCT MONTH(order_date)) AS months_ordered
FROM orders
WHERE YEAR(order_date) = 2024
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT MONTH(order_date)) = 12;
-- 12 = all 12 months
Q38. Display running total of stock quantities as products are added. ▼
SQL — Running Total with Window Function
SELECT
  id,
  product_name,
  stock_qty,
  SUM(stock_qty) OVER (
    ORDER BY id
    ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
  ) AS running_stock_total
FROM products
ORDER BY id;
Q39. Find pairs of products frequently bought together (market basket). ▼
SQL — Product Pairs
SELECT
  p1.product_name AS product_a,
  p2.product_name AS product_b,
  COUNT(DISTINCT oi1.order_id) AS times_bought_together
FROM order_items oi1
JOIN order_items oi2
  ON  oi1.order_id   = oi2.order_id
  AND oi1.product_id < oi2.product_id   -- avoid self-pairs and duplicates
JOIN products p1 ON oi1.product_id = p1.id
JOIN products p2 ON oi2.product_id = p2.id
GROUP BY p1.product_name, p2.product_name
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT oi1.order_id) >= 5
ORDER BY times_bought_together DESC
LIMIT 20;
Q40. Find the day of week with the highest average order value. ▼
SQL
SELECT
  DAYNAME(order_date)       AS day_of_week,
  COUNT(*)                   AS order_count,
  ROUND(AVG(total), 2)      AS avg_order_value,
  SUM(total)                 AS total_revenue
FROM orders
GROUP BY DAYOFWEEK(order_date), DAYNAME(order_date)
ORDER BY avg_order_value DESC;
Q41–45. Employee tenure analysis | Cohort retention | Inventory below reorder | Multi-step CTE | LEAD for next order ▼
Q41 — Employee Tenure Buckets
SELECT
  name, hire_date,
  TIMESTAMPDIFF(YEAR, hire_date, CURDATE()) AS years_tenure,
  CASE
    WHEN TIMESTAMPDIFF(YEAR, hire_date, CURDATE()) < 1  THEN 'New (<1yr)'
    WHEN TIMESTAMPDIFF(YEAR, hire_date, CURDATE()) < 3  THEN 'Junior (1-3yr)'
    WHEN TIMESTAMPDIFF(YEAR, hire_date, CURDATE()) < 7  THEN 'Mid (3-7yr)'
    ELSE 'Senior (7yr+)'
  END AS tenure_bucket
FROM employees
ORDER BY years_tenure DESC;
Q42 — Products below reorder level
SELECT
  product_name, category,
  stock_qty,
  reorder_level,
  reorder_level - stock_qty AS units_to_order
FROM products
WHERE stock_qty <= reorder_level
  AND is_active = 1
ORDER BY units_to_order DESC;
Q43 — LEAD: days until next order per customer
SELECT
  customer_id,
  order_date         AS this_order,
  LEAD(order_date) OVER (
    PARTITION BY customer_id
    ORDER BY order_date
  )                    AS next_order,
  DATEDIFF(
    LEAD(order_date) OVER (
      PARTITION BY customer_id
      ORDER BY order_date
    ),
    order_date
  ) AS days_to_next_order
FROM orders
ORDER BY customer_id, order_date;
Q44 — Multi-step CTE: monthly cohort size
WITH
first_orders AS (
  SELECT
    customer_id,
    MIN(order_date) AS first_order_date
  FROM orders
  GROUP BY customer_id
),
cohort_sizes AS (
  SELECT
    DATE_FORMAT(first_order_date, '%Y-%m') AS cohort_month,
    COUNT(*) AS new_customers
  FROM first_orders
  GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT * FROM cohort_sizes
ORDER BY cohort_month;
Q45 — Count distinct active users per week
SELECT
  YEARWEEK(logged_in_at, 1) AS iso_week,
  DATE(MIN(logged_in_at))    AS week_start,
  COUNT(DISTINCT user_id)   AS wau  -- weekly active users
FROM user_logins
GROUP BY YEARWEEK(logged_in_at, 1)
ORDER BY iso_week;
Q46–55. SCD Type 2 query | Percentile per department | Sales funnel | New vs returning customers | DAU/WAU/MAU ▼
Q46 — Percentile rank of salary within department
SELECT
  name, department, salary,
  ROUND(PERCENT_RANK() OVER (
    PARTITION BY department
    ORDER BY salary
  ) * 100, 1) AS dept_percentile
FROM employees;
Q47 — New vs returning customers this month
WITH cust_orders AS (
  SELECT
    customer_id,
    MIN(order_date) AS first_order
  FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id
)
SELECT
  CASE
    WHEN DATE_FORMAT(first_order,'%Y-%m') = DATE_FORMAT(NOW(),'%Y-%m')
      THEN 'New'
    ELSE 'Returning'
  END AS customer_type,
  COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) AS count
FROM cust_orders GROUP BY 1;
Q48 — DAU, WAU, MAU in one query
SELECT
  COUNT(DISTINCT CASE
    WHEN DATE(logged_in_at) = CURDATE()
    THEN user_id END)    AS dau,
  COUNT(DISTINCT CASE
    WHEN logged_in_at >= DATE_SUB(CURDATE(), INTERVAL 7 DAY)
    THEN user_id END)    AS wau,
  COUNT(DISTINCT CASE
    WHEN logged_in_at >= DATE_SUB(CURDATE(), INTERVAL 30 DAY)
    THEN user_id END)    AS mau
FROM user_logins;

More Intermediate Questions (Q36–Q55)

Q36. Explain the difference between a clustered and a non-clustered index with an example. ▼

A clustered index determines the physical order of rows in the table — data rows ARE the leaf nodes of the B-tree. There can be only one per table (the PRIMARY KEY in InnoDB). Range scans are fast because physically adjacent rows are close on disk. A non-clustered index is a separate B-tree structure that stores indexed values + pointers (row IDs/PKs) back to the actual rows. Multiple allowed per table. Requires two lookups: one to find the pointer, one to fetch the row (unless a covering index eliminates the second step).

Q37. What are window functions and how do they differ from regular aggregates? ▼

Regular aggregates (with GROUP BY) collapse multiple rows into one per group — the original rows are lost. Window functions perform calculations across a "window" of related rows but preserve all rows in the output — each row gets an additional computed column. The OVER() clause defines the window. Window functions cannot be used in WHERE (use a subquery/CTE to filter on window results).

SQL — Window vs GROUP BY
-- GROUP BY: collapses rows — one result per dept
SELECT department, AVG(salary) AS avg_sal
FROM employees
GROUP BY department;

-- Window: keeps all rows, adds avg as a column on each row
SELECT
  name, department, salary,
  AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY department) AS dept_avg,
  salary - AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY department) AS diff_from_avg
FROM employees;
Q38. How does PARTITION BY differ from GROUP BY? ▼

Both divide rows into groups for calculations. GROUP BY reduces multiple rows into one summary row per group — you lose individual row details. PARTITION BY (inside OVER) divides rows into groups for window calculations but keeps every row visible. PARTITION BY is only valid inside window function OVER clauses — it never appears in a standalone position like GROUP BY does.

Q39. Write a query to get the 3 highest-paid employees in each department. ▼
SQL
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT
    name, department, salary,
    DENSE_RANK() OVER (
      PARTITION BY department
      ORDER BY salary DESC
    ) AS rnk
  FROM employees
)
SELECT name, department, salary, rnk
FROM  ranked
WHERE rnk <= 3
ORDER BY department, rnk;
Q40. What is a CTE and how is it different from a subquery? ▼

A CTE (Common Table Expression) is defined with the WITH clause before a SELECT and can be referenced by name within that query. A subquery is embedded directly inside another query. Key differences: CTEs are named and can be referenced multiple times in the same query (write once, use many); CTEs support recursion (WITH RECURSIVE); CTEs improve readability, especially with multiple levels of logic; subqueries are better for one-time simple lookups. Both are not persisted — they exist only for the duration of the query.

Q41. Write a query to calculate a running total using a window function. ▼
SQL
SELECT
  sale_date,
  amount,
  SUM(amount) OVER (
    ORDER BY sale_date
    ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
  ) AS running_total,
  SUM(amount) OVER (
    PARTITION BY MONTH(sale_date)
    ORDER BY sale_date
  ) AS monthly_running_total
FROM daily_sales
ORDER BY sale_date;
Q42. What is an execution plan? How do you force a specific index? ▼

An execution plan is the optimizer's strategy for running a query — which indexes to use, join order, sort methods. EXPLAIN shows the plan. The optimizer usually makes the right choice, but occasionally picks a bad plan (e.g., on stale statistics). You can hint or force index usage with USE INDEX, FORCE INDEX, or IGNORE INDEX.

SQL
-- View execution plan
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 42 AND status = 'shipped';

-- Suggest an index
SELECT * FROM orders
USE INDEX (idx_orders_customer)
WHERE customer_id = 42;

-- Force an index (override optimizer completely)
SELECT * FROM orders
FORCE INDEX (idx_orders_customer)
WHERE customer_id = 42;
Q43. How does GROUP_CONCAT work? What are its options? ▼
SQL
-- Basic: comma-separated list
SELECT department,
  GROUP_CONCAT(name) AS employee_list
FROM employees
GROUP BY department;

-- With ORDER BY + custom SEPARATOR
SELECT department,
  GROUP_CONCAT(name ORDER BY salary DESC SEPARATOR ' | ') AS by_salary
FROM employees
GROUP BY department;

-- With DISTINCT (no duplicates)
SELECT customer_id,
  GROUP_CONCAT(DISTINCT product_category ORDER BY product_category) AS categories
FROM orders o
JOIN order_items oi ON o.id = oi.order_id
JOIN products    p  ON oi.product_id = p.id
GROUP BY customer_id;
Q44. Write a query to find customers who ordered every product in a given set. ▼
SQL — Relational Division
-- Customers who ordered ALL products in category 'Electronics'
WITH elec_products AS (
  SELECT id FROM products WHERE category = 'Electronics'
),
customer_elec AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT o.customer_id, oi.product_id
  FROM orders      o
  JOIN order_items oi ON o.id = oi.order_id
  WHERE oi.product_id IN (SELECT id FROM elec_products)
)
SELECT customer_id
FROM  customer_elec
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT product_id) = (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM elec_products);
Q45. How do you find records that exist in one table but not another (set difference)? ▼
SQL — Three Methods
-- Method 1: LEFT JOIN anti-join (fastest in most cases)
SELECT a.* FROM table_a a
LEFT JOIN table_b b ON a.id = b.id
WHERE b.id IS NULL;

-- Method 2: NOT EXISTS
SELECT * FROM table_a a
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM table_b WHERE id = a.id
);

-- Method 3: EXCEPT (PostgreSQL, SQL Server — not MySQL)
SELECT id FROM table_a
EXCEPT
SELECT id FROM table_b;
Q46. Explain the difference between RANK, DENSE_RANK, and ROW_NUMBER with a worked example. ▼
SQL
SELECT
  name, score,
  ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY score DESC) AS row_num,
  RANK()       OVER (ORDER BY score DESC) AS rank_,
  DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY score DESC) AS dense_rank_
FROM quiz_results;
Output for scores: 95, 90, 90, 85
namescorerow_numrankdense_rank
Alice95111
Bob90222
Carol90322
Dave8544 (skipped 3)3 (no skip)
Q47. How does the HAVING clause filter on aggregate conditions? Write an example. ▼

HAVING is evaluated after GROUP BY and aggregation — it is the only place where you can filter based on aggregate function results. WHERE cannot reference aggregates because it executes before aggregation happens.

SQL
-- Categories where average price exceeds 100 AND have 5+ products
SELECT
  category,
  COUNT(*) AS product_count,
  ROUND(AVG(price), 2) AS avg_price
FROM products
WHERE is_active = TRUE         -- filters rows BEFORE aggregation
GROUP BY category
HAVING AVG(price) > 100      -- filters groups AFTER aggregation
   AND COUNT(*) >= 5
ORDER BY avg_price DESC;
Q48. Write a query to show employee number, name, and number of direct reports for each manager. ▼
SQL — Self-Join for Org Data
SELECT
  m.id         AS manager_id,
  m.name       AS manager_name,
  m.department AS department,
  COUNT(e.id)  AS direct_reports
FROM      employees m
LEFT JOIN employees e ON e.manager_id = m.id
GROUP BY m.id, m.name, m.department
HAVING   COUNT(e.id) > 0       -- only show actual managers
ORDER BY direct_reports DESC;
Q49. What is EXPLAIN ANALYZE and how does it differ from EXPLAIN? ▼

EXPLAIN shows the optimizer's estimated execution plan — what it plans to do. EXPLAIN ANALYZE (PostgreSQL) or EXPLAIN FORMAT=JSON (MySQL 8.0+) actually runs the query and shows the real execution statistics — actual rows processed, actual time taken, number of loops. This reveals when the optimizer's estimates were wrong (e.g., estimated 10 rows but scanned 1 million). Always use EXPLAIN ANALYZE on a read replica or development environment, never in production on slow queries.

Q50. Write a stored procedure that accepts a table name and returns row count dynamically. ▼
SQL — Dynamic SQL in Procedure
DELIMITER $$
CREATE PROCEDURE GetTableRowCount(IN p_table VARCHAR(100))
BEGIN
  SET @sql = CONCAT('SELECT COUNT(*) AS row_count FROM ', p_table);
  PREPARE stmt FROM @sql;
  EXECUTE stmt;
  DEALLOCATE PREPARE stmt;
END$$
DELIMITER ;

CALL GetTableRowCount('orders');
CALL GetTableRowCount('customers');

Dynamic SQL via CONCAT is vulnerable to SQL injection if the table name comes from untrusted user input. Always validate or whitelist table names against a known list before using in dynamic SQL.

Q51. What is a transaction savepoint? Write an example. ▼
SQL
START TRANSACTION;

  INSERT INTO orders (customer_id, total) VALUES (42, 299.00);
  SAVEPOINT sp_order;   -- checkpoint after order insert

  INSERT INTO payments (order_id, amount) VALUES (LAST_INSERT_ID(), 299.00);
  -- Simulate payment failure
  ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT sp_order;
  -- Order still in transaction, payment rolled back
  -- Can retry payment with different method

  INSERT INTO payments (order_id, method, amount)
  VALUES (LAST_INSERT_ID(), 'card', 299.00);

COMMIT;  -- both order and retried payment committed
Q52. What is denormalization? When is it acceptable? ▼

Denormalization is the deliberate introduction of redundancy into a database schema to improve read performance. Instead of joining 6 tables to get a customer's order summary, you store a pre-computed order_count column directly on the customer record. Acceptable when: query latency is measurably too slow and no index can fix it; data is read far more often than it changes; the redundant data is easily maintained (via triggers or application logic). Common in data warehouses (star schemas), analytics tables, and caching layers. Never denormalize without first proving that normalized queries with proper indexes are too slow.

Q53. Write a query to detect and count orphaned records (FK violations). ▼
SQL
-- Orders with no matching customer (orphaned orders)
SELECT
  COUNT(*) AS orphaned_orders
FROM orders o
LEFT JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE c.id IS NULL;

-- Show the actual orphaned records
SELECT
  o.id          AS order_id,
  o.customer_id AS missing_customer,
  o.total,
  o.order_date
FROM orders o
LEFT JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE c.id IS NULL
ORDER BY o.order_date DESC;
Q54. Write a query using LEAD and LAG to compare each sale with the previous and next day. ▼
SQL
SELECT
  sale_date,
  amount                                                              AS today,
  LAG(amount)  OVER (ORDER BY sale_date)                            AS yesterday,
  LEAD(amount) OVER (ORDER BY sale_date)                            AS tomorrow,
  amount - LAG(amount) OVER (ORDER BY sale_date)                   AS day_over_day_change,
  ROUND(
    (amount - LAG(amount) OVER (ORDER BY sale_date)) * 100.0
    / NULLIF(LAG(amount) OVER (ORDER BY sale_date), 0), 1)            AS pct_change
FROM  daily_sales
ORDER BY sale_date;
Q55. What is an inline view (derived table)? Write a practical example. ▼

An inline view (derived table) is a subquery used in the FROM clause — it is materialized on-the-fly and given an alias to reference in the outer query. Unlike CTEs, derived tables cannot be referenced more than once. They are useful for computing aggregates first, then filtering or joining on those results.

SQL
-- Find departments where average salary exceeds the company median
SELECT
  dept_avgs.department,
  dept_avgs.avg_salary,
  company.median_salary
FROM
  -- Derived table 1: per-department averages
  (
    SELECT department, ROUND(AVG(salary),0) AS avg_salary
    FROM employees
    GROUP BY department
  ) dept_avgs,
  -- Derived table 2: company-level median (scalar)
  (
    SELECT AVG(salary) AS median_salary
    FROM employees
  ) company
WHERE dept_avgs.avg_salary > company.median_salary
ORDER BY dept_avgs.avg_salary DESC;
🔴 Practice & Interview Prep

Q&A — Advanced (40 Questions)

Window functions, CTEs, recursion, optimization, transactions, and classic interview scenarios from top tech companies.

Theoretical (Q1–Q10)

Q1. Window functions vs GROUP BY — what is the difference? ▼

GROUP BY collapses rows into one per group (destructive). Window functions add a computed column to every row without reducing row count. Both can compute aggregates, but window functions preserve all rows. Syntax: function() OVER (PARTITION BY col ORDER BY col ROWS/RANGE BETWEEN...). Examples: ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK, LEAD, LAG, SUM (running total), AVG (moving average), FIRST_VALUE, LAST_VALUE, NTILE.

Q2. RANK vs DENSE_RANK vs ROW_NUMBER — how do they differ on ties? ▼
salaryROW_NUMBERRANKDENSE_RANK
90000111
80000222
80000322
70000443
  • ROW_NUMBER: Unique sequential — ties arbitrarily numbered
  • RANK: Ties same rank, then skips (1,2,2,4)
  • DENSE_RANK: Ties same rank, no skip (1,2,2,3)
Q3. CTE vs subquery — when to prefer each? ▼

Use CTE when: the same result is referenced multiple times; logic is multi-level and would deeply nest subqueries; you need recursion. CTEs improve readability significantly. Subqueries are fine for simple one-time use. Performance: most databases optimize similarly, but PostgreSQL can materialize CTEs which may hurt performance if the CTE result is large.

Q4. What is a recursive CTE? When is it used? ▼

A recursive CTE has an anchor member (base case) and a recursive member (references itself) joined by UNION ALL. Runs iteratively until no new rows. Used for: org chart traversal (employee → manager → CEO), tree/category hierarchies, generating number sequences, graph traversal. Always include a termination condition to prevent infinite loops.

Q5. What are the four SQL isolation levels? ▼
  • READ UNCOMMITTED: Dirty reads allowed. Sees uncommitted data. Fastest but dangerous.
  • READ COMMITTED: Only sees committed data. Prevents dirty reads.
  • REPEATABLE READ: Same query returns same results within a transaction. MySQL InnoDB default.
  • SERIALIZABLE: Full isolation — slowest, safest. No concurrency anomalies.
Q6. What is query optimization? What techniques do you use? ▼
  • EXPLAIN / EXPLAIN ANALYZE: Identify full scans, missing indexes, join order
  • Proper indexing: WHERE, JOIN, ORDER BY columns; composite indexes for multi-column filters
  • Avoid functions on indexed columns: WHERE YEAR(date)=2024 → use range instead
  • SELECT only needed columns: Avoid SELECT * with large blob/text fields
  • Keyset pagination: WHERE id > last_id LIMIT n instead of OFFSET on large tables
  • Covering indexes: Include all query columns in index to avoid table fetch
Q7. What is a deadlock? How do you prevent it? ▼

A deadlock occurs when transaction A holds lock 1 and waits for lock 2, while transaction B holds lock 2 and waits for lock 1 — circular wait, neither can proceed. Prevention: access tables/rows in a consistent order; keep transactions short; avoid user interaction inside transactions; use optimistic locking where possible. Most DBs auto-detect and roll back the "cheapest" transaction.

Q8. Optimistic vs pessimistic locking? ▼

Pessimistic: Lock before read/write (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE). Safe but blocks other transactions. Good for high-conflict scenarios. Optimistic: No locks — read with version number; on update, verify version unchanged. If version changed, retry. Implemented with a version or updated_at column. Best for high-read, low-conflict scenarios.

Q9. What is a covering index? ▼

A covering index includes ALL columns a query needs — so the DB answers the query entirely from the index without touching base table rows, eliminating the second lookup. Example: CREATE INDEX idx ON orders (customer_id, order_date) INCLUDE (total, status) covers a query selecting total/status and filtering on customer_id/order_date. Shows as "Using index" in EXPLAIN Extra column.

Q10. What is the N+1 query problem? ▼

1 query fetches N rows, then N additional queries are run for each row to fetch related data. Example: fetch 100 orders (1 query), then for each order fetch the customer (100 queries) = 101 total queries. Fix: use a JOIN to get both in one query, or batch load. Common in ORM-heavy apps. Always inspect generated SQL when using ORMs.

Query Practice (Q11–Q40)

Q11. Nth highest salary using DENSE_RANK. ▼
SQL — Nth Highest Salary
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT name, salary,
    DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk
  FROM employees
)
SELECT name, salary FROM ranked
WHERE rnk = 3;  -- change N here
Q12. Month-over-month revenue growth using LAG. ▼
SQL — MoM Growth
WITH monthly AS (
  SELECT
    DATE_FORMAT(created_at,'%Y-%m') AS month,
    SUM(amount) AS revenue
  FROM orders GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT
  month, revenue,
  LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS prev_month,
  ROUND(
    (revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month))
    * 100.0 / NULLIF(LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month), 0), 1
  ) AS mom_growth_pct
FROM monthly
ORDER BY month;
Q13. Recursive CTE org chart. ▼
SQL — Recursive CTE
WITH RECURSIVE org AS (
  SELECT id, name, manager_id, 0 AS lvl, name AS path
  FROM employees WHERE manager_id IS NULL   -- CEO
  UNION ALL
  SELECT e.id, e.name, e.manager_id,
    o.lvl+1,
    CONCAT(o.path, ' → ', e.name)
  FROM employees e
  JOIN org o ON e.manager_id = o.id
)
SELECT REPEAT('  ',lvl)||name AS tree, path
FROM org ORDER BY path;
Q14. 7-day moving average of daily sales. ▼
SQL — Moving Average
SELECT
  sale_date, amount,
  ROUND(
    AVG(amount) OVER (
      ORDER BY sale_date
      ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
    ), 2
  ) AS ma_7d
FROM daily_sales
ORDER BY sale_date;
Q15. First and last purchase date per customer. ▼
SQL
SELECT
  customer_id,
  MIN(order_date) AS first_purchase,
  MAX(order_date) AS last_purchase,
  DATEDIFF(MAX(order_date), MIN(order_date)) AS days_as_customer
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id;
Q16. Consecutive login streaks (gaps and islands). ▼
SQL — Gaps and Islands
WITH rn_logins AS (
  SELECT user_id, login_date,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY login_date) AS rn
  FROM (SELECT DISTINCT user_id, DATE(logged_in_at) login_date
        FROM user_logins) d
),
islands AS (
  SELECT user_id, login_date,
    DATE_SUB(login_date, INTERVAL rn DAY) AS grp
  FROM rn_logins
)
SELECT
  user_id,
  MIN(login_date) AS streak_start,
  MAX(login_date) AS streak_end,
  COUNT(*) AS streak_len
FROM islands
GROUP BY user_id, grp
ORDER BY streak_len DESC;

If days 1,2,3 have row numbers 1,2,3, then date − rownumber = the same constant for all three. Any gap breaks this pattern, creating a new group key.

Q17. Calculate median salary. ▼
SQL — Median
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT
    salary,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY salary) AS rn,
    COUNT(*) OVER () AS total
  FROM employees
)
SELECT AVG(salary) AS median
FROM ranked
WHERE rn IN (FLOOR((total+1)/2), CEIL((total+1)/2));
Q18. Detect churning customers with risk tiers. ▼
SQL — Churn Detection
WITH activity AS (
  SELECT
    customer_id,
    MAX(order_date) AS last_order,
    COUNT(*) AS orders,
    SUM(amount) AS ltv,
    DATEDIFF(CURDATE(), MAX(order_date)) AS days_ago
  FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id
)
SELECT
  c.name, c.email, a.days_ago, a.ltv,
  CASE
    WHEN a.days_ago >= 90 THEN 'High Risk'
    WHEN a.days_ago >= 60 THEN 'Medium Risk'
    WHEN a.days_ago >= 30 THEN 'Low Risk'
    ELSE 'Active'
  END AS churn_risk
FROM activity a
JOIN customers c ON c.id = a.customer_id
WHERE a.days_ago >= 30
ORDER BY a.ltv DESC;
Q19. Detect salary promotions using LAG on title history. ▼
SQL — LAG for Promotion Detection
WITH hist AS (
  SELECT
    employee_id, job_title, salary, effective_date,
    LAG(job_title) OVER (
      PARTITION BY employee_id ORDER BY effective_date
    ) AS prev_title,
    LAG(salary) OVER (
      PARTITION BY employee_id ORDER BY effective_date
    ) AS prev_salary
  FROM employee_history
)
SELECT
  e.name, h.prev_title, h.job_title,
  h.salary - h.prev_salary AS raise
FROM hist h
JOIN employees e ON e.id = h.employee_id
WHERE h.prev_title IS NOT NULL
  AND h.salary > h.prev_salary
ORDER BY raise DESC;
Q20. Products never ordered (two methods). ▼
SQL
-- LEFT JOIN anti-join
SELECT p.id, p.product_name
FROM products p
LEFT JOIN order_items oi ON p.id = oi.product_id
WHERE oi.product_id IS NULL;

-- NOT EXISTS
SELECT id, product_name FROM products p
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM order_items WHERE product_id = p.id
);
Q21–25. Stored proc with OUT | Audit trigger | NTILE quartiles | Multi-CTE chain | Generate date series ▼
Q21 — Stored Proc with OUT param
DELIMITER $$
CREATE PROCEDURE GetDeptStats(
  IN  p_dept    VARCHAR(50),
  OUT p_count   INT,
  OUT p_avg_sal DECIMAL(10,2)
)
BEGIN
  SELECT COUNT(*), AVG(salary)
  INTO   p_count, p_avg_sal
  FROM   employees
  WHERE  department = p_dept;
END$$
DELIMITER ;
CALL GetDeptStats('Engineering', @cnt, @avg);
SELECT @cnt, @avg;
Q22 — Audit Trigger
CREATE TRIGGER trg_salary_audit
AFTER UPDATE ON employees
FOR EACH ROW
BEGIN
  IF OLD.salary != NEW.salary THEN
    INSERT INTO audit_log
      (emp_id, old_sal, new_sal, changed_at)
    VALUES
      (NEW.id, OLD.salary, NEW.salary, NOW());
  END IF;
END;
Q23 — NTILE quartiles
SELECT name, salary,
  CASE NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY salary)
    WHEN 1 THEN 'Q1 Bottom 25%'
    WHEN 2 THEN 'Q2'
    WHEN 3 THEN 'Q3'
    WHEN 4 THEN 'Q4 Top 25%'
  END AS quartile
FROM employees;
Q24 — Multi-CTE chain
WITH
rev_monthly AS (
  SELECT DATE_FORMAT(order_date,'%Y-%m') mo, SUM(total) rev
  FROM orders GROUP BY 1
),
with_growth AS (
  SELECT mo, rev,
    ROUND((rev-LAG(rev)OVER(ORDER BY mo))*100.0/NULLIF(LAG(rev)OVER(ORDER BY mo),0),1) pct
  FROM rev_monthly
)
SELECT * FROM with_growth WHERE pct > 20;
Q25 — Generate date series (recursive CTE)
WITH RECURSIVE ds AS (
  SELECT DATE('2024-01-01') AS dt
  UNION ALL
  SELECT DATE_ADD(dt, INTERVAL 1 DAY)
  FROM ds WHERE dt < '2024-12-31'
)
SELECT ds.dt, COALESCE(s.amount,0) AS sales
FROM ds
LEFT JOIN daily_sales s ON ds.dt = s.sale_date
ORDER BY ds.dt;
-- Days with no sales show 0 instead of missing
Q26–30. PERCENT_RANK | RFM segmentation | Performance rewrite | Keyset pagination | Materialized views ▼
Q26 — PERCENT_RANK
SELECT name, salary,
  ROUND(PERCENT_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary) * 100, 1) AS percentile
FROM employees;
Q27 — RFM Customer Segmentation
WITH rfm AS (
  SELECT
    customer_id,
    DATEDIFF(NOW(), MAX(order_date)) AS recency,
    COUNT(*) AS frequency,
    SUM(amount) AS monetary
  FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id
)
SELECT c.name, r.*,
  CASE
    WHEN recency<=30 AND frequency>=5 AND monetary>1000 THEN 'Champion'
    WHEN recency<=90 AND frequency>=3                    THEN 'Loyal'
    WHEN recency>90  AND monetary>500                    THEN 'At Risk'
    ELSE 'Needs Attention'
  END AS segment
FROM rfm r
JOIN customers c ON c.id = r.customer_id;
Q28 — Avoid function on indexed column
-- SLOW: function prevents index scan
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE YEAR(order_date)=2024;

-- FAST: range uses index
SELECT * FROM orders
WHERE order_date >= '2024-01-01'
  AND order_date  < '2025-01-01';
Q29 — Keyset pagination
-- SLOW for large offsets (scans 100k rows)
SELECT * FROM orders ORDER BY id LIMIT 20 OFFSET 100000;

-- FAST: cursor from last page (uses index)
SELECT * FROM orders
WHERE id > 100000   -- last seen id
ORDER BY id LIMIT 20;

A materialized view stores query results physically (unlike regular views). Must be refreshed periodically. Great for expensive aggregations on dashboards where slightly stale data is acceptable. MySQL doesn't natively support them — simulate with a scheduled job that repopulates a summary table.

Q31–40. JSON queries | CTE UPDATE | Batch DELETE | SELECT FOR UPDATE | SAVEPOINT | EXPLAIN reading | Duplicate transactions ▼
Q31 — JSON column queries (MySQL 5.7+)
SELECT id,
  metadata ->> '$.color'  AS color,
  metadata ->> '$.size'   AS size
FROM products
WHERE metadata ->> '$.color' = 'blue';
Q32 — UPDATE with subquery (top earners)
UPDATE employees
SET salary = salary * 1.10
WHERE id IN (
  SELECT id FROM (
    SELECT id,
      PERCENT_RANK() OVER (
        PARTITION BY department ORDER BY salary
      ) AS pct
    FROM employees
  ) t WHERE pct >= 0.9
);
Q33 — Schema migration best practices
-- 1. Add nullable column (never add NOT NULL without DEFAULT to large tables)
ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN tier VARCHAR(20) DEFAULT NULL;

-- 2. Backfill in batches to avoid long locks
UPDATE users SET tier = 'standard'
WHERE tier IS NULL LIMIT 1000;  -- run in loop

-- 3. Apply NOT NULL constraint after backfill
ALTER TABLE users
MODIFY COLUMN tier VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'standard';
Q34 — Batch DELETE
-- Delete in batches — never delete millions at once
DELETE FROM logs
WHERE created_at < DATE_SUB(NOW(), INTERVAL 90 DAY)
ORDER BY id
LIMIT 1000;
-- Run in a loop until 0 rows affected
Q35 — SELECT FOR UPDATE (pessimistic lock)
START TRANSACTION;
SELECT balance FROM accounts
WHERE id = 42 FOR UPDATE; -- row lock acquired
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 500 WHERE id = 42;
COMMIT;
Q36 — SAVEPOINT for partial rollback
START TRANSACTION;
  INSERT INTO orders (...) VALUES (...);
  SAVEPOINT after_order;
  INSERT INTO payments (...) VALUES (...);
  -- If payment fails:
  ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT after_order;
  -- Order row stays; retry payment logic
COMMIT;
  • type = ALL: Full table scan — add an index
  • type = ref / range: Index in use — good
  • type = const / eq_ref: Optimal — direct PK lookup
  • rows: Estimated rows examined — lower is better
  • Extra = Using filesort: In-memory sort — add ORDER BY column to index
  • Extra = Using temporary: Temp table — expensive GROUP BY / DISTINCT
  • Extra = Using index: Covering index — best case

A star schema has a central fact table with denormalized dimension tables — simple JOINs, fast analytics. A snowflake schema normalizes dimensions into sub-tables — more joins but less redundancy. Star schemas dominate in data warehouses (Redshift, BigQuery, Snowflake) for query speed.

Fix with a JOIN
-- N+1 BAD: 1 query to get orders + N queries for each customer
-- GOOD: single JOIN gets everything at once
SELECT
  o.id, o.total,
  c.name AS customer_name,
  c.email
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id;
-- 1 query replaces 101 queries
Find charges with same user+amount within 5 minutes
SELECT
  p1.id     AS payment_id,
  p1.user_id,
  p1.amount,
  p1.created_at,
  p2.id     AS duplicate_of
FROM payments p1
JOIN payments p2
  ON  p1.user_id = p2.user_id
  AND p1.amount  = p2.amount
  AND p1.id      > p2.id
  AND ABS(TIMESTAMPDIFF(SECOND,p1.created_at,p2.created_at)) <= 300
ORDER BY p1.user_id, p1.created_at;

Expert Level (Q41–Q50)

Q41. What is a lateral join (LATERAL / CROSS APPLY)? ▼

A LATERAL join (called CROSS APPLY in SQL Server) allows a subquery in the FROM clause to reference columns from tables listed earlier in the FROM clause — something regular derived tables cannot do. In MySQL 8.0+, LATERAL is supported. It's used for "top N per group" queries and correlated table-valued expressions.

SQL — LATERAL JOIN (MySQL 8+)
-- Top 3 orders per customer using LATERAL
SELECT
  c.id, c.name,
  top_orders.id    AS order_id,
  top_orders.total AS order_total
FROM customers c
JOIN LATERAL (
  SELECT id, total
  FROM   orders
  WHERE  customer_id = c.id   -- references outer c.id
  ORDER BY total DESC
  LIMIT  3
) top_orders ON TRUE
ORDER BY c.id;
Q42. How do you implement SCD Type 2 in a modern data stack (dbt)? ▼

In dbt (data build tool), SCD Type 2 is implemented via dbt snapshots. You define a snapshot YAML config specifying the source table, unique_key, strategy (timestamp or check), and which columns to track. dbt automatically adds dbt_scd_id, dbt_valid_from, dbt_valid_to, and dbt_updated_at columns. On each run, dbt issues a MERGE (or equivalent) that expires old rows and inserts new ones — no manual stored procedure needed.

YAML — dbt Snapshot Config
-- snapshots/customers_snapshot.sql
{% snapshot customers_snapshot %}
  {{
    config(
      target_schema = 'snapshots',
      unique_key    = 'customer_id',
      strategy      = 'timestamp',
      updated_at    = 'updated_at'
    )
  }}
  SELECT * FROM {{ source('raw', 'customers') }}
{% endsnapshot %}
Q43. Explain the difference between OLTP and OLAP databases. ▼
DimensionOLTPOLAP
PurposeDay-to-day transactionsAnalytics & reporting
OperationsINSERT, UPDATE, DELETE heavySELECT heavy (complex aggregations)
Row count per queryFew rows (PK lookup)Millions of rows scanned
SchemaNormalized (3NF)Denormalized (star/snowflake)
IndexesMany narrow indexesFewer, wider (columnar storage)
ExamplesMySQL, PostgreSQL, SQL ServerBigQuery, Redshift, Snowflake, ClickHouse
ConcurrencyThousands of usersTens of analysts
Data freshnessReal-timeMinutes to hours (ETL lag)
Q44. What is a partitioned table? Show RANGE partitioning. ▼

Partitioning divides a large table into smaller physical segments (partitions) while keeping a single logical view. Queries that touch only one partition skip all others — this is called partition pruning. Partition types: RANGE (by value range), LIST (by discrete values), HASH (distributed evenly), KEY (hash on primary key).

SQL — RANGE Partitioning
CREATE TABLE orders_partitioned (
  id         INT,
  order_date DATE,
  total      DECIMAL(10,2)
)
PARTITION BY RANGE (YEAR(order_date)) (
  PARTITION p2022 VALUES LESS THAN (2023),
  PARTITION p2023 VALUES LESS THAN (2024),
  PARTITION p2024 VALUES LESS THAN (2025),
  PARTITION pmax  VALUES LESS THAN MAXVALUE
);

-- This query ONLY scans the p2024 partition (partition pruning)
SELECT * FROM orders_partitioned
WHERE order_date BETWEEN '2024-01-01' AND '2024-12-31';

-- Drop old partition instantly (no DELETE needed)
ALTER TABLE orders_partitioned DROP PARTITION p2022;
Q45. What are common table expression (CTE) materialization issues in PostgreSQL? ▼

In PostgreSQL, CTEs prior to version 12 were always materialized — their results were computed and stored in memory regardless of how the outer query used them. This prevented the optimizer from pushing filters down into the CTE, often causing full scans. From PG 12+, CTEs are automatically inlined (not materialized) unless they're recursive or contain side effects (writes). You can force behavior with MATERIALIZED or NOT MATERIALIZED hints. In MySQL and most other DBs, CTEs are treated more like inline views and can be optimized through.

SQL — PostgreSQL CTE Hints
-- Force materialization (compute once, cache result)
WITH expensive_calc AS MATERIALIZED (
  SELECT customer_id, SUM(total) ltv
  FROM orders GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT * FROM expensive_calc WHERE ltv > 5000;

-- Force inline (allow optimizer to push filter into CTE)
WITH filtered AS NOT MATERIALIZED (
  SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status = 'completed'
)
SELECT * FROM filtered WHERE total > 1000;
Q46–50. Window frame specs | Dynamic SQL | Hierarchical query | ETL merge pattern | Query plan forcing ▼
Q46 — Window Frame Specifications
-- ROWS vs RANGE in window frames
-- ROWS: physical row count (3 preceding rows literally)
SELECT
  sale_date,
  SUM(revenue) OVER (
    ORDER BY sale_date
    ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
  ) AS rolling_3d
FROM daily_sales;

-- RANGE: value-based window (all rows with same ORDER BY value)
SELECT
  dept, salary,
  SUM(salary) OVER (
    PARTITION BY dept
    ORDER BY salary
    RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
  ) AS cumulative_salary
FROM employees;
Q47 — Dynamic SQL with PREPARE
-- Build and execute SQL dynamically (use with caution — SQL injection risk)
SET @table_name = 'orders';
SET @sql = CONCAT('SELECT COUNT(*) FROM ', @table_name);

PREPARE stmt FROM @sql;
EXECUTE stmt;
DEALLOCATE PREPARE stmt;

-- Safer: use prepared statements in application layer (?, :param)
-- In procedures: use EXECUTE IMMEDIATE (PostgreSQL/Oracle) or PREPARE/EXECUTE
Q48 — Full Hierarchical Category Query
-- Get all subcategories under 'Electronics' at any depth
WITH RECURSIVE cat_tree AS (
  SELECT id, name, parent_id, 0 depth, name path
  FROM categories
  WHERE name = 'Electronics'
  UNION ALL
  SELECT
    c.id, c.name, c.parent_id,
    ct.depth + 1,
    CONCAT(ct.path, ' > ', c.name)
  FROM categories c
  JOIN cat_tree    ct ON c.parent_id = ct.id
)
SELECT REPEAT('--', depth)||name AS category_tree, path
FROM cat_tree
ORDER BY path;
Q49 — MERGE / UPSERT ETL Pattern
-- Standard MERGE (SQL Server / Oracle / BigQuery)
-- MySQL equivalent: INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE

-- MySQL ETL upsert: sync staging → production
INSERT INTO dim_products
  (product_id, name, price, category, updated_at)
SELECT
  product_id, name, price, category, NOW()
FROM staging_products
ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE
  name       = VALUES(name),
  price      = VALUES(price),
  category   = VALUES(category),
  updated_at = VALUES(updated_at);

Sometimes the optimizer makes sub-optimal decisions. You can override it with hints:

MySQL Query Hints
-- Force use of a specific index
SELECT * FROM orders USE INDEX (idx_order_date)
WHERE order_date > '2024-01-01';

-- Force ignore of an index
SELECT * FROM orders IGNORE INDEX (idx_status)
WHERE status = 'pending';

-- MySQL 8+ optimizer hints (more granular)
SELECT /*+ INDEX(orders idx_order_date) */
  * FROM orders
WHERE order_date > '2024-01-01';

Ace your SQL Interview

  • Think out loud: Explain your approach before writing — interviewers care about reasoning.
  • Start simple: Write a working basic version first, then optimize.
  • Consider edge cases: NULLs, ties, empty results, division by zero.
  • Know your audience: Analyst roles → aggregations, JOINs, CTEs. Engineering roles → transactions, indexes, performance.
  • Practice platforms: LeetCode SQL (50 problems), StrataScratch, Mode Analytics SQL Tutorial.

Advanced Theory — Deep Dives (Q41–Q55)

Q41. What is a star schema vs snowflake schema? With diagrams. ▼

Star schema: A central fact table surrounded by denormalized dimension tables. Each dimension is a single table, even if logically it has sub-attributes. Simple JOINs (fact → dim), fast for analytics. Used in most data marts.

Snowflake schema: Dimensions are normalized into multiple related tables (e.g., dim_product → dim_category → dim_department). Saves storage, enforces referential integrity, but requires more JOINs. Common in enterprise warehouses where storage or update anomalies matter.

Comparison
FeatureStarSnowflake
Dimension tablesDenormalized, flatNormalized, hierarchical
JOIN complexitySimple (1 join per dim)Complex (multiple joins per dim)
Query speedFaster (fewer joins)Slower (more joins)
StorageMore (some redundancy)Less (normalized)
ETL complexitySimpleComplex
Preferred inPower BI, Tableau, data martsLarge enterprise EDW
Q42. Explain database sharding. How does it differ from partitioning? ▼

Partitioning splits a large table into smaller pieces on a single database server. The application still connects to one database — the partition is transparent. Solves storage and query performance for large tables on one machine.

Sharding distributes data across multiple database servers (shards). Each shard holds a subset of data (e.g., users A-M on shard 1, N-Z on shard 2). Enables horizontal scaling beyond a single server's capacity. Adds complexity: cross-shard queries (e.g., aggregating across all users) require application-level coordination or a query router. Used at very large scale: hundreds of millions of users, petabyte-scale data.

Q43. What are window frame clauses? Explain ROWS vs RANGE. ▼
SQL — Window Frame Examples
-- ROWS: physical rows relative to current row (most common)
SUM(amount) OVER (
  ORDER BY date
  ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW  -- 3-row running sum
)

-- RANGE: logical range (peers with same ORDER BY value)
SUM(amount) OVER (
  ORDER BY date
  RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL 7 DAY PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
)  -- all rows within last 7 days (not just 7 rows)

-- Common frame boundaries:
ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW  -- cumulative sum
ROWS BETWEEN CURRENT ROW AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING   -- reverse cumulative
ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING -- entire partition
ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW          -- 7-row window

ROWS counts physical rows. RANGE groups all rows with the same ORDER BY value as peers (useful for date-based windows where multiple rows share the same date). For most running totals and moving averages, ROWS is preferred for its predictable behavior.

Q44. What is a hash join vs nested loop join vs merge join? ▼
Join AlgorithmHow It WorksBest WhenCost
Nested LoopFor each row in outer table, scan inner tableSmall inner table, indexed inner columnO(n × m) worst case
Hash JoinBuild hash table on smaller table, probe with largerLarge unsorted tables, equality joinsO(n + m) average
Merge JoinSort both tables, merge like zipperBoth tables already sorted/indexedO(n log n + m log m)

MySQL's InnoDB primarily uses nested loop joins. PostgreSQL and SQL Server use all three and choose based on statistics. You can influence join strategy with optimizer hints.

Q45. What is an execution plan cache? How does it affect performance? ▼

When a query runs, the optimizer creates an execution plan (which indexes to use, join order, etc.). This planning has a cost. The plan cache (query cache in MySQL, plan cache in SQL Server) stores compiled plans and reuses them for identical queries — avoiding re-planning on every execution. Stored procedures benefit most from this: they are compiled once on first call and cached. Ad-hoc SQL with different literal values every time (e.g., WHERE id = 42 vs WHERE id = 43) may not reuse plans unless parameterized. In MySQL 8.0+, the query cache was removed — use stored procedures and prepared statements for plan reuse.

Q46. Explain SCD (Slowly Changing Dimensions) and when to use Type 2. ▼

SCDs handle how dimension data changes over time in data warehouses. Type 2 is most commonly used because it provides complete point-in-time accuracy: when a customer's city changes, a new row is inserted with the new city, the old row is expired with an end date. Fact table JOINs use both the business key AND the date to match the right dimension row. Use Type 2 whenever you need to answer questions like "where was this customer when they placed this order?" or "what department was this employee in when they made this sale?" — any time the historical context of a transaction matters.

Q47–50. OLAP vs OLTP | CAP theorem | Connection pooling | Database normalization anomalies ▼

Q47 — OLAP vs OLTP: OLTP (Online Transaction Processing) handles frequent, small, fast reads/writes for day-to-day operations — highly normalized, low latency, ACID-compliant. OLAP (Online Analytical Processing) handles complex aggregation queries over large historical datasets for analytics — denormalized (star/snowflake), column-oriented storage, batch-loaded. Examples: MySQL for OLTP, Redshift/BigQuery/Snowflake for OLAP.

Q48 — CAP Theorem: Distributed systems can guarantee at most two of three: Consistency (all nodes see same data), Availability (every request gets a response), Partition Tolerance (system continues during network splits). Traditional RDBMS prioritize CP (Consistency + Partition Tolerance). Cassandra/DynamoDB prioritize AP. You can't have all three when network partitions occur.

Q49 — Connection pooling: Opening a new database connection is expensive (TCP handshake, auth, session setup). A connection pool maintains a set of pre-opened connections and reuses them. Applications borrow a connection from the pool, use it, and return it. Tools: PgBouncer, HikariCP, ProxySQL. Prevents "connection exhaustion" and dramatically reduces latency under high concurrency.

Q50 — Normalization anomalies: Without normalization, three types of anomalies occur: (1) Update anomaly: same data in multiple rows — update one and others become stale. (2) Insert anomaly: can't insert a fact without inserting another unrelated fact (e.g., can't add a department without an employee). (3) Delete anomaly: deleting a row removes important data (e.g., deleting last employee in a department removes the department's name). Normalization eliminates these by ensuring each fact is stored exactly once.

Advanced Query Practice (Q41–Q60)

Q41. Find the employee with the highest salary in each department using FIRST_VALUE. ▼
SQL — FIRST_VALUE
SELECT DISTINCT
  department,
  FIRST_VALUE(name) OVER (
    PARTITION BY department
    ORDER BY salary DESC
    ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING
  ) AS top_earner,
  FIRST_VALUE(salary) OVER (
    PARTITION BY department
    ORDER BY salary DESC
    ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING
  ) AS top_salary
FROM employees;
Q42. Write a query to detect sudden spikes in daily revenue (>2x previous day). ▼
SQL — Revenue Spike Detection
WITH daily_rev AS (
  SELECT
    DATE(created_at) AS dt,
    SUM(total)       AS revenue
  FROM orders
  GROUP BY 1
),
with_prev AS (
  SELECT
    dt,
    revenue,
    LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY dt) AS prev_day
  FROM daily_rev
)
SELECT
  dt, revenue, prev_day,
  ROUND(revenue / NULLIF(prev_day, 0), 2) AS revenue_ratio
FROM with_prev
WHERE revenue > prev_day * 2  -- more than 2x the previous day
ORDER BY dt;
Q43. Implement SCD Type 2 update as a stored procedure. ▼
SQL — SCD Type 2 ETL Procedure
DELIMITER $$
CREATE PROCEDURE UpdateCustomerSCD2(
  IN p_customer_id  INT,
  IN p_name         VARCHAR(100),
  IN p_city         VARCHAR(100),
  IN p_country      VARCHAR(50)
)
BEGIN
  DECLARE v_changed BOOLEAN DEFAULT FALSE;

  -- Check if any tracked attribute changed
  SELECT (city != p_city OR country != p_country)
  INTO v_changed
  FROM dim_customer
  WHERE customer_id = p_customer_id AND is_current = 1;

  IF v_changed THEN
    -- Step 1: expire the old row
    UPDATE dim_customer
    SET   is_current   = 0,
          eff_end_date = DATE_SUB(CURDATE(), INTERVAL 1 DAY)
    WHERE customer_id  = p_customer_id
      AND   is_current    = 1;

    -- Step 2: insert new current row
    INSERT INTO dim_customer
      (customer_id, name, city, country,
       is_current, eff_start_date, eff_end_date)
    VALUES
      (p_customer_id, p_name, p_city, p_country,
       1, CURDATE(), '9999-12-31');

    SELECT 'UPDATED' AS result;
  ELSE
    -- No tracked attribute changed — just update non-SCD fields
    UPDATE dim_customer
    SET   name = p_name
    WHERE customer_id = p_customer_id AND is_current = 1;
    SELECT 'NO CHANGE' AS result;
  END IF;
END$$
DELIMITER ;

CALL UpdateCustomerSCD2(42, 'Alice', 'Delhi', 'India');
Q44. Write a query for a retention heatmap (cohort × months after signup). ▼
SQL — Cohort Retention Heatmap
WITH
cohorts AS (
  SELECT
    customer_id,
    DATE_FORMAT(MIN(order_date), '%Y-%m') AS cohort_month
  FROM orders
  GROUP BY customer_id
),
retention AS (
  SELECT
    c.cohort_month,
    TIMESTAMPDIFF(MONTH,
      STR_TO_DATE(CONCAT(c.cohort_month,'-01'),'%Y-%m-%d'),
      o.order_date
    ) AS months_since_first,
    COUNT(DISTINCT o.customer_id) AS active_users
  FROM cohorts c
  JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
  GROUP BY c.cohort_month, 2
)
SELECT
  cohort_month,
  MAX(CASE WHEN months_since_first=0  THEN active_users END) AS m0,
  MAX(CASE WHEN months_since_first=1  THEN active_users END) AS m1,
  MAX(CASE WHEN months_since_first=2  THEN active_users END) AS m2,
  MAX(CASE WHEN months_since_first=3  THEN active_users END) AS m3,
  MAX(CASE WHEN months_since_first=6  THEN active_users END) AS m6
FROM retention
GROUP BY cohort_month
ORDER BY cohort_month;
Q45. Write a dynamic SQL query to calculate revenue for any configurable date range. ▼
SQL — Dynamic Date Range Revenue
DELIMITER $$
CREATE PROCEDURE RevenueByDateRange(
  IN p_start   DATE,
  IN p_end     DATE,
  IN p_group   VARCHAR(10)  -- 'day', 'week', 'month', 'year'
)
BEGIN
  DECLARE v_format VARCHAR(20);
  DECLARE v_sql    TEXT;

  SET v_format = CASE p_group
    WHEN 'day'   THEN '%Y-%m-%d'
    WHEN 'week'  THEN '%Y-W%u'
    WHEN 'month' THEN '%Y-%m'
    WHEN 'year'  THEN '%Y'
    ELSE '%Y-%m'
  END;

  SET v_sql = CONCAT(
    "SELECT DATE_FORMAT(order_date, '", v_format, "') AS period, ",
    "COUNT(*) AS orders, ROUND(SUM(total),2) AS revenue, ROUND(AVG(total),2) AS aov ",
    "FROM orders WHERE order_date BETWEEN ? AND ? ",
    "GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1"
  );

  PREPARE stmt FROM v_sql;
  EXECUTE stmt USING p_start, p_end;
  DEALLOCATE PREPARE stmt;
END$$
DELIMITER ;

CALL RevenueByDateRange('2024-01-01', '2024-12-31', 'month');
CALL RevenueByDateRange('2024-01-01', '2024-12-31', 'week');
Q46–55. Advanced Analytics: LTV prediction prep | Product funnel | Inventory turns | Price elasticity | Anomaly detection ▼
Q46 — Customer LTV prediction inputs
SELECT
  customer_id,
  DATEDIFF(NOW(), MIN(order_date))  AS customer_age_days,
  COUNT(*)                            AS total_orders,
  SUM(total)                          AS total_revenue,
  AVG(total)                          AS aov,
  DATEDIFF(NOW(), MAX(order_date))  AS days_since_last,
  DATEDIFF(MAX(order_date), MIN(order_date))
    / NULLIF(COUNT(*)-1, 0)           AS avg_days_between_orders
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2;               -- need at least 2 orders for interval calc
Q47 — Inventory turnover rate
-- Inventory turnover = Cost of Goods Sold / Average Inventory
SELECT
  p.product_name,
  p.category,
  SUM(oi.quantity * p.cost_price)  AS cogs,
  p.stock_qty * p.cost_price        AS current_inventory_value,
  ROUND(
    SUM(oi.quantity * p.cost_price)
    / NULLIF(p.stock_qty * p.cost_price, 0), 2
  ) AS inventory_turnover
FROM products p
LEFT JOIN order_items oi ON p.id = oi.product_id
GROUP BY p.id, p.product_name, p.category,
         p.stock_qty, p.cost_price
ORDER BY inventory_turnover DESC;
Q48 — Sessions with no orders (conversion rate)
SELECT
  DATE(s.started_at)         AS date,
  COUNT(DISTINCT s.id)       AS total_sessions,
  COUNT(DISTINCT o.id)       AS sessions_with_orders,
  ROUND(
    COUNT(DISTINCT o.id) * 100.0
    / COUNT(DISTINCT s.id), 2
  ) AS conversion_rate_pct
FROM sessions s
LEFT JOIN orders o
  ON s.user_id = o.customer_id
  AND DATE(o.created_at) = DATE(s.started_at)
GROUP BY DATE(s.started_at)
ORDER BY date;
