📌 Chapter 1

What is DAX?

DAX (Data Analysis Expressions) is a collection of functions, operators, and constants used in formulas to calculate and return values in Power BI, Power Pivot (Excel), and Azure Analysis Services. It combines the feel of Excel formulas with the power of relational database query concepts.

DAX vs SQL — Key Differences

AspectSQLDAX
PurposeQuery & manipulate databasesDefine calculations in a data model
Execution styleSet-based, writes full queriesExpression-based, defines formulas
Filter awarenessWHERE clause explicitly filtersContext (visual, slicer, row) filters automatically
Runs inRDBMS (MySQL, PostgreSQL, etc.)Power BI, Power Pivot, SSAS Tabular
ResultsReturns rows & columnsReturns a scalar value or table
Time intelligenceManual date calculationsBuilt-in: TOTALYTD, SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR, etc.

Where DAX Lives in Power BI

📏

Measures

Dynamic calculations that respond to filters and slicers. Computed at query time. No new column in table. Example: [Total Sales]

➕

Calculated Columns

New column added to a table in the data model. Computed at data refresh time. Stored in memory. Example: [Full Name] = [First] & " " & [Last]

🗂️

Calculated Tables

Virtual tables created from DAX expressions. Used for date tables, disconnected parameter tables, bridging. Example: CALENDAR(), CROSSJOIN()

Always prefer Measures over Calculated Columns for aggregations. Measures are computed dynamically and don't consume RAM. Calculated Columns are materialized and stored — use them only for row-level attributes like concatenating name fields or categorizing rows.

DAX Syntax Basics

DAX — Syntax Reference
-- Measure (defined in Power BI Measure pane)
Total Sales = SUM(Sales[Amount])

-- Calculated Column (added to a table)
Sales[Profit Margin %] =
  DIVIDE(Sales[Profit], Sales[Revenue], 0)

-- Referencing a table column: TableName[ColumnName]
Products[Price]

-- Referencing a measure: [MeasureName] (no table prefix)
[Total Sales]

-- Variables improve readability and performance
Profit % =
VAR vRevenue = SUM(Sales[Revenue])
VAR vCost    = SUM(Sales[Cost])
RETURN
  DIVIDE(vRevenue - vCost, vRevenue, 0)

-- Comments: -- single line, /* multi line */
Sales Tax = Sales[Amount] * 0.18  -- 18% GST
🔢 Chapter 2

Data Types & Operators

DAX has a small set of native data types and a rich operator set. Understanding type coercion prevents subtle bugs.

DAX Data Types

DAX TypeDescriptionExample
Whole Number64-bit integer42, -100, 0
Decimal NumberDouble-precision float3.14, 99.99
Fixed DecimalCurrency (4 decimal places)1234.5678
TextUnicode string"Hello", "India"
Boolean (TRUE/FALSE)Logical valueTRUE, FALSE
Date/TimeDate, Time, DateTime, DateTimeZoneDATE(2024,1,1)
TableUsed in table-valued functionsFILTER(Sales, ...)
BlankAbsence of value (like SQL NULL)BLANK()

Operators

DAX — Operators
-- Arithmetic
Sales[Revenue] + Sales[Tax]         -- addition
Sales[Price] * Sales[Qty]           -- multiplication
DIVIDE(Sales[Profit], Sales[Revenue]) -- safe division (avoids /0 error)

-- Comparison (return TRUE/FALSE)
Sales[Amount] >  1000
Sales[Status] =  "Paid"
Sales[Status] <> "Cancelled"         -- not equal

-- Text concatenation
Customers[FirstName] & " " & Customers[LastName]

-- Logical
AND(Sales[Amount]>0, Sales[Status]="Paid")   -- both true
OR(Sales[Region]="North", Sales[Region]="South")

-- IN operator (list membership)
Products[Category] IN {"Electronics", "Mobiles", "Laptops"}

BLANK propagates through arithmetic: BLANK() + 5 = 5 (treats BLANK as 0). But BLANK() = BLANK() returns TRUE. Always use ISBLANK([Measure]) to check for blank rather than [Measure] = BLANK().

🎯 Chapter 3 — Foundation

Evaluation Context

Evaluation context is the single most important concept in DAX. Every DAX formula is evaluated inside a context that determines which rows and columns are visible. Miss this and DAX will never make sense. Get it and everything clicks.

Two Types of Context

📋

Row Context

Created when DAX iterates over a table row by row. Each row is the "current row." Calculated columns always have row context. Iterator functions (SUMX, FILTER) create row context. Important: measures do NOT have row context by themselves — they aggregate.

🔍

Filter Context

The set of active filters applied to the data model. Comes from: visual filters, slicers, page filters, report filters, row/column headers in a matrix, and the CALCULATE function. Filter context restricts which rows participate in aggregations.

When a measure is evaluated, it always runs inside the filter context of the visual. When a calculated column or iterator runs, it uses row context. CALCULATE is the bridge — it creates a new filter context, optionally building on the existing one.

Row Context in Action

DAX — Row Context Examples
-- Calculated column: row context exists — each row knows its own values
Sales[Line Total] = Sales[Unit Price] * Sales[Quantity]
-- [Unit Price] and [Quantity] refer to THIS ROW's values

-- SUMX creates row context as it iterates
Revenue (X) =
SUMX(
  Sales,                               -- iterate over Sales table
  Sales[Unit Price] * Sales[Quantity]  -- expression evaluated for EACH row
)
-- Different from SUM(Sales[Amount]) if Amount column doesn't pre-compute the product

-- FILTER creates row context
High Value Sales =
CALCULATE(
  SUM(Sales[Amount]),
  FILTER(Sales, Sales[Amount] > 10000)
  -- FILTER iterates Sales row by row (row context), keeping rows where Amount > 10000
)

Filter Context in Action

DAX — Filter Context Examples
-- A simple SUM measure: affected by whatever filter context exists
Total Sales = SUM(Sales[Amount])

-- In a matrix with Region on rows:
--   Row "North" → filter context filters Sales to Region = North
--   Row "South" → filter context filters Sales to Region = South
--   Grand Total → no region filter, all rows included

-- CALCULATE changes filter context
Electronics Sales =
CALCULATE(
  SUM(Sales[Amount]),
  Products[Category] = "Electronics"
  -- Regardless of what category filter the visual applies,
  -- this measure ALWAYS filters to Electronics
)

-- ALL() removes filter context from a column
% of Total =
DIVIDE(
  [Total Sales],
  CALCULATE([Total Sales], ALL(Sales))
  -- ALL(Sales) removes ALL filters from the Sales table
  -- numerator is filtered (current context), denominator is grand total
)

Context Transition

When CALCULATE is used inside a row context (calculated column or SUMX), it automatically converts the row context into an equivalent filter context. This is called context transition. Every unique combination of column values in the current row becomes a filter. This is powerful but can cause performance issues — be aware when nesting CALCULATE inside iterators.

DAX — Context Transition
-- Context transition example in a calculated column
Customers[Total Purchases] =
CALCULATE(SUM(Sales[Amount]))
-- Row context (CustomerID = 42) transitions to filter context
-- CALCULATE sees: filter Sales where CustomerID = 42
-- Result: total sales for THIS customer only

-- Without CALCULATE, SUM would return the grand total (no row context in measures)
Customers[Wrong Total] = SUM(Sales[Amount])
-- Returns GRAND TOTAL for every row — wrong!
➕ Chapter 4

Calculated Columns & Tables

Calculated columns extend a table with new attributes. Calculated tables create new virtual tables. Both are computed at data refresh time and stored in memory (VertiPaq engine).

Calculated Columns — Examples

DAX — Calculated Column Patterns
-- Concatenate text columns
Employees[Full Name] =
  Employees[First Name] & " " & Employees[Last Name]

-- Categorize with IF
Products[Price Tier] =
IF(Products[Unit Price] >= 50000, "Premium",
IF(Products[Unit Price] >= 10000, "Mid-Range", "Budget"))

-- SWITCH for cleaner multi-branch logic
Sales[Quarter] =
SWITCH(
  MONTH(Sales[OrderDate]),
  1, "Q1", 2, "Q1", 3, "Q1",
  4, "Q2", 5, "Q2", 6, "Q2",
  7, "Q3", 8, "Q3", 9, "Q3",
  "Q4"
)

-- Date parts
Sales[Year]    = YEAR(Sales[OrderDate])
Sales[MonthNum] = MONTH(Sales[OrderDate])
Sales[WeekDay]  = WEEKDAY(Sales[OrderDate], 2) -- 2 = Mon=1

-- Lookup from related table (requires relationship)
Sales[Product Category] = RELATED(Products[Category])

-- Age calculation
Customers[Age] =
  DATEDIFF(Customers[DOB], TODAY(), YEAR)

Calculated Tables

DAX — Calculated Table Examples
-- Date table (essential for time intelligence)
Dim Date =
ADDCOLUMNS(
  CALENDAR(DATE(2020,1,1), DATE(2026,12,31)),
  "Year",        YEAR([Date]),
  "Month",       MONTH([Date]),
  "MonthName",   FORMAT([Date], "MMMM"),
  "Quarter",     CONCATENATE("Q", QUARTER([Date])),
  "WeekNum",     WEEKNUM([Date]),
  "DayOfWeek",   WEEKDAY([Date],2),
  "DayName",     FORMAT([Date], "dddd"),
  "IsWeekend",   IF(WEEKDAY([Date],2)>=6, TRUE, FALSE),
  "YearMonth",   FORMAT([Date], "YYYY-MM"),
  "FiscalYear",  "FY" & IF(MONTH([Date])>=4, YEAR([Date])+1, YEAR([Date]))
)

-- Disconnected parameter table (for what-if slicers)
Discount Rates =
DATATABLE(
  "Rate Label", STRING,
  "Rate Value", DOUBLE,
  {
    {"5%",  0.05},
    {"10%", 0.10},
    {"15%", 0.15},
    {"20%", 0.20}
  }
)

-- Filter + transform an existing table
High Value Customers =
FILTER(
  Customers,
  CALCULATE(SUM(Sales[Amount])) > 100000
)
📏 Chapter 5

Measures — Theory & Practice

Measures are the heart of Power BI analytics. They are dynamic formulas that evaluate in the filter context of whatever visual they're placed in. A single measure adapts to every visual without rewriting.

Implicit vs Explicit Measures

Implicit measures are created when you drag a numeric field into a visual and Power BI auto-sums it. They are inflexible — you can't reference them from other measures, format them precisely, or apply complex logic. Always create explicit measures with the Measure pane. Professional Power BI models have zero implicit measures.

Essential Measure Patterns

DAX — Core Measure Patterns
-- 1. Basic aggregation measures
Total Revenue    = SUM(Sales[Revenue])
Total Orders     = COUNTROWS(Sales)
Distinct Customers = DISTINCTCOUNT(Sales[CustomerID])
Avg Order Value  = AVERAGE(Sales[Amount])

-- 2. Safe division (returns 0 or BLANK on divide-by-zero)
Profit Margin % =
DIVIDE(
  [Total Revenue] - [Total Cost],
  [Total Revenue],
  0  -- alternate result when denominator = 0
)

-- 3. Conditional measure with CALCULATE + filter
Online Revenue =
CALCULATE(
  [Total Revenue],
  Sales[Channel] = "Online"
)

-- 4. % of Total (grand total stays in denominator)
Revenue % of Total =
DIVIDE(
  [Total Revenue],
  CALCULATE([Total Revenue], ALL(Sales))
)

-- 5. % of parent row (for matrix visuals)
Revenue % of Category =
DIVIDE(
  [Total Revenue],
  CALCULATE([Total Revenue], ALLSELECTED(Products[Category]))
)

-- 6. Rank within context
Product Rank =
RANKX(
  ALL(Products[ProductName]),
  [Total Revenue],
  ,
  DESC
)

-- 7. Cumulative (running) total
Cumulative Revenue =
CALCULATE(
  [Total Revenue],
  FILTER(
    ALL(Date[Date]),
    Date[Date] <= MAX(Date[Date])
  )
)

-- 8. Dynamic title based on slicer selection
Selected Region Title =
IF(
  HASONEVALUE(Regions[Region]),
  SELECTEDVALUE(Regions[Region]) & " — Revenue Summary",
  "All Regions — Revenue Summary"
)

Measure Organization — Display Folders

Create a dedicated empty table called "_Measures" (using DATATABLE with no rows) and store all your measures there. This keeps measures organized, separate from data tables, and easy to find. Use Display Folders within that table to group measures by category (Sales, Finance, HR, Time Intelligence).

📊 Chapter 6

Aggregation Functions

DAX aggregation functions summarize data across multiple rows. They automatically respect the current filter context.

Complete Aggregation Reference

DAX — All Aggregation Functions
── Numeric aggregations ──────────────────────────────────
SUM(Sales[Amount])              -- sum of numeric column
AVERAGE(Sales[Amount])          -- mean (ignores BLANK)
MIN(Sales[Amount])              -- minimum value
MAX(Sales[Amount])              -- maximum value
MEDIAN(Sales[Amount])           -- median (50th percentile)

── Count aggregations ────────────────────────────────────
COUNT(Sales[Amount])             -- count of non-blank numeric values
COUNTA(Sales[OrderID])          -- count of non-blank values (any type)
COUNTROWS(Sales)                 -- count all rows (including blanks)
DISTINCTCOUNT(Sales[CustomerID]) -- count unique values
DISTINCTCOUNTNOBLANK(Sales[CustomerID]) -- unique non-blank values
COUNTBLANK(Sales[Phone])         -- count blank/null values

── Statistical ───────────────────────────────────────────
STDEV.P(Sales[Amount])          -- population std deviation
STDEV.S(Sales[Amount])          -- sample std deviation
VAR.P(Sales[Amount])            -- population variance
PERCENTILE.INC(Sales[Amount],0.9) -- 90th percentile

── Real-world measure examples ───────────────────────────
Total Units Sold    = SUM(Sales[Quantity])
Avg Selling Price   = AVERAGE(Sales[Unit Price])
Unique Customers    = DISTINCTCOUNT(Sales[CustomerID])
Total Transactions  = COUNTROWS(Sales)
Highest Sale        = MAX(Sales[Amount])
🔍 Chapter 7

FILTER, ALL & ALLEXCEPT

These functions control which rows are included in calculations by adding, removing, or modifying filter context. They are used almost exclusively inside CALCULATE.

FILTER — Row-by-Row Selection

DAX — FILTER Examples
-- FILTER returns a table (subset of rows)
Revenue > 10K Orders =
CALCULATE(
  [Total Revenue],
  FILTER(Sales, Sales[Amount] > 10000)
)

-- Multiple conditions in FILTER
Premium Online Sales =
CALCULATE(
  [Total Revenue],
  FILTER(Sales,
    Sales[Amount] > 5000 &&
    Sales[Channel] = "Online"
  )
)

-- FILTER with RELATED (from related table)
Electronics Revenue =
CALCULATE(
  [Total Revenue],
  FILTER(Sales,
    RELATED(Products[Category]) = "Electronics"
  )
)
-- Note: prefer simple column filter in CALCULATE over FILTER+RELATED for performance

-- Better: direct column filter (uses VertiPaq index, faster)
Electronics Revenue v2 =
CALCULATE([Total Revenue], Products[Category] = "Electronics")

ALL, ALLEXCEPT, ALLSELECTED

DAX — ALL Family
-- ALL(table): removes ALL filters from entire table
Grand Total Revenue =
CALCULATE([Total Revenue], ALL(Sales))

-- ALL(column): removes filter from one column only
Revenue % of All Products =
DIVIDE(
  [Total Revenue],
  CALCULATE([Total Revenue], ALL(Products[ProductName]))
)

-- ALLEXCEPT: remove all filters EXCEPT specified columns
-- Useful: % of total per category, keeping category filter
Revenue % of Category =
DIVIDE(
  [Total Revenue],
  CALCULATE([Total Revenue], ALLEXCEPT(Products, Products[Category]))
)

-- ALLSELECTED: respects slicer selections, removes row/column header filters
-- Perfect for "% of filtered total" in matrix visuals
Revenue % of Filtered Total =
DIVIDE(
  [Total Revenue],
  CALCULATE([Total Revenue], ALLSELECTED(Products[ProductName]))
)

-- REMOVEFILTERS: modern cleaner syntax for ALL inside CALCULATE
Total Revenue No Date Filter =
CALCULATE([Total Revenue], REMOVEFILTERS(Date))
⚡ Chapter 8 — Key Function

CALCULATE & CALCULATETABLE

CALCULATE is the most powerful and most used function in DAX. It evaluates an expression while modifying the filter context. Mastering CALCULATE is mastering DAX.

CALCULATE Syntax & How It Works

CALCULATE( <expression>, [<filter1>], [<filter2>], ... )

Filters can be: boolean predicates (Sales[Channel] = "Online"), table functions (FILTER, ALL, VALUES), or time intelligence functions (SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR). Filters are AND-ed together. CALCULATE first adds/overrides filters, then evaluates the expression in the new context.

DAX — CALCULATE Deep Examples
-- Single filter override
North Region Sales =
CALCULATE([Total Revenue], Regions[Name] = "North")

-- Multiple filters (AND logic)
North Online 2024 =
CALCULATE(
  [Total Revenue],
  Regions[Name]   = "North",
  Sales[Channel]  = "Online",
  YEAR(Sales[OrderDate]) = 2024
)

-- IN operator for multiple values
Top Category Revenue =
CALCULATE(
  [Total Revenue],
  Products[Category] IN {"Electronics", "Mobiles"}
)

-- Preserve existing filter + add new one (default behavior)
Budget Sales (Excl. Returns) =
CALCULATE(
  [Total Revenue],
  Sales[Type] <> "Return"
  -- The visual's existing filters (date, region, etc.) still apply
  -- We only ADD a new filter: exclude returns
)

-- KEEPFILTERS: add filter without overriding existing
Electronics in Context =
CALCULATE(
  [Total Revenue],
  KEEPFILTERS(Products[Category] = "Electronics")
)

-- CALCULATETABLE: same as CALCULATE but returns a table
Online Sales Table =
CALCULATETABLE(
  Sales,
  Sales[Channel] = "Online"
)
-- Use in COUNTROWS, SUMX, TOPN, etc.

-- Nested CALCULATE — inner overrides outer for same column
Always North =
CALCULATE(
  CALCULATE([Total Revenue], Regions[Name] = "North"),
  Regions[Name] = "South"
)
-- Inner wins: returns North revenue regardless of outer filter
🕐 Time Intelligence — Deep Dive

Time Intelligence

Time intelligence functions automatically navigate your date table to calculate period-over-period comparisons, year-to-date totals, rolling averages, and more. They require a properly marked Date table with a continuous date range.

Date Table Requirements

  • Must have a column of type Date with no gaps — every calendar date must exist
  • Must be marked as a Date Table in Power BI (Table Tools → Mark as Date Table)
  • The date column must be unique — one row per date
  • Your fact table must have a relationship to the Date table's date column

Period-to-Date Functions

DAX — YTD, QTD, MTD
-- Year-to-Date (from Jan 1 to the last visible date)
Revenue YTD =
TOTALYTD([Total Revenue], Date[Date])

-- YTD with custom fiscal year end (e.g., March 31 for Indian FY)
Revenue FY-YTD =
TOTALYTD([Total Revenue], Date[Date], "03-31")

-- Quarter-to-Date
Revenue QTD =
TOTALQTD([Total Revenue], Date[Date])

-- Month-to-Date
Revenue MTD =
TOTALMTD([Total Revenue], Date[Date])

-- Equivalent CALCULATE version (more flexible)
Revenue YTD (Manual) =
CALCULATE(
  [Total Revenue],
  DATESYTD(Date[Date])
)

Same Period Last Year (SPLY) & Comparisons

DAX — Prior Period Comparisons
-- Revenue same period last year
Revenue LY =
CALCULATE(
  [Total Revenue],
  SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR(Date[Date])
)

-- YoY Growth Amount
Revenue YoY Δ = [Total Revenue] - [Revenue LY]

-- YoY Growth %
Revenue YoY % =
DIVIDE(
  [Revenue YoY Δ],
  [Revenue LY]
)

-- Previous month
Revenue Prev Month =
CALCULATE(
  [Total Revenue],
  PREVIOUSMONTH(Date[Date])
)

-- Previous quarter
Revenue Prev Quarter =
CALCULATE([Total Revenue], PREVIOUSQUARTER(Date[Date]))

-- YTD Last Year (for YTD comparison)
Revenue YTD LY =
CALCULATE(
  [Revenue YTD],
  SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR(Date[Date])
)

-- DATESINPERIOD: flexible trailing period
Revenue Last 30 Days =
CALCULATE(
  [Total Revenue],
  DATESINPERIOD(Date[Date], MAX(Date[Date]), -30, DAY)
)

-- DATEADD: offset by any period
Revenue Same Month 2 Years Ago =
CALCULATE(
  [Total Revenue],
  DATEADD(Date[Date], -2, YEAR)
)
📈 Time Intelligence Patterns

YoY, QoQ, MoM — Complete Patterns

Period-over-period comparisons are the most requested analytics patterns in any business. Here is the complete production-ready DAX for each.

DAX — Full Comparison Measure Set
╔══════════════ YEAR-OVER-YEAR ══════════════╗
Revenue LY     = CALCULATE([Total Revenue], SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR(Date[Date]))
YoY Amount     = [Total Revenue] - [Revenue LY]
YoY %          = DIVIDE([YoY Amount], [Revenue LY])
YoY Icon       = IF([YoY %] > 0, "▲ " & FORMAT([YoY %],"0.0%"),
                              "▼ " & FORMAT([YoY %],"0.0%"))

╔══════════════ QUARTER-OVER-QUARTER ════════╗
Revenue PQ     = CALCULATE([Total Revenue], PREVIOUSQUARTER(Date[Date]))
QoQ Amount     = [Total Revenue] - [Revenue PQ]
QoQ %          = DIVIDE([QoQ Amount], [Revenue PQ])

╔══════════════ MONTH-OVER-MONTH ════════════╗
Revenue PM     = CALCULATE([Total Revenue], PREVIOUSMONTH(Date[Date]))
MoM Amount     = [Total Revenue] - [Revenue PM]
MoM %          = DIVIDE([MoM Amount], [Revenue PM])

╔══════════════ YTD COMPARISON ══════════════╗
Revenue YTD    = TOTALYTD([Total Revenue], Date[Date])
Revenue YTD LY = CALCULATE([Revenue YTD], SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR(Date[Date]))
YTD vs LY %    = DIVIDE([Revenue YTD] - [Revenue YTD LY], [Revenue YTD LY])
🔄 Rolling Calculations

Rolling Totals & Moving Averages

DAX — Rolling Calculations
-- 3-Month Rolling Total
Revenue Rolling 3M =
CALCULATE(
  [Total Revenue],
  DATESINPERIOD(Date[Date], LASTDATE(Date[Date]), -3, MONTH)
)

-- 12-Month Rolling Total (trailing twelve months)
Revenue TTM =
CALCULATE(
  [Total Revenue],
  DATESINPERIOD(Date[Date], LASTDATE(Date[Date]), -12, MONTH)
)

-- 3-Month Moving Average
Revenue MA 3M =
AVERAGEX(
  DATESINPERIOD(Date[Date], LASTDATE(Date[Date]), -3, MONTH),
  [Total Revenue]
)

-- 7-Day Moving Average (daily granularity)
Revenue MA 7D =
CALCULATE(
  DIVIDE([Total Revenue], DISTINCTCOUNT(Date[Date])),
  DATESINPERIOD(Date[Date], MAX(Date[Date]), -7, DAY)
)

-- Cumulative total (running sum)
Cumulative Revenue =
CALCULATE(
  [Total Revenue],
  FILTER(
    ALL(Date[Date]),
    Date[Date] <= MAX(Date[Date])
  )
)
🔁 Chapter 9 — Advanced

Iterator Functions (X-Functions)

Iterator functions iterate over every row of a table, evaluate an expression in that row's context, then aggregate the results. They are the DAX equivalent of SQL's row-by-row calculations.

DAX — X-Functions Complete Reference
-- SUMX: sum of an expression per row
Revenue (SUMX) =
SUMX(Sales, Sales[Quantity] * Sales[Unit Price])
-- Use when you need row-level calculation before summing
-- (Quantity × Price per row, THEN sum all rows)

-- AVERAGEX: average of an expression per row
Avg Margin =
AVERAGEX(
  Sales,
  DIVIDE(Sales[Profit], Sales[Revenue], 0)
)

-- MAXX / MINX: max/min of expression across rows
Max Order Value =
MAXX(Sales, Sales[Quantity] * Sales[Unit Price])

-- COUNTX: count rows where expression is non-blank/non-zero
Profitable Lines =
COUNTX(Sales, IF(Sales[Profit] > 0, Sales[Profit], BLANK()))

-- RANKX: rank a value against a table of values
Product Rank by Revenue =
RANKX(
  ALL(Products[ProductName]),  -- table to rank against
  [Total Revenue],               -- expression to rank by
  ,                               -- value (blank = current context)
  DESC,                           -- direction
  DENSE                           -- tie handling: DENSE or SKIP
)

-- Conditional SUMX with FILTER
Weekend Revenue =
SUMX(
  FILTER(Sales, WEEKDAY(Sales[OrderDate], 2) >= 6),
  Sales[Quantity] * Sales[Unit Price]
)

-- GENERATE / GENERATEALL for cross-join iterations
Weighted Score =
SUMX(
  FILTER(
    ADDCOLUMNS(Products, "Score", [Total Revenue] / [Grand Total Revenue]),
    [Score] > 0.05
  ),
  [Score] * Products[Weight]
)
📦 Chapter 10

Variables — VAR / RETURN

Variables make DAX formulas readable, maintainable, and faster. They capture the result of an expression once — avoiding repeated calculation and preventing confusing context shifts inside nested expressions.

DAX — Variables Best Practices
-- Basic VAR usage
Profit Margin =
VAR vRevenue = SUM(Sales[Revenue])
VAR vCost    = SUM(Sales[Cost])
VAR vProfit  = vRevenue - vCost
RETURN
  DIVIDE(vProfit, vRevenue, 0)

-- Variables in conditional logic (avoids evaluating [Revenue LY] twice)
YoY Status =
VAR vCurrentRev = [Total Revenue]
VAR vLastYearRev = [Revenue LY]
VAR vGrowth      = DIVIDE(vCurrentRev - vLastYearRev, vLastYearRev)
RETURN
  SWITCH(TRUE(),
    ISBLANK(vLastYearRev), "No Prior Year",
    vGrowth > 0.10,         "🟢 Strong Growth",
    vGrowth > 0,            "🔵 Moderate Growth",
    vGrowth > -0.10,        "🟡 Slight Decline",
                             "🔴 Significant Decline"
  )

-- Variable capturing a table expression
Top 10 Revenue =
VAR vTop10 =
  TOPN(10, ALL(Products[ProductName]), [Total Revenue], DESC)
RETURN
  CALCULATE(
    [Total Revenue],
    vTop10
  )

-- Multi-return debugging pattern (swap which var you RETURN)
Debug Measure =
VAR vRevenue     = [Total Revenue]
VAR vRevenueLY   = [Revenue LY]
VAR vGrowthAmt   = vRevenue - vRevenueLY
RETURN vGrowthAmt  -- change to vRevenue, vRevenueLY to inspect each stage
🔀 Chapter 11

Logical & Conditional Functions

DAX — Logical Functions
-- IF: basic conditional
IF(Sales[Amount] > 10000, "High", "Low")

-- SWITCH(TRUE()): cleaner multi-branch (replaces nested IF)
Sales Tier =
SWITCH(TRUE(),
  [Total Revenue] >= 1000000, "Platinum",
  [Total Revenue] >=  500000, "Gold",
  [Total Revenue] >=  100000, "Silver",
  "Bronze"
)

-- SWITCH on value
Date[Day Type] =
SWITCH(WEEKDAY(Date[Date],2),
  6, "Weekend",
  7, "Weekend",
  "Weekday"
)

-- AND / OR
AND(Sales[Amount]>0, Sales[Status]="Paid")
Sales[Amount]>0 && Sales[Status]="Paid"   -- same with &&
OR(Sales[Region]="North", Sales[Region]="South")
Sales[Region]="North" || Sales[Region]="South"

-- IFERROR: handle errors gracefully
IFERROR(Sales[Amount] / Sales[Units], 0)

-- ISBLANK: check for blank values
IF(ISBLANK([Revenue LY]), "N/A", FORMAT([YoY %], "0.0%"))

-- COALESCE: return first non-blank (DAX 2020+)
COALESCE(Customers[Phone], Customers[Mobile], "No Contact")
🔤 Chapter 12

Text Functions

DAX — Text Functions
LEN(Customers[Name])                        -- character count
UPPER(Customers[Name])                       -- uppercase
LOWER(Customers[Email])                      -- lowercase
TRIM(Customers[Name])                        -- remove leading/trailing spaces
LEFT(Products[Code], 3)                     -- first 3 chars
RIGHT(Products[Code], 4)                    -- last 4 chars
MID(Products[Code], 3, 5)                  -- 5 chars starting at position 3
FIND("@", Customers[Email])                 -- position of @ (1-based, error if not found)
SEARCH("@", Customers[Email], 1, BLANK())  -- like FIND but case-insensitive, returns blank if not found
SUBSTITUTE(Sales[Notes], "old", "new")      -- replace all occurrences
REPLACE(Sales[Code], 1, 2, "XX")            -- replace by position
REPT("★", Products[Rating])                 -- repeat star rating times
CONCATENATE(Emp[First], Emp[Last])          -- join two strings
Emp[First] & " " & Emp[Last]               -- same using & operator
FORMAT([Total Revenue], "₹#,##0.00")        -- format number as Indian currency
FORMAT(Date[Date], "DD MMM YYYY")           -- "15 Jan 2024"
VALUE("42")                                   -- string to number
TEXT(1234.5, "#,##0.00")                     -- number to string
EXACT("abc", "ABC")                          -- case-sensitive comparison: FALSE
CONTAINS(Products, Products[Name], "Phone") -- TRUE if any row has Name = "Phone"
📅 Chapter 13

Date & Time Functions

DAX — Date Functions
── Create dates ──────────────────────────────────────────
TODAY()                              -- current date
NOW()                                -- current date + time
DATE(2024, 1, 15)                   -- Jan 15, 2024
DATEVALUE("2024-01-15")             -- parse string to date

── Extract parts ─────────────────────────────────────────
YEAR(Sales[OrderDate])              -- 2024
MONTH(Sales[OrderDate])             -- 1-12
DAY(Sales[OrderDate])               -- 1-31
HOUR(Sales[OrderTime])              -- 0-23
MINUTE(Sales[OrderTime])            -- 0-59
WEEKDAY(Sales[OrderDate], 2)        -- 1=Mon, 7=Sun
WEEKNUM(Sales[OrderDate], 2)        -- week number of year
QUARTER(Sales[OrderDate])           -- 1-4
EOMONTH(Sales[OrderDate], 0)        -- last day of same month
EOMONTH(Sales[OrderDate], -1)       -- last day of previous month

── Date arithmetic ───────────────────────────────────────
DATEDIFF(Customers[DOB], TODAY(), YEAR)  -- age in years
EDATE(TODAY(), 3)                          -- 3 months from today
EDATE(TODAY(), -1)                         -- 1 month ago

── Practical examples ────────────────────────────────────
-- Days since last order per customer
Customers[Days Since Last Order] =
  DATEDIFF(
    CALCULATE(MAX(Sales[OrderDate])),
    TODAY(),
    DAY
  )

-- Is the selected date in the last 7 days?
In Last 7 Days =
  IF(MAX(Date[Date]) >= TODAY()-7, "Yes", "No")
🔗 Chapter 14

Relationships & USERELATIONSHIP

DAX formulas automatically follow active relationships in the data model. USERELATIONSHIP lets you use an inactive relationship inside a CALCULATE expression.

DAX — Relationship Functions
-- RELATED: lookup value from the "one" side of a relationship (in calculated column)
Sales[Product Category] = RELATED(Products[Category])
Sales[Customer Name]   = RELATED(Customers[Name])

-- RELATEDTABLE: get all related rows from "many" side (in calculated column)
Customers[Order Count] = COUNTROWS(RELATEDTABLE(Sales))

-- USERELATIONSHIP: use inactive relationship
-- Scenario: Sales table has OrderDate AND ShipDate, both related to Date table
-- Only OrderDate relationship is active. To analyze by ShipDate:
Revenue by Ship Date =
CALCULATE(
  [Total Revenue],
  USERELATIONSHIP(Sales[ShipDate], Date[Date])
)

-- CROSSFILTER: change filter direction within CALCULATE
Products with Sales =
CALCULATE(
  DISTINCTCOUNT(Products[ProductID]),
  CROSSFILTER(Sales[ProductID], Products[ProductID], BOTH)
)

-- TREATAS: treat a table as if it has a relationship
Revenue for Top Products =
CALCULATE(
  [Total Revenue],
  TREATAS(
    {"Product A", "Product B", "Product C"},
    Products[ProductName]
  )
)
🏆 Chapter 15

RANKX, TOPN & Advanced Row Context

DAX — Ranking & Top N
-- RANKX across all products (rank 1 = highest revenue)
Product Rank =
RANKX(ALL(Products[ProductName]), [Total Revenue])

-- RANKX within category (partition by category)
Rank in Category =
RANKX(
  ALLSELECTED(Products[ProductName]),
  [Total Revenue], , DESC, DENSE
)

-- TOPN: get table of top N rows
Top 5 Customers Revenue =
CALCULATE(
  [Total Revenue],
  TOPN(5,
    ALL(Customers[CustomerName]),
    [Total Revenue],
    DESC
  )
)

-- TOPN in a visual — show only top 5 products
Is Top 5 =
VAR vTop5 = TOPN(5, ALL(Products), [Total Revenue])
RETURN
  IF(CONTAINS(vTop5, Products[ProductID], MAX(Products[ProductID])), TRUE)
📡 Chapter 16

Semi-Additive Measures

Fully additive measures (like Revenue) can be summed across any dimension. Semi-additive measures (like Inventory, Balance) cannot be summed across time — you should take the last value or average instead.

DAX — Semi-Additive Patterns
-- End of Period Inventory (LASTNONBLANK)
Inventory End of Period =
CALCULATE(
  SUM(Inventory[Quantity]),
  LASTNONBLANK(Date[Date], CALCULATE(SUM(Inventory[Quantity])))
)

-- Bank balance — last day of period
Balance EoP =
CALCULATE(
  SUM(Accounts[Balance]),
  LASTDATE(Date[Date])
)

-- Headcount — count employees as of last date in period
Headcount =
CALCULATE(
  COUNTROWS(Employees),
  LASTDATE(Date[Date])
)

-- Average daily balance across the period
Avg Daily Balance =
AVERAGEX(
  DATESINPERIOD(Date[Date], LASTDATE(Date[Date]), -30, DAY),
  CALCULATE(SUM(Accounts[Balance]))
)
🔒 Chapter 17

Row-Level Security (RLS)

RLS restricts which data rows a user can see when they view a Power BI report. You define roles with DAX filter expressions — each role limits the data model based on the logged-in user.

DAX — RLS Patterns
-- Static RLS: all users in this role see only North region
-- (Table filter on Regions table)
[Region] = "North"

-- Dynamic RLS: each user sees only their own region
-- Username comes from the Security table (email mapped to region)
[Email] = USERPRINCIPALNAME()

-- Dynamic RLS via bridge table (many-to-many user-region mapping)
Regions[RegionID] IN
  CALCULATETABLE(
    VALUES(UserRegions[RegionID]),
    UserRegions[UserEmail] = USERPRINCIPALNAME()
  )

-- Manager sees own data + all direct reports (hierarchy RLS)
Employees[Email] = USERPRINCIPALNAME()
  || Employees[ManagerEmail] = USERPRINCIPALNAME()
🚀 Chapter 18

DAX Performance & Best Practices

Well-written DAX can be 100x faster than naive DAX. These patterns separate professional Power BI developers from beginners.

Performance Rules

DAX — Optimization Patterns
-- ❌ SLOW: FILTER on a table with RELATED (iterates every row)
CALCULATE([Revenue], FILTER(Sales, RELATED(Products[Category])="Elec"))

-- ✅ FAST: Direct column filter (uses VertiPaq compression index)
CALCULATE([Revenue], Products[Category] = "Electronics")

-- ❌ SLOW: Repeating the same expression multiple times
Bad Measure =
IF(
  DIVIDE([Revenue]-[Cost], [Revenue]) > 0.2,
  DIVIDE([Revenue]-[Cost], [Revenue]),   -- recalculated!
  0
)
-- ✅ FAST: Use variables to capture once
Good Measure =
VAR vMargin = DIVIDE([Revenue]-[Cost], [Revenue])
RETURN IF(vMargin > 0.2, vMargin, 0)

-- ❌ SLOW: COUNTROWS(FILTER()) for counting with conditions
COUNTROWS(FILTER(Sales, Sales[Amount] > 1000))
-- ✅ FAST: CALCULATE(COUNTROWS()) — avoids materializing filtered table
CALCULATE(COUNTROWS(Sales), Sales[Amount] > 1000)

-- ❌ SLOW: Using measures inside FILTER (recalculates in row context each row)
FILTER(Sales, [Total Revenue] > 10000)
-- ✅ FAST: Use column directly if available
FILTER(Sales, Sales[Amount] > 10000)

Best Practices Checklist

RuleWhy
Always use explicit measures (never implicit)Reusable, formattable, referenceable from other measures
Use VAR to capture repeated expressionsComputed once, avoids context shift bugs, faster
Prefer column filters over FILTER+RELATEDVertiPaq segment elimination is much faster
Use DIVIDE() not /Built-in divide-by-zero protection
Mark your Date tableRequired for time intelligence functions
Avoid many calculated columnsThey consume RAM (VertiPaq materialization)
Use CALCULATE(COUNTROWS()) over COUNTROWS(FILTER())CALCULATE uses indices; FILTER materializes full table
Store all measures in a _Measures tableOrganization, cleanliness, professional model structure
Use SELECTEDVALUE() for slicer-driven logicReturns blank (not error) when multiple values selected
Analyze with DAX Studio + VertiPaq AnalyzerFind slow queries, large columns, and model bloat
🟢 DAX Practice

DAX Q&A — Beginner (25 Questions)

Fundamental DAX concepts and formulas. Perfect for beginners and Power BI interview prep.

Theory (Q1–Q12)

Q1. What is DAX and what is it used for? ▼

DAX (Data Analysis Expressions) is a formula language used in Power BI, Power Pivot (Excel), and Azure Analysis Services. It's used to define: Measures (dynamic calculations like Total Sales, Profit %), Calculated Columns (new table columns computed row by row), and Calculated Tables (virtual tables like a Date dimension). DAX is expression-based — you define what to calculate, not how to loop through data.

Q2. What is the difference between a Measure and a Calculated Column? ▼
AspectMeasureCalculated Column
Computed whenQuery time (dynamic)Refresh time (static)
Stored in RAMNoYes
Filter-awareYes — adapts to every visual filterNo — fixed at refresh
Has row contextNo (unless inside SUMX etc.)Yes — sees each row
Used inVisual values, KPIs, cardsSlicer fields, row-level attributes
Q3. What is filter context? ▼

Filter context is the set of active filters that determine which rows participate in a DAX calculation. It comes from: report-level filters, page filters, visual-level filters, slicer selections, and row/column headers in a matrix. A measure like SUM(Sales[Amount]) automatically returns different results on each row of a matrix because the row header creates a different filter context for each cell.

Q4. What is row context? ▼

Row context is created when DAX iterates over a table row by row. It exists in: calculated column definitions (each row has its own context), and iterator functions like SUMX, FILTER, ADDCOLUMNS. In row context, Sales[Amount] refers to THIS row's Amount value. Measures don't have row context by default — they need SUMX or CALCULATE to work row by row.

Q5. What does CALCULATE do? ▼

CALCULATE evaluates an expression while modifying the filter context. It is the most important function in DAX. Syntax: CALCULATE(expression, filter1, filter2, ...). The filters add to, override, or remove existing filters before the expression is evaluated. Without CALCULATE, you cannot change the context a measure runs in — it will always use whatever the visual provides.

Q6. What is the difference between SUM and SUMX? ▼

SUM(Table[Column]) sums a single column directly — fast, no row context created. SUMX(Table, expression) iterates over every row of Table, evaluates the expression in each row's context, then sums the results. Use SUMX when you need to calculate something per row first: SUMX(Sales, Sales[Qty] * Sales[Price]) multiplies then sums — you can't do this with a single SUM if there's no pre-computed total column.

Q7. What is ALL() used for? ▼

ALL() removes filter context from a table or column. Used inside CALCULATE to create "ignore filter" measures. CALCULATE([Total Sales], ALL(Products)) returns total sales for all products regardless of which product the visual is filtering on. It's essential for % of total calculations: divide the filtered value by the ALL() version to get the proportion.

Q8. What is BLANK() in DAX? How is it different from NULL? ▼

BLANK() is DAX's equivalent of absence of value — similar to NULL in SQL but with key differences. Arithmetic with BLANK treats it as 0 or empty string (BLANK() + 5 = 5). Comparisons: BLANK() = BLANK() returns TRUE. BLANK() propagates through most functions but not through arithmetic. Use ISBLANK() to test for it. In Power BI visuals, measures returning BLANK() are hidden (cell appears empty), which is useful for hiding zero rows.

Q9. Why do time intelligence functions require a Date table? ▼

Time intelligence functions (TOTALYTD, SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR, PREVIOUSMONTH, etc.) navigate the date dimension to find "same period" dates. They need: (1) a Date table marked as a Date Table in Power BI, (2) a column of DATE type with no gaps (every calendar day present), (3) unique dates (one row per day), and (4) a relationship from the fact table to this Date table. Without these, the functions produce incorrect or blank results.

Q10. What is DIVIDE() and why is it preferred over /? ▼

DIVIDE(numerator, denominator, [alternate]) is a safe division function. If the denominator is 0 or BLANK, it returns the alternate value (default: BLANK()) instead of throwing an error. Using / directly can cause "division by zero" errors visible in visuals. Always use DIVIDE for any division involving measures or user data where the denominator might be 0.

Q11. What is the purpose of VAR in DAX? ▼

VAR stores the result of an expression in a named variable, and RETURN specifies what the measure ultimately returns. Benefits: (1) Performance — the variable is computed once even if referenced multiple times; (2) Readability — complex formulas become readable step-by-step; (3) Debugging — temporarily RETURN a variable to inspect its value; (4) Context safety — a variable captures the value at the point of declaration, preventing confusing context shifts in nested calculations.

Q12. What is SELECTEDVALUE() and HASONEVALUE()? ▼

SELECTEDVALUE(column, default) returns the value of a column when it is filtered to exactly one value (e.g., one item selected in a slicer). Returns the default (or BLANK) when multiple values are selected. HASONEVALUE(column) returns TRUE when exactly one value is visible in the filter context. Use them for dynamic titles, conditional formatting, and single-selection-dependent logic.

🟡 DAX Practice

DAX Q&A — Intermediate (30 Questions)

CALCULATE, time intelligence, X-functions, context transition, and real-world Power BI patterns.

Theory (Q1–Q12)

Q1. Explain context transition in DAX. ▼

Context transition happens when CALCULATE is used inside a row context (calculated column or iterator). CALCULATE converts each unique combination of column values in the current row into an equivalent filter context. Example: in a calculated column, CALCULATE(SUM(Sales[Amount])) doesn't return the grand total — it applies the current row's CustomerID as a filter and returns that customer's total sales. This is a key advanced concept that enables powerful row-level aggregation in calculated columns.

Q2. What is the difference between ALL() and ALLSELECTED()? ▼

ALL() removes ALL filters — including those from slicers, page filters, and visual filters. The result is always the absolute grand total. ALLSELECTED() removes row/column header filters from the visual but keeps slicer and external filter selections. This makes ALLSELECTED perfect for "% of what's currently filtered" — if a user filters to 2024 via a slicer, ALLSELECTED keeps that year filter while removing product/region filters from the matrix.

Q3. When would you use KEEPFILTERS()? ▼

Normally, CALCULATE overrides an existing filter on the same column with the new one. KEEPFILTERS makes CALCULATE intersect filters instead. Example: if the visual has Category = "Electronics" and you use CALCULATE([Revenue], KEEPFILTERS(Category = "Mobiles")), the result is BLANK (Electronics AND Mobiles is an empty intersection). Without KEEPFILTERS, it would override to Mobiles. Use KEEPFILTERS when you want the new filter to narrow down the existing context rather than replace it.

Q4. What is USERELATIONSHIP() and when do you need it? ▼

USERELATIONSHIP activates an inactive relationship for the duration of a CALCULATE expression. Common scenario: a Sales table has both an OrderDate and a ShipDate, both with a relationship to the Date table — but only one can be active at a time. To build a "Revenue by Ship Date" measure without changing the model's active relationship, you use CALCULATE([Total Revenue], USERELATIONSHIP(Sales[ShipDate], Date[Date])). This temporarily uses the ShipDate→Date relationship for that one calculation.

Q5. What is RANKX() and what are its parameters? ▼

RANKX ranks a value against a table of values. Parameters: RANKX(table, expression, [value], [order], [ties]). table: the set of values to rank against (usually ALL or ALLSELECTED of a dimension). expression: what to rank by (usually a measure). value: the value to rank (blank = use current context). order: DESC (default, 1=highest) or ASC. ties: DENSE (no gaps: 1,2,2,3) or SKIP (1,2,2,4). DENSE is usually preferred for clean rankings.

Q6. Explain the difference between EARLIER() and VAR in row context. ▼

Both solve the "access outer row context" problem but VAR is the modern approach. EARLIER() references the row context one level "up" from a nested row context — it was the only way before variables. Example: comparing each row's salary to the average salary of its category in a calculated column. With EARLIER: AVERAGEX(FILTER(Employees, [Category]=EARLIER([Category])), [Salary]). With VAR (cleaner): VAR vCat = [Category] RETURN AVERAGEX(FILTER(Employees, [Category]=vCat), [Salary]). Always use VAR in modern DAX — EARLIER is legacy.

Q7. What is a semi-additive measure? Give examples. ▼

A semi-additive measure cannot be meaningfully summed across the time dimension, even though it can be summed across other dimensions (like product or region). Examples: Inventory quantity (summing Jan + Feb stock is meaningless — you want the end-of-month balance), Bank account balance, Headcount, Active subscribers. For these, use LASTDATE(), LASTNONBLANK(), or AVERAGEX over time rather than SUM across dates.

Q8. What is the VertiPaq engine and why does it matter for DAX? ▼

VertiPaq is Power BI's in-memory columnar storage engine. It compresses data by column using dictionary encoding and RLE (Run-Length Encoding) — this is why a column with many repeated values (like "Country") is tiny in memory. DAX formulas execute against this engine via Storage Engine queries (fast, parallelized) and Formula Engine computations (single-threaded, slower). Good DAX pushes as much work as possible to the Storage Engine (column filters, aggregations) and minimizes Formula Engine work (which happens when using FILTER with measures, context transition, etc.).

Q9. What is ALLEXCEPT() and how does it differ from ALL()? ▼

ALL(Table) removes all filters from the entire table. ALLEXCEPT(Table, col1, col2) removes all filters from the table except the specified columns. This is useful for "% of subtotal" in a matrix: if you have Region and Category on rows, and you want % of region total (keeping Region filter but removing Category), use ALLEXCEPT(Products, Products[Region]) in the denominator's CALCULATE.

Q10. What are the main time intelligence functions in DAX? ▼
  • TOTALYTD / TOTALQTD / TOTALMTD: Accumulate from start of period to current date
  • SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR: Same date range, one year back
  • PREVIOUSYEAR / PREVIOUSQUARTER / PREVIOUSMONTH: Full prior period
  • DATEADD: Shift dates by N intervals (days, months, quarters, years)
  • DATESINPERIOD: All dates in a rolling window (e.g., last 90 days)
  • DATESMTD / DATESQTD / DATESYTD: Return table of dates from start of period
  • FIRSTDATE / LASTDATE: First or last date in current context
  • LASTNONBLANK: Last date with data — essential for semi-additive measures
Q11. What is the difference between RELATED() and RELATEDTABLE()? ▼

RELATED() follows a many-to-one relationship and returns a single value from the "one" side. Used in calculated columns on the "many" side. Example: Sales[Category] = RELATED(Products[Category]) — each Sales row gets its product's category. RELATEDTABLE() follows a one-to-many relationship and returns a table of all related rows from the "many" side. Used in calculated columns on the "one" side. Example: Customers[OrderCount] = COUNTROWS(RELATEDTABLE(Sales)).

Q12. What is Row-Level Security (RLS) in Power BI? ▼

RLS restricts which rows of data each user can see in a published report. You define Roles in Power BI Desktop, and each role has a DAX filter expression applied to one or more tables (e.g., [Region] = "North"). When a user views the report, Power BI applies the filter of their assigned role — they only see North data. Dynamic RLS uses USERPRINCIPALNAME() to filter based on the logged-in user's identity, matching against a security mapping table.

🔴 DAX Practice

DAX Q&A — Advanced (35 Questions)

Complex context scenarios, performance optimization, data modeling patterns, and senior-level DAX interview questions.

Theory (Q1–Q15)

Q1. Explain the Storage Engine vs Formula Engine in Power BI. ▼

DAX execution uses two engines. The Storage Engine (SE) is multi-threaded, reads VertiPaq compressed columns, performs aggregations and simple filters extremely fast using columnar indexes. The Formula Engine (FE) is single-threaded, handles complex logic, iterators, context transitions, and non-SARGable operations. Good DAX pushes work to the SE (column equality filters, simple aggregations) and minimizes FE work (FILTER with measures, nested iterators). Tools like DAX Studio show SE and FE query logs, helping you identify which operations are bottlenecks.

Q2. What is cardinality in Power BI and how does it affect performance? ▼

Cardinality = number of unique values in a column. High-cardinality columns (UUIDs, timestamps, free text) compress poorly in VertiPaq, consume more RAM, and slow down filter operations. Reduce cardinality by: rounding timestamps to date (remove time component), using integer keys instead of string keys for relationships, removing high-cardinality columns that aren't needed in visuals, using a date table instead of datetime in the fact table. Low cardinality columns (country, status, boolean) compress extremely well and are fast to filter.

Q3. What is bidirectional cross-filtering and when is it dangerous? ▼

In a standard relationship, filters flow from the one-side to the many-side. With bidirectional cross-filtering, filters also flow from many to one. This enables some convenient patterns (counting products that have been sold, filtering dimension by fact data) but is dangerous in complex models: it can cause circular filter propagation, ambiguous filter paths, and significant performance degradation. Best practice: use single-direction relationships by default, and use CROSSFILTER() inside CALCULATE when you need bidirectional behavior for a specific measure.

Q4. What is the difference between GENERATE() and ADDCOLUMNS()? ▼

ADDCOLUMNS(table, colName, expr, ...) adds calculated columns to an existing table — it returns the original table with new columns appended. GENERATE(table1, table2expr) creates a row-by-row cross-join: for each row in table1, evaluates table2expr in that row's context and appends the results. ADDCOLUMNS is used when you just want to enrich a table with computed columns. GENERATE is used when you need to expand a table by attaching related row sets to each row — like a lateral join in SQL.

Q5. How do you implement ABC analysis (segmenting products by revenue contribution) in DAX? ▼
DAX — ABC Analysis
ABC Segment =
VAR vRevShare =
  DIVIDE(
    [Total Revenue],
    CALCULATE([Total Revenue], ALL(Products))
  )
VAR vCumShare =
  SUMX(
    FILTER(
      ALL(Products[ProductName]),
      CALCULATE([Total Revenue]) >= [Total Revenue]
    ),
    DIVIDE(CALCULATE([Total Revenue]), CALCULATE([Total Revenue], ALL(Products)))
  )
RETURN
  SWITCH(TRUE(),
    vCumShare <= 0.70, "A — Top 70%",
    vCumShare <= 0.90, "B — Next 20%",
    "C — Bottom 10%"
  )
Q6–10. DAX Studio workflow | Disconnected tables | What-if parameters | Dynamic segmentation | Many-to-many ▼

Q6 — DAX Studio: Free tool for measuring and optimizing DAX. Use it to: run measures and see execution time, read Server Timings (SE vs FE time), run VertiPaq Analyzer to find large columns, check query plan, and test measures without publishing. For production models, every complex measure should be profiled in DAX Studio before deployment.

Q7 — Disconnected tables: Tables with no relationship to the data model, used as parameter sources. Example: a "Sales Target" table where each row is a target option (₹1M, ₹5M, ₹10M). The user picks one via a slicer; the measure uses SELECTEDVALUE() to read it and apply it. Enables dynamic benchmarking and what-if scenarios without actual data relationships.

Q8 — What-If parameters: Power BI's built-in feature creates a disconnected parameter table with a numeric slicer. The automatically generated measure captures the selected value. Use it for price elasticity modeling, scenario analysis, discount simulation, target-setting dashboards — anywhere the user needs to adjust a parameter dynamically.

Q9 — Dynamic segmentation: Segment customers into tiers based on live measures (not stored data). Example: classify each customer as Gold/Silver/Bronze based on their current-context revenue. Use a calculated measure with SWITCH(TRUE(), ...) referencing [Total Revenue]. The tier updates in real time as filters change.

Q10 — Many-to-many relationships: When both sides of a relationship have non-unique values (e.g., a product in multiple categories, a salesperson covering multiple regions), you need a bridge table. Create a junction table (ProductCategory) and use it as an intermediary. With bidirectional cross-filtering on both relationships, filters flow through the bridge. Alternatively, use TREATAS or INTERSECT in DAX to handle M:N without bridge tables.

Q11–15. Composite models | Aggregations | DirectQuery limitations | CALCULATE without filters | Tabular model roles ▼

Q11 — Composite models: Power BI composite models mix Import mode (VertiPaq in-memory) and DirectQuery mode tables in the same model. Small dimension tables import for speed; huge fact tables query live from the database. The Import dimensions filter DirectQuery facts via the relationship. Enables interactive performance with up-to-date large data.

Q12 — User-Defined Aggregations: For composite models with huge DirectQuery tables, you can define pre-aggregated summary tables in Import mode. Power BI automatically uses the aggregation table when possible and falls back to DirectQuery for detail queries. Dramatically speeds up high-level reports while still allowing drill-through to transaction data.

Q13 — DirectQuery DAX limitations: DAX functions that materialize large intermediate tables (complex FILTER, ADDCOLUMNS, GENERATE) can be extremely slow in DirectQuery as they translate to SQL subqueries. Avoid: complex iterator patterns, measures with many nested CALCULATEs, high-cardinality DISTINCTCOUNT. Prefer: simple aggregations, direct column filters, simple time intelligence.

Q14 — CALCULATE() with no filters: CALCULATE(expression) with no filter arguments still triggers context transition — it converts any active row context into filter context. This is essential for using measures inside calculated columns. Always call CALCULATE when you want a measure to be "context-aware" inside an iterator or calculated column.

Q15 — Object-Level Security: Beyond RLS (row-level), Power BI supports Object-Level Security (OLS) via Tabular Editor — you can hide entire tables or columns from specific roles. A user in a restricted role can't see the table exists at all, not just filtered rows.

Advanced Formula Practice (Q16–Q35)

Q16. Write a complete DAX Date Table using ADDCOLUMNS + CALENDAR. ▼
DAX — Full Date Table
Dim Date =
ADDCOLUMNS(
  CALENDAR(DATE(2020,1,1), DATE(2026,12,31)),
  "Year",         YEAR([Date]),
  "Quarter",      "Q" & QUARTER([Date]),
  "Month",        MONTH([Date]),
  "MonthName",    FORMAT([Date], "MMMM"),
  "MonthShort",   FORMAT([Date], "MMM"),
  "YearMonth",    FORMAT([Date], "YYYY-MM"),
  "WeekNum",      WEEKNUM([Date],2),
  "DayOfWeek",    WEEKDAY([Date],2),
  "DayName",      FORMAT([Date], "dddd"),
  "IsWeekend",    WEEKDAY([Date],2) >= 6,
  "FiscalYear",   "FY" & IF(MONTH([Date])>=4,YEAR([Date])+1,YEAR([Date])),
  "FiscalQuarter","FQ" & SWITCH(MONTH([Date]),
    4,"1",5,"1",6,"1",7,"2",8,"2",9,"2",
    10,"3",11,"3",12,"3","4")
)
Q17. Write Dynamic RLS for a manager hierarchy. ▼
DAX — Hierarchical RLS Filter
-- Filter on Employees table (role definition)
-- Each user sees themselves + everyone they manage directly
[Email] = USERPRINCIPALNAME()
|| [ManagerEmail] = USERPRINCIPALNAME()
Q18. Write a measure for Customer Lifetime Value with recency weighting. ▼
DAX — Weighted LTV
Weighted LTV =
SUMX(
  Sales,
  Sales[Revenue] *
  EXP(
    -0.01 *
    DATEDIFF(Sales[OrderDate], TODAY(), DAY)
  )
)
-- Exponential decay: recent orders weighted more heavily than old ones
Q19–25. Budget vs Actual | Customer cohort month | Product velocity | Waterfall chart measure | Forecast | Pareto | Dynamic target line ▼
Q19 — Budget vs Actual Variance
Budget Variance =
VAR vActual = [Total Revenue]
VAR vBudget = SUM(Budget[Target])
RETURN
  DIVIDE(vActual - vBudget, vBudget)
Q20 — Customer Acquisition Cohort Month
Customers[Cohort Month] =
FORMAT(
  CALCULATE(MIN(Sales[OrderDate])),
  "YYYY-MM"
)
Q21 — Product Velocity (Units Sold per Day)
Velocity =
VAR vDays = DISTINCTCOUNT(Date[Date])
RETURN
  DIVIDE(SUM(Sales[Quantity]), vDays)
Q22 — Pareto / Cumulative % for Combo Chart
Cumulative % of Total =
DIVIDE(
  SUMX(
    FILTER(
      ALL(Products[ProductName]),
      CALCULATE([Total Revenue]) >= [Total Revenue]
    ),
    CALCULATE([Total Revenue])
  ),
  CALCULATE([Total Revenue], ALL(Products))
)
Q23 — Forecast: Linear trend extension
Forecast Revenue =
IF(
  MAX(Date[Date]) > TODAY(),
  [Revenue YTD] * DIVIDE(365,
    DATEDIFF(DATE(YEAR(TODAY()),1,1), TODAY(), DAY)),
  BLANK()
)
-- Projects current YTD run rate to end of year (simple linear)
Q26–35. Performance patterns | SUMMARIZE | INTERSECT | EXCEPT | New vs returning customers | Market share | Churn rate | Days in stock | Revenue bridge | KPI status ▼
Q26 — SUMMARIZE for virtual table aggregation
Avg Revenue per Region =
VAR vRegionRevs =
  SUMMARIZE(
    Sales,
    Regions[Region],
    "RegionRev", [Total Revenue]
  )
RETURN
  AVERAGEX(vRegionRevs, [RegionRev])
Q27 — New vs Returning Customers
New Customers =
COUNTROWS(
  FILTER(
    VALUES(Sales[CustomerID]),
    CALCULATE(
      MIN(Sales[OrderDate]),
      ALL(Date)
    ) >= MIN(Date[Date])
  )
)
Q28 — Market Share %
Market Share % =
DIVIDE(
  [Total Revenue],
  CALCULATE([Total Revenue],
    ALL(Products[Brand]))
)
Q29 — Customer Churn Rate
Churn Rate =
VAR vActive  = DISTINCTCOUNT(Sales[CustomerID])
VAR vActiveLY =
  CALCULATE(
    DISTINCTCOUNT(Sales[CustomerID]),
    SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR(Date[Date])
  )
RETURN
  DIVIDE(vActiveLY - vActive, vActiveLY)
Q30 — KPI Status with color coding
KPI Color =
VAR vGrowth = [YoY %]
RETURN
  SWITCH(TRUE(),
    ISBLANK(vGrowth),  "Grey",
    vGrowth >  0.05,   "Green",
    vGrowth >= 0,      "Yellow",
    "Red"
  )
Q31–35 — Advanced Interview Scenarios
-- Q31: Revenue for products that also sold last year (INTERSECT)
Retained Products Revenue =
CALCULATE(
  [Total Revenue],
  INTERSECT(
    VALUES(Sales[ProductID]),
    CALCULATE(VALUES(Sales[ProductID]),
      PREVIOUSYEAR(Date[Date]))
  )
)

-- Q32: Revenue for NEW products (sold this year but not last year - EXCEPT)
New Product Revenue =
CALCULATE(
  [Total Revenue],
  EXCEPT(
    VALUES(Sales[ProductID]),
    CALCULATE(VALUES(Sales[ProductID]),
      PREVIOUSYEAR(Date[Date]))
  )
)

-- Q33: Days inventory on hand
Days on Hand =
VAR vDailySales = DIVIDE([Total Units Sold], DISTINCTCOUNT(Date[Date]))
RETURN
  DIVIDE(SUM(Inventory[Qty]), vDailySales)

-- Q34: Revenue contribution of top N% products
Top 20% Products Revenue =
VAR vTotalProducts = COUNTROWS(ALL(Products))
VAR vTop20 = ROUNDUP(vTotalProducts * 0.2, 0)
RETURN
  CALCULATE(
    [Total Revenue],
    TOPN(vTop20, ALL(Products), [Total Revenue])
  )

-- Q35: Complete Measure Folder structure (display folders best practice)
-- In Power BI, set "Display Folder" property:
-- [Total Revenue]     → "Sales\Base Measures"
-- [Revenue YTD]       → "Sales\Time Intelligence"
-- [YoY %]             → "Sales\Time Intelligence"
-- [Profit Margin %]   → "Finance\Profitability"
-- [Product Rank]      → "Products\Rankings"

How to Ace DAX Interviews

  • Always start with context: Explain whether you need row context or filter context before writing the formula.
  • Know your CALCULATE inside out: It's in ~70% of real DAX formulas.
  • Use VAR: It shows you understand both performance and readability.
  • Explain ALL() vs ALLSELECTED(): This trips up most candidates.
  • Know time intelligence prerequisites: Date table requirements are frequently asked.
  • Practice in DAX Studio: Being able to profile and optimize a slow measure is a senior-level differentiator.
