📌 Chapter 1

What is PySpark?

Apache Spark is a unified analytics engine for large-scale data processing. PySpark is its Python API, allowing distributed computation on clusters of machines.

Architecture & SparkSession

🎛️

Driver

The main program coordinating the job. Hosts the SparkContext and DAGScheduler. Runs on master node.

⚙️

Executors

Worker processes that run tasks. Each executor has a fixed number of cores and memory. Results are sent back to the driver.

🗂️

Partitions

Data is split into partitions — each partition is processed by one task on one executor. More partitions = more parallelism.

📊

DAG

Directed Acyclic Graph of stages and tasks. Spark optimises the DAG before execution using the Catalyst optimizer.

PySpark — SparkSession
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession

spark = (SparkSession.builder
    .appName("MyETL")
    .config("spark.executor.memory", "4g")
    .config("spark.executor.cores",  "2")
    .config("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions", "200")
    .getOrCreate())

spark.version          # e.g. '3.5.0'
spark.sparkContext     # underlying SparkContext
spark.stop()           # always stop when done
🔢 Chapter 2

RDDs — Resilient Distributed Datasets

RDDs are the low-level building block of Spark — immutable, distributed collections. Most modern code uses DataFrames, but understanding RDDs is essential for debugging and performance tuning.

RDD Operations

PySpark — RDD
sc = spark.sparkContext

# Create RDD
rdd = sc.parallelize([1,2,3,4,5], numSlices=4)
rdd2 = sc.textFile("s3://bucket/logs/*.txt")

# Transformations (lazy)
doubled = rdd.map(lambda x: x * 2)
evens   = rdd.filter(lambda x: x % 2 == 0)
words   = rdd2.flatMap(lambda line: line.split())

# Key-Value RDD
pairs = words.map(lambda w: (w, 1))
counts = pairs.reduceByKey(lambda a, b: a + b)

# Actions (trigger execution)
rdd.collect()          # bring all to driver (careful!)
rdd.take(5)            # first 5 elements
rdd.count()            # total elements
rdd.reduce(lambda a,b: a+b)  # fold to single value
counts.sortBy(lambda x: -x[1]).take(10)  # top 10
📋 Chapter 3

DataFrames & Datasets

Spark DataFrames provide a higher-level, schema-aware API — similar to Pandas but distributed. They use the Catalyst optimizer for automatic query optimisation.

Core DataFrame Operations

PySpark — DataFrame
from pyspark.sql import functions as F
from pyspark.sql.types import StructType, StructField, StringType, IntegerType

# Read
df = spark.read.parquet("s3://bucket/orders/")
df = spark.read.csv("data.csv", header=True, inferSchema=True)

# Inspect
df.printSchema()
df.show(5, truncate=False)
df.describe().show()

# Select & Filter
df.select("id", "amount", F.col("status").alias("order_status"))
df.filter(F.col("amount") > 100)
df.where("status = 'shipped' AND amount > 50")

# New columns
df.withColumn("tax",   F.col("amount") * 0.18) \
  .withColumn("total", F.col("amount") + F.col("tax"))

# UDF — user-defined function (slow, avoid if possible)
from pyspark.sql.functions import udf
@udf(returnType=StringType())
def tier(amt): return "High" if amt > 1000 else "Low"
df.withColumn("tier", tier(F.col("amount")))
🗄️ Chapter 4

Spark SQL

SQL on Distributed DataFrames

PySpark — Spark SQL
# Register as temp view
df.createOrReplaceTempView("orders")
df_customers.createOrReplaceTempView("customers")

# Run SQL — same as on a traditional DB
result = spark.sql("""
  SELECT
    c.name,
    COUNT(o.id)        AS total_orders,
    SUM(o.amount)      AS total_spent,
    AVG(o.amount)      AS avg_order,
    MAX(o.order_date)  AS last_order
  FROM orders    o
  JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
  WHERE o.status = 'completed'
  GROUP BY c.name
  HAVING SUM(o.amount) > 1000
  ORDER BY total_spent DESC
""")
result.show()

# Global temp view — visible across sessions
df.createGlobalTempView("global_orders")
spark.sql("SELECT * FROM global_temp.global_orders LIMIT 10")

# Cache a table for repeated queries
spark.catalog.cacheTable("orders")
🔄 Chapter 5

Transformations & Actions

Lazy vs Eager Execution

Transformations (select, filter, join, groupBy) are lazy — they build a plan but don't execute. Actions (show, count, collect, write) trigger execution — Spark sends the optimised DAG to the cluster. This means you can chain many transformations cheaply.

PySpark — Transformations vs Actions
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

# TRANSFORMATIONS — no computation yet
t1 = df.filter(F.col("status") == "active")
t2 = t1.select("id", "amount")
t3 = t2.withColumn("taxed", F.col("amount") * 1.18)
t4 = t3.orderBy("amount", ascending=False)

# ACTION — triggers the entire plan
t4.show(10)                    # print to console
t4.count()                     # returns int
t4.collect()                   # list of Row objects (careful with large data)
t4.first()                     # first Row
t4.write.parquet("s3://out/")  # write to storage

# Explain — see the query plan
t4.explain(mode="formatted")
🔗 Chapter 6

Joins & Aggregations

All Join Types + GroupBy

PySpark — Joins & Aggregations
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

# Join types: inner, left, right, full, left_semi, left_anti, cross
joined = orders.join(customers, on="customer_id", how="left")

# Broadcast join — small table fit in memory (avoids shuffle)
from pyspark.sql.functions import broadcast
joined = orders.join(broadcast(lookup_df), "product_id")

# GroupBy aggregations
df.groupBy("dept").agg(
    F.count("id").alias("headcount"),
    F.avg("salary").alias("avg_salary"),
    F.sum("salary").alias("total_salary"),
    F.max("salary").alias("max_salary"),
    F.countDistinct("location").alias("offices")
).show()

# Pivot
df.groupBy("dept").pivot("quarter").sum("revenue")
🪟 Chapter 7

Window Functions

rank, lag, rolling — partitioned over distributed data

PySpark — Window Functions
from pyspark.sql import functions as F
from pyspark.sql.window import Window

# Define window spec
w_dept = Window.partitionBy("dept").orderBy(F.desc("salary"))

# Ranking
df.withColumn("rank",       F.rank().over(w_dept)) \
  .withColumn("dense_rank", F.dense_rank().over(w_dept)) \
  .withColumn("row_num",    F.row_number().over(w_dept))

# Lag/Lead
w_time = Window.partitionBy("user_id").orderBy("event_time")
df.withColumn("prev_event", F.lag("event", 1).over(w_time)) \
  .withColumn("next_event", F.lead("event", 1).over(w_time))

# Running total
w_run = Window.partitionBy("dept").orderBy("hire_date").rowsBetween(Window.unboundedPreceding, Window.currentRow)
df.withColumn("running_salary", F.sum("salary").over(w_run))

# Percent of group
df.withColumn("dept_total", F.sum("salary").over(Window.partitionBy("dept"))) \
  .withColumn("pct_of_dept", F.col("salary") / F.col("dept_total"))
📁 Chapter 8

I/O — Parquet, Delta, Hive

Reading & Writing Formats

PySpark — I/O
# Parquet (recommended — columnar, compressed, schema)
df.write.mode("overwrite").partitionBy("year", "month").parquet("s3://datalake/orders/")
df = spark.read.parquet("s3://datalake/orders/year=2024/")

# Delta Lake (ACID transactions, versioning)
df.write.format("delta").mode("overwrite").save("/delta/orders")
df = spark.read.format("delta").load("/delta/orders")
# Time travel
spark.read.format("delta").option("versionAsOf", 3).load("/delta/orders")

# Hive Metastore
df.write.mode("overwrite").saveAsTable("analytics.orders_fact")
df = spark.sql("SELECT * FROM analytics.orders_fact")

# JDBC (relational DBs)
df = (spark.read.format("jdbc")
    .option("url",      "jdbc:postgresql://host:5432/db")
    .option("dbtable",  "orders")
    .option("user",     "user")
    .option("password", "pass")
    .option("numPartitions", "8")
    .load())
🚀 Chapter 9

Optimization & Tuning

Caching, Partitioning, Shuffle

PySpark — Optimization
from pyspark.storagelevel import StorageLevel

# Cache / Persist — reuse computed data
df_hot.cache()                                   # memory only
df_hot.persist(StorageLevel.MEMORY_AND_DISK)    # spill to disk
df_hot.unpersist()                              # free memory

# Partitioning
df.repartition(200)           # full shuffle, even distribution
df.repartition(50, "dept")   # hash partition on column
df.coalesce(10)               # reduce partitions, no full shuffle

# Shuffle tuning
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions", "50")  # default 200
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold", "50mb")

# Avoid data skew — salt the join key
import pyspark.sql.functions as F
df_large.withColumn("salted_key",
    F.concat(F.col("key"), F.lit("_"), (F.rand() * 10).cast("int")))

# Adaptive Query Execution (Spark 3.0+)
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.adaptive.enabled", "true")
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.adaptive.coalescePartitions.enabled", "true")
🟢 Practice

Q&A — PySpark Beginner (20 Questions)

Core Concepts

Q1. What is Apache Spark and how does it differ from Hadoop MapReduce? ▼

Spark is an in-memory distributed computing engine. Hadoop MapReduce writes intermediate results to disk after every stage — Spark keeps data in memory across stages, making it 10–100× faster for iterative algorithms (ML, graph processing). Spark also offers a unified API (batch, streaming, SQL, ML, graph) vs Hadoop's specialised tools. Spark can run on Hadoop YARN, Mesos, Kubernetes, or standalone.

Q2. What is the difference between a Transformation and an Action in Spark? ▼

Transformations (filter, map, join, groupBy) are lazy — they define a computation plan (DAG) but don't execute until an Action is called. Actions (show, count, collect, write) trigger the actual computation. This lazy model lets Spark optimise the entire plan before executing. Key benefit: Spark can push predicates early, combine steps, and avoid unnecessary data movement.

Q3. What is a partition in Spark? ▼

A partition is a logical chunk of data processed by one task on one executor core. More partitions = more parallelism (up to the number of available cores). Too few partitions = underutilised cluster. Too many = overhead from task scheduling. Rule of thumb: 2–4 partitions per CPU core. Default for shuffles is 200 (spark.sql.shuffle.partitions). Read from HDFS/S3: typically one partition per file block (128MB).

Q4. What is a broadcast join and when should you use it? ▼

A broadcast join sends a small DataFrame to all executor nodes, eliminating the expensive shuffle needed for a regular join. Use when one DataFrame is small enough to fit in executor memory (default threshold: 10MB, configurable). Always use broadcast for dimension tables joined with large fact tables. Syntax: orders.join(broadcast(lookup), 'key'). Spark may auto-broadcast below the threshold.

Q5. What is data skew and how do you handle it in Spark? ▼

Skew occurs when one partition has vastly more data than others — one task takes 10× longer, becoming the bottleneck. Causes: joining on low-cardinality keys (e.g., country with 80% US), hot keys in groupBy. Solutions: (1) Salting — append a random number to the key to distribute load; (2) broadcast join the skewed small table; (3) AQE (Adaptive Query Execution) in Spark 3.0+ auto-detects and splits skewed partitions; (4) filter and process hot keys separately.

Q6. What is a DAG in Spark and what role does it play? ▼

A DAG (Directed Acyclic Graph) is Spark's representation of the series of computations to perform. When you call an action, Spark builds a DAG of stages from your transformation chain. The DAGScheduler divides the DAG into stages separated by shuffle boundaries. Each stage contains tasks that can run in parallel (one per partition). The Catalyst optimizer also rewrites the logical plan before DAG generation, pushing predicates down, eliminating redundant projections.

Q7. What is the difference between map() and flatMap() in PySpark? ▼

map(func) applies func to each element and returns exactly one output per input — always a 1:1 mapping. flatMap(func) applies func to each element and then flattens the results — one input can produce 0, 1, or many outputs. Classic use: flatMap(lambda line: line.split()) turns each line into many words. For DataFrames, the equivalent is explode() for array/map columns.

Q8. What is caching in Spark and when should you cache a DataFrame? ▼

df.cache() stores the DataFrame in executor memory (MEMORY_ONLY). Call an action after to materialise it. Use when: the DataFrame is computed from a slow source AND used multiple times in your job. Avoid caching if used only once (wastes memory). Always unpersist() when done. persist(StorageLevel.MEMORY_AND_DISK) spills to disk when memory is full. Over-caching is a common cause of OOM errors in Spark jobs.

Q9. How does Spark handle schema inference vs explicit schema? ▼

inferSchema=True in read.csv scans the data to guess types — runs an extra pass over the data (slow for large files) and may infer incorrectly (e.g. "001" as int, not string). Explicit schema with StructType: faster, correct, self-documenting. Always define schema explicitly in production pipelines. For JSON: same trade-off. For Parquet: schema is embedded in the file — no inference needed.

Q10. What is a UDF in PySpark and why should you avoid it when possible? ▼

A UDF (User-Defined Function) wraps a Python function for use in Spark SQL/DataFrame operations. The problem: each row must be serialised from JVM → Python, processed, and deserialised back → Python → JVM. This adds 10-100× overhead vs native Spark SQL functions. Alternatives: use built-in pyspark.sql.functions (run in JVM), or Pandas UDFs (@pandas_udf) which use Apache Arrow for vectorised batch transfer — much faster than row-level UDFs.

Q11. What are Spark Structured Streaming's watermarks? ▼

Watermarks handle late-arriving data in streaming. A watermark says: "I will wait up to X time after the current max event time for late data". Events arriving later than the watermark are dropped. Define with: df.withWatermark("timestamp", "10 minutes"). Required for stateful operations (window aggregations, stream-stream joins) to bound state size and enable correct output semantics. Without watermarks, Spark must retain state indefinitely.

Q12. What is Adaptive Query Execution (AQE) in Spark 3.0+? ▼

AQE re-optimises query plans at runtime using actual statistics collected mid-query: (1) Coalescing post-shuffle partitions — combines small partitions from an oversized shuffle.partitions setting; (2) Converting sort-merge joins to broadcast joins when one side turns out smaller than expected; (3) Skew join optimisation — splits skewed partitions automatically. Enable with spark.sql.adaptive.enabled=true. Dramatically reduces tuning needed for production jobs.

Q13. How do you write a Spark Structured Streaming job? ▼

spark.readStream.format("kafka") or format("csv").option("path","dir") creates a streaming DataFrame. Apply transformations normally. df.writeStream.format("delta").option("checkpointLocation","path").outputMode("append").trigger(processingTime="1 minute").start(). Three output modes: append (new rows only), update (updated rows), complete (full result every trigger). Checkpoint saves offset progress for fault tolerance and exactly-once semantics.

Q14. What is the Tungsten execution engine in Spark? ▼

Tungsten is Spark's physical execution engine, introduced in Spark 1.4. It improves performance via: (1) Off-heap memory management — bypasses JVM GC for binary data; (2) Cache-aware computation — data structures designed for CPU cache lines; (3) Whole-stage code generation (WSCG) — generates specialised JVM bytecode for each query, collapsing multiple operators into one tight loop, eliminating virtual function calls and boxing overhead. Result: 10-20× faster than interpreted execution.

Q15. How do you read partitioned data efficiently in PySpark? ▼

Partitioned Parquet/Delta: spark.read.parquet("s3://bucket/year=2024/month=3/") — specify the partition path to skip irrelevant data. Or use the full path and add a filter: df.filter(col("year")==2024) — Spark pushes the filter to the file listing and only reads matching partitions (partition pruning). Never read the entire partitioned dataset and filter in memory — this negates the purpose of partitioning. Always align your filter columns with your partition columns.

Q16. What is the difference between a Spark job, stage, and task? ▼

Job: triggered by one action (show, count, write). A job may contain multiple stages. Stage: a group of transformations that can be executed without a shuffle. Stages are separated at shuffle boundaries (groupBy, join, orderBy, distinct). Task: one unit of work — processes one partition within a stage. A stage with 200 partitions launches 200 tasks. Viewing the Spark UI: Jobs → Stages → Tasks gives the complete execution breakdown.

Q17. How do you use PySpark to process JSON files with nested/complex schemas? ▼

spark.read.json("path") auto-infers schema including nested structs and arrays. Access nested fields: df.select("address.city") or col("address.city"). Flatten a struct: df.select("id", "address.*"). Explode arrays: df.withColumn("tag", explode(col("tags"))). For schema evolution: mergeSchema=True in Parquet options. Define explicit schema with StructType nesting for production reliability.

Q18. What is Delta Lake and what problems does it solve? ▼

Delta Lake is an open storage format (Parquet + transaction log) that adds ACID transactions to data lakes. Solves: (1) Concurrent writes — optimistic concurrency control; (2) Schema enforcement — rejects writes with wrong schema; (3) Time travel — df.read.format("delta").option("versionAsOf", N); (4) Upserts/Deletes — DeltaTable.forPath().merge(); (5) Data lake GDPR compliance — delete by user ID across history. Maintained by Databricks, now open-sourced under Linux Foundation.

Q19. How do you estimate the number of shuffle partitions to use? ▼

Default is 200. Rule of thumb: target 100MB–1GB per partition post-shuffle. Formula: num_partitions = (total_shuffle_data_GB * 1000) / 100 (for ~100MB partitions). Too many partitions: excessive task scheduling overhead, many tiny files. Too few: large partitions, OOM risk, slow tasks. With AQE enabled: Spark auto-coalesces post-shuffle partitions — set shuffle.partitions higher than needed (e.g. 2000) and let AQE merge small partitions.

Q20. What is the difference between Spark's client mode and cluster mode? ▼

Client mode: the driver runs on the machine that submitted the job (your laptop or edge node). Logs appear locally. Easy debugging. Not suitable for long-running production jobs (if your machine disconnects, the job fails). Cluster mode: the driver is submitted to the cluster and runs on a worker node. Job survives client disconnection. Used for all production workloads. Specify with spark-submit --deploy-mode cluster.

🔴 Practice

Q&A — PySpark Advanced (20 Questions)

Advanced Topics

Q1. Explain Spark's Catalyst Optimizer. ▼

Catalyst is Spark's query optimisation framework. It takes a logical plan (your transformations) through: (1) Analysis — resolves column names and types; (2) Logical Optimization — predicate pushdown, constant folding, column pruning; (3) Physical Planning — generates multiple physical plans, picks the best via cost model; (4) Code Generation — generates JVM bytecode (Tungsten). Result: your high-level Python code runs as optimised compiled code.

Q2. What is the difference between narrow and wide transformations? ▼

Narrow transformations: each input partition produces exactly one output partition — no data movement across executors. Examples: map, filter, select, withColumn. Can be pipelined into one stage. Wide transformations: require data from multiple partitions to produce one output partition — causes a shuffle (data moves across the network). Examples: groupBy, join, orderBy, distinct, repartition. Shuffles are the main performance bottleneck — minimise them.

Q3. How does Spark handle fault tolerance? ▼

Spark uses lineage — every RDD/DataFrame tracks the sequence of transformations that created it. If a partition is lost (executor failure), Spark recomputes only that partition from the lineage, not the entire dataset. For long lineages or after shuffles, checkpointing (df.checkpoint()) saves data to HDFS, breaking the lineage and providing a recovery point. Structured Streaming uses write-ahead logs (WAL) for exactly-once guarantees.

Q4. Explain Spark's memory management model. ▼

Spark memory is divided into: Execution memory (for joins, sorts, aggregations), Storage memory (for caching/broadcasting), User memory (Python data, UDF state), and Reserved memory (300MB for Spark itself). In unified memory model (default since Spark 1.6): execution and storage share a common pool, each can borrow from the other. Storage memory that gets evicted triggers re-computation. spark.memory.fraction (0.6) controls execution+storage share of heap; spark.memory.storageFraction (0.5) of that is storage's protected amount.

Q5. How do you write a Pandas UDF in PySpark and when does it outperform regular UDFs? ▼

@pandas_udf(returnType=DoubleType()) or PandasUDFType.SCALAR. The function receives a pd.Series (scalar) or pd.DataFrame (grouped_map) instead of individual values. Uses Apache Arrow for zero-copy serialisation between JVM and Python — 10-100× faster than row-level UDFs. Best for: vectorised transformations (normalisation, custom string parsing), functions that benefit from NumPy/Pandas operations on batches. Still slower than native Spark functions — always prefer built-ins first.

Q6. How does Spark handle OOM (Out of Memory) errors and how do you diagnose them? ▼

Types: Driver OOM — from collect(), too-large broadcast, excessive driver-side data. Fix: avoid collect on large data; use head()/take(); increase spark.driver.memory. Executor OOM — from large joins, too-wide partitions, UDF memory leaks. Fix: increase partitions (smaller per-partition), increase executor memory, use broadcast join, persist intermediate results. Diagnose: Spark UI → Executors tab → GC time (>10% = memory pressure), storage tab for cached sizes. Enable GC logging: spark.executor.extraJavaOptions=-verbose:gc.

Q7. What are the differences between HashAggregate, SortAggregate, and ObjectHashAggregate in Spark? ▼

All implement groupBy aggregation, chosen by the Catalyst planner based on data properties. HashAggregate: builds a hash map in memory — fastest, used for most aggregations with numeric/primitive types. SortAggregate: sort-based, used when hash map doesn't fit in memory or when handling non-orderable types (maps, arrays) — spills to disk. ObjectHashAggregate: for aggregations involving complex types (like collect_list) that can't be stored as binary in hash map. Visible in explain() output.

Q8. How does Spark Streaming achieve exactly-once semantics end-to-end? ▼

Three components needed: (1) Idempotent sources: replayable (Kafka with committed offsets, S3 files); (2) Checkpoint: saves progress (offsets + state) to HDFS/S3 — engine restores from here on failure; (3) Idempotent sinks: writes must be repeatable — Delta Lake with txnVersion, databases with upsert logic, or Kafka with idempotent producer. If all three are in place, Spark Structured Streaming guarantees exactly-once. Kafka direct source + Delta Lake sink is the standard exactly-once pattern.

Q9. How do you monitor and debug a slow Spark job? ▼

Step 1: Spark UI → Jobs/Stages — find the slow stage. Step 2: look at task distribution — is one task 10× slower? (skew). Step 3: check GC time (>10% = memory pressure). Step 4: check shuffle read/write sizes — large shuffles indicate wide transformations on large data. Step 5: check stage DAG for unnecessary shuffles. Tools: df.explain("formatted") shows physical plan. spark.eventLog.enabled=true for post-mortem analysis with Spark History Server. For production: Datadog, Ganglia, or Grafana + Prometheus scraping Spark metrics.

Q10. What is the difference between repartition and partitionBy when writing? ▼

df.repartition(N): redistributes data into exactly N in-memory partitions via a full shuffle — used before writing to control parallelism. df.write.partitionBy("year","month"): writes data to folder structure (year=2024/month=3/) — a Hive-style partition for read-time partition pruning. These are different: repartition controls number of in-memory tasks; partitionBy controls directory structure of output files. Combine: df.repartition("year","month").write.partitionBy("year","month") for one file per partition directory.

Q11. How do you handle schema evolution in Spark with Parquet and Delta Lake? ▼

Parquet: spark.read.option("mergeSchema","true").parquet(path) merges schemas across files — adds new columns, marks missing ones as null. No support for column type changes. Delta Lake: spark.conf.set("spark.databricks.delta.schema.autoMerge.enabled","true") or mode("append").option("mergeSchema","true"). Delta also supports schema evolution via ALTER TABLE: DeltaTable.forPath(path).alterTable().addColumns(...). Column reordering, type evolution (int→long), and nullable changes are supported.

Q12. What is Z-ordering in Delta Lake and when does it help? ▼

Z-ordering (data skipping optimisation) co-locates related data in the same Parquet files by sorting rows on multiple columns simultaneously using a Z-curve space-filling algorithm. OPTIMIZE delta.table ZORDER BY (customer_id, product_id). After Z-ordering, queries filtering on those columns read fewer files — Delta's file statistics (min/max per column per file) can skip entire files. Helps most for high-cardinality filter columns (IDs, timestamps). Does NOT help for low-cardinality (e.g. status with 3 values).

Q13. How do you implement streaming aggregations with late data in Structured Streaming? ▼

Use watermarks + window aggregations: df.withWatermark("event_time","10 minutes").groupBy(window("event_time","1 hour"),"device_id").agg(sum("value")). Output modes: update (emit updated windows after each trigger) or append (emit windows only after watermark passes — fully late-safe). For correctness: watermark defines how late data is accepted. Late data outside the watermark is silently dropped. Balance: wider watermarks → more correct but more state memory; narrower → less memory but more dropped data.

Q14. What are Delta Lake MERGE operations and when are they used? ▼

DeltaTable.forPath(spark, path).alias("target").merge(source_df.alias("source"), "target.id = source.id").whenMatchedUpdate(set={...}).whenNotMatchedInsert(values={...}).execute(). Supports full SCD2 patterns, deduplication, CDC (change data capture) upserts. Under the hood: Spark reads matching files, processes updates in memory, rewrites affected files, records new version in transaction log. MERGE is the foundation of CDC-based lakehouse ingestion patterns.

Q15. How would you design a PySpark pipeline for processing 10TB of daily logs? ▼

Architecture: (1) Ingest raw logs to S3/ADLS (Bronze) via Kafka or batch upload; (2) Spark Structured Streaming or scheduled batch job to parse, validate, and enrich → Silver layer (Delta Parquet, partitioned by date); (3) Scheduled dbt or Spark batch to aggregate → Gold (fact tables); Key tuning: partition Silver by date+hour, Z-order on user_id or session_id, 200-500 shuffle partitions, broadcast dimension tables (<1GB), cache frequently reused DataFrames, use AQE. Write one Spark job per layer with checkpointing and Delta ACID for reliability.

Q16. What is speculative execution in Spark and when should it be disabled? ▼

Speculative execution launches duplicate copies of slow tasks on different executors — the first to finish "wins", the other is killed. Helps when stragglers are caused by bad hardware. Enable: spark.speculation=true. Disable when: tasks have side effects (e.g. writing to external DBs — speculative writes would create duplicates), when stragglers are due to data skew (speculation wastes resources instead of fixing the root cause), or when running on spot instances (duplicate tasks increase cost). Default: disabled.

Q17. How do you tune Spark for writing to object storage (S3/ADLS/GCS)? ▼

(1) Use committer = "magic" or "directory": spark.sql.sources.commitProtocolClass=org.apache.spark.internal.io.cloud.PathOutputCommitProtocol — avoids the slow rename-based commit protocol; (2) write Parquet with Snappy or ZSTD compression; (3) target 128MB–1GB output files — use repartition() or coalesce() to control file count; (4) enable spark.hadoop.fs.s3a.fast.upload=true; (5) increase max connections: fs.s3a.connection.maximum=100. Avoid many small files — they slow down listing and read.

Q18. What is the Catalyst optimizer and how does it work step-by-step? ▼

Catalyst transforms your query through 4 phases: (1) Parsing: SQL or DataFrame API → unresolved logical plan (AST); (2) Analysis: resolve column names/types against the catalog → resolved logical plan; (3) Logical Optimisation: apply rules (predicate pushdown, column pruning, constant folding, boolean simplification, join reordering) → optimised logical plan; (4) Physical Planning: generate multiple physical plans, estimate costs, choose best → physical plan; (5) Code Generation: Tungsten WSCG compiles to JVM bytecode. Each step is rule-based, extensible.

Q19. How do you handle CDC (Change Data Capture) in PySpark? ▼

Common pattern with Delta Lake MERGE: (1) read CDC events from Kafka (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE ops); (2) group by primary key, keep latest change per key per micro-batch; (3) MERGE into Delta target table — MATCHED+UPDATE, NOT MATCHED+INSERT, MATCHED+DELETE (if op=D); (4) commit offsets after successful merge. For SCD2: MERGE with additional logic to close existing rows (set is_current=false, expiry_date) and insert new rows. Delta MERGE is atomic — partial failures are rolled back.

Q20. What are the key differences between Apache Flink and Apache Spark Structured Streaming? ▼

Spark Structured Streaming: micro-batch model (default), SQL/DataFrame API, strong batch+streaming unification, Delta Lake integration, huge ecosystem. Apache Flink: true event-by-event streaming (row-at-a-time), lower latency (sub-second vs seconds for Spark micro-batch), native event time + watermarks, richer stateful processing (keyed state, process functions), better for CEP (complex event processing). Choose Spark for: batch+streaming on same codebase, Delta Lake integration, Databricks. Choose Flink for: ultra-low latency, complex stateful streaming, event-time correctness is paramount.

📌 Chapter 1

What is a Data Warehouse?

A data warehouse is a centralised analytical repository optimised for reading, aggregation, and reporting — not transactional writes.

OLTP vs OLAP

AspectOLTP (Transactional)OLAP (Analytical)
PurposeDaily operations (orders, payments)Analysis, reporting, BI
Query typeINSERT/UPDATE/DELETE, small SELECTsLarge aggregations, JOINs across years
SchemaNormalised (3NF)Denormalised (Star/Snowflake)
Data volumeGBs — current dataTBs–PBs — historical data
UsersThousands of concurrent app usersTens to hundreds of analysts
ExamplesMySQL, PostgreSQL, OracleSnowflake, BigQuery, Redshift

Inmon vs Kimball

🏛️

Inmon — Corporate Information Factory

Build a normalised enterprise DWH first (3NF), then build data marts from it. Top-down. Single source of truth. Harder to build initially but very flexible.

⭐

Kimball — Dimensional Modeling

Build dimensional data marts first (star schema), integrate via conformed dimensions. Bottom-up. Faster to deliver value. Most common in practice today.

🏛️ Chapter 2

Architecture Patterns

From Data Lake to Lakehouse

🗄️

Traditional DWH

Structured data only. Schema-on-write. Expensive proprietary hardware. Examples: Teradata, Oracle Exadata. High reliability, limited flexibility.

🏞️

Data Lake

All data types (structured, semi, unstructured). Schema-on-read. Cheap storage (S3/ADLS/GCS). Risk: becomes a "data swamp" without governance.

🏠

Lakehouse

Best of both: data lake storage + DWH query performance. ACID transactions, schema enforcement, time travel. Examples: Databricks Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg, Apache Hudi.

☁️

Cloud DWH

Fully managed, serverless scaling. Separate compute and storage. Pay per query or per second. Examples: Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift Serverless, Azure Synapse.

🗂️ Chapter 3

Dimensional Modeling

Dimensional modeling organises data into Fact tables (measurements, metrics) and Dimension tables (context, attributes). Designed for query performance and analytical intuition.

Facts vs Dimensions

📊

Fact Table

Contains measurable events. Each row is a business event at a specific grain. Has foreign keys to dimensions + numeric measures (amount, quantity, duration). Can be additive, semi-additive, or non-additive.

📋

Dimension Table

Provides context for facts. Denormalised, wide tables with descriptive attributes. Examples: dim_customer, dim_product, dim_date. Supports filtering, grouping, labeling.

📅

Date Dimension

Every DWH needs one. Columns: date_key (int YYYYMMDD), full_date, day_name, month, quarter, year, fiscal_period, is_holiday, is_weekend. Join on date_key for instant time filtering.

🎯

Grain

The grain defines what one row in the fact table represents. "One row per order line item" vs "one row per daily sales total by store". Choosing the right grain is the most important design decision.

  • Transaction: one row per event (most common). Grain: one row per order line.
  • Periodic snapshot: one row per period per entity. Grain: one row per account per month.
  • Accumulating snapshot: one row per process instance, updated as it progresses. Grain: one row per order, columns for each stage date.
🔷 Chapter 4

Star vs Snowflake Schema

Design Trade-offs

AspectStar SchemaSnowflake Schema
StructureFact + denormalised flat dimensionsFact + normalised dimensions (sub-tables)
Query complexityFewer JOINs — simpler queriesMore JOINs — complex queries
StorageMore storage (data redundancy)Less storage (normalised)
PerformanceFaster reads (BI tools optimised for it)Slower reads (more JOINs)
MaintenanceEasier — fewer tablesHarder — referential integrity
Best forMost BI / analytics workloadsWhen storage is critical or dimensions are huge
🔄 Chapter 5

ETL vs ELT

Pipeline Patterns

🔄

ETL (Extract → Transform → Load)

Transform data BEFORE loading into the warehouse. Used with traditional DWHs (limited compute). Transformation happens in a dedicated ETL server or middleware (Informatica, SSIS). Transformations are defined upfront — schema-on-write.

➡️

ELT (Extract → Load → Transform)

Load raw data INTO the warehouse first, then transform using SQL/dbt. Used with modern cloud DWHs (Snowflake, BigQuery) that can handle massive compute. More flexible — raw data always available. Schema-on-read for exploration.

In ELT, always land raw data in a staging layer before transforming. This gives you a re-runnable audit trail, enables reprocessing when business logic changes, and separates ingestion failures from transformation failures.

📦 Chapter 6

Slowly Changing Dimensions

Dimensions change over time — a customer moves city, a product changes category. SCDs define how to track these changes in the warehouse.

SCD Types

TypeStrategyHistoryUse When
Type 0Never update (retain original)NoneFixed attributes like date of birth
Type 1Overwrite the old valueNoneError corrections, non-analytical changes
Type 2 ⭐New row + effective/expiry dates + is_current flagFullNeed point-in-time historical accuracy
Type 3Add previous_value columnOne prior valueOnly one prior value matters
Type 4Separate history tableFull (separate table)High-churn dim, keep main table clean
Type 6Type 1 + 2 + 3 combinedFull + current stampedNeed history AND easy current-state queries
📐 Chapter 7

Data Layers — Medallion Architecture

Bronze → Silver → Gold

🥉

Bronze (Raw)

Exact copy of source data. No transformations. Append-only or insert-only. JSON, CSV, or Parquet as received. Serves as audit trail and replay source. Never delete.

🥈

Silver (Cleaned)

Validated, deduplicated, standardised data. Applied data types, null handling, schema enforcement. Still close to source — one record per entity per event. Used by data engineers.

🥇

Gold (Aggregated)

Business-level aggregations, star schema facts and dimensions. Optimised for BI tools and reports. Domain-specific (Sales Gold, Marketing Gold). Used by analysts and executives.

Ingest → Bronze (S3/ADLS) → Silver (Delta Lake, dbt cleaning models) → Gold (dbt mart models, Snowflake) → BI tool (Tableau, Power BI, Looker)

⚙️ Chapter 9

dbt — Data Build Tool

dbt is the T in ELT — it manages SQL transformations in your data warehouse using software engineering practices: version control, testing, documentation, and lineage.

Core dbt Concepts

🏗️

Models

Each model is a .sql file containing a SELECT statement. dbt compiles it into CREATE TABLE/VIEW. Organised in staging/, marts/, intermediate/ folders.

🔗

ref()

{{ ref('stg_orders') }} creates a dependency. dbt builds a DAG and executes models in the correct order. Enables lineage tracking.

✅

Tests

Built-in: not_null, unique, accepted_values, relationships. Custom: write SQL tests. Run with dbt test. Catches data quality issues before they reach dashboards.

📚

Documentation

dbt docs generate creates a searchable data catalog with column descriptions, model lineage DAG, and test results — all from your .yml files.

dbt — Model Example
-- models/marts/fct_orders.sql
{{ config(
    materialized = 'table',
    partition_by = {'field': 'order_date', 'data_type': 'date'},
    cluster_by   = ['customer_id']
) }}

WITH orders AS (
    SELECT * FROM {{ ref('stg_orders') }}
),
customers AS (
    SELECT * FROM {{ ref('stg_customers') }}
)
SELECT
    o.order_id,
    o.order_date,
    o.amount,
    c.customer_name,
    c.segment
FROM orders o
LEFT JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
🟢 Practice

Q&A — Data Warehousing Beginner (20 Questions)

Core Concepts

Q1. What is the difference between OLTP and OLAP? ▼

OLTP (Online Transaction Processing): designed for day-to-day operations — fast inserts, updates, deletes, small reads. Normalised schema. Thousands of concurrent users. Examples: order management, banking. OLAP (Online Analytical Processing): designed for complex analytical queries — massive aggregations, JOINs across millions of rows, historical analysis. Denormalised schema (Star/Snowflake). Tens of analysts. A data warehouse is an OLAP system fed from one or more OLTP sources.

Q2. What is a fact table and a dimension table? ▼

A fact table contains measurable events (sales, clicks, logins). It has a foreign key to each dimension and numeric measures (amount, quantity). A dimension table provides context — who, what, when, where, how. It's usually wide and denormalised (customer name, city, segment, tier all in one row). Facts are deep (many rows), dimensions are wide (many columns).

Q3. What is the grain of a fact table? ▼

The grain is the precise definition of what one row in the fact table represents. Examples: "one row per order line item", "one row per daily store sales total", "one row per customer login event". Defining the grain is the most critical design decision — it determines which dimensions can be attached and what questions can be answered. All measures must be facts at the declared grain.

Q4. What is a surrogate key and why use it? ▼

A surrogate key is a system-generated meaningless integer PK (AUTO_INCREMENT or sequence). Use it instead of natural/business keys because: (1) natural keys change (email, phone); (2) integers join faster than strings; (3) SCD Type 2 requires multiple rows for the same entity — you need a unique key per version, not per entity. The natural/business key is stored as a separate indexed column for lookups.

Q5. What is the Medallion architecture? ▼

A three-layer data organisation pattern: Bronze (raw, exact copy of sources — never modified), Silver (cleaned, validated, deduplicated — production-quality data), Gold (business-level aggregations, dimensional models — optimised for BI). Common in Delta Lake / Databricks but applicable anywhere. Benefits: clear separation of concerns, reprocessability from any layer, data quality gates between layers.

Q6. What is a conformed dimension? ▼

A conformed dimension is shared identically across multiple data marts. Example: a dim_date or dim_customer that is the same in both the Sales and Finance marts. When dimension tables are conformed, you can drill across marts (combine results from different subjects). Conformed dimensions are the "glue" of the Kimball enterprise data warehouse — they allow consistent reporting across business domains without building a monolithic DWH.

Q7. What is the difference between additive, semi-additive, and non-additive facts? ▼

Additive: can be summed across all dimensions. Example: order amount, units sold. Most flexible. Semi-additive: can be summed across some dimensions but not all. Example: account balance — summing across customers is valid; summing across time (last day of month + last day of quarter) is not. Use LASTNONBLANK in DAX or LAST_VALUE in SQL. Non-additive: cannot be summed at all. Example: ratios, percentages, temperatures. Store the components (numerator + denominator) and compute the ratio at query time.

Q8. What is a junk dimension? ▼

A junk dimension consolidates low-cardinality flags, indicators, and codes that don't belong to any existing dimension — rather than cluttering the fact table with many small flag columns. Example: order_type_flag, is_rush, is_gift, payment_status — combine all combinations into a junk dimension with a surrogate key. The fact table gets one foreign key instead of many flag columns. Reduces fact table width and groups related miscellaneous attributes logically.

Q9. What is the difference between a fact-less fact table and a bridge table? ▼

A fact-less fact table has no measures — only dimension keys. Used to capture events that simply happened. Example: student_attendance (student_key, class_key, date_key) — the fact that a student attended class IS the fact. Count the rows to measure attendance. A bridge table (or association table) handles many-to-many dimension relationships — e.g., a customer belonging to multiple segments, or a product having multiple categories. Bridge tables have a FK to both dimensions.

Q10. What are the four steps of Kimball's dimensional modeling process? ▼

(1) Select the business process: what organisational activity are you measuring? (orders, shipments, support tickets). (2) Declare the grain: what does one row represent? (one order line item). (3) Identify the dimensions: who, what, when, where, how, why for each fact row. (4) Identify the facts: numeric measurements at the declared grain. This order matters — grain must be declared before dimensions or facts can be identified. Changing grain after design invalidates the model.

Q11. What is the difference between ETL staging tables and landing zones? ▼

A landing zone (or raw layer/Bronze) is where source data arrives unmodified — files, API payloads, DB extracts exactly as received. No transformation. Append-only. Staging tables are intermediate work-in-progress tables used during ETL — data from sources is loaded here, then transformed and merged into the target. Staging tables are typically truncated-and-reloaded each run. Landing zones are permanent audit trails; staging tables are transient. Modern ELT collapses staging into the Bronze layer of the Medallion architecture.

Q12. How do you handle late-arriving facts vs late-arriving dimensions? ▼

Late-arriving fact: a transaction received after its period closes. Insert it with the correct historical date. If the dimension existed at that time, look up the correct surrogate key using effective/expiry dates. Late-arriving dimension: the dimension member arrives after facts referencing it. Options: (1) Use a "Unknown" placeholder key until the dimension arrives, then update facts; (2) Insert the dimension record with an estimated effective date; (3) Use an inferred member flag. Late-arriving data handling is a key difference between operational and analytical systems.

Q13. What is a role-playing dimension? ▼

A single physical dimension table used multiple times in the same fact table for different roles. Example: dim_date used as order_date, ship_date, and return_date in the same fact table — three different foreign keys all pointing to the same physical date dimension. In the data model, represent as three aliases/views of dim_date: dim_order_date, dim_ship_date, dim_return_date. Each role gets its own surrogate key column in the fact table.

Q14. What is change data capture (CDC) and how does it work? ▼

CDC captures row-level changes (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) from source databases in near-real-time. Methods: (1) Log-based CDC: reads database transaction logs (MySQL binlog, PostgreSQL WAL, SQL Server CDC) — non-intrusive, most popular; (2) Trigger-based: DB triggers write changes to a shadow table — adds overhead; (3) Timestamp-based: query rows modified since last_run — misses deletes, requires reliable updated_at column; (4) Diff-based: compare full snapshots — expensive. Tools: Debezium (open-source), Fivetran, AWS DMS, Airbyte.

Q15. What is data vault modeling and how does it differ from Kimball? ▼

Data Vault is a modeling methodology for the raw layer of enterprise DWHs. Three entity types: Hubs (business keys: customer_id, order_id), Links (relationships between hubs: order-customer association), Satellites (descriptive attributes with history). Designed for: auditability (full lineage), parallel loading (no dependencies between entities), adaptability to source changes. Kimball: query-optimised, star schema, harder to change. Data Vault: load-optimised, more normalised, easier to add new sources. Many organisations use Data Vault for raw/Silver, Kimball-style marts for Gold.

Q16. How do you implement incremental loading in a DWH pipeline? ▼

Track high-watermark: store last successful load timestamp/ID, load only rows where updated_at > last_run. For full replacement: truncate-and-reload (simple but slow). For append-only: insert new records where id > max_id. For slowly changing: upsert using MERGE (match on natural key, update if changed, insert if new). For CDC-based: apply change events from Debezium/Fivetran. Key: reliable updated_at index on source. Incremental loading is the core challenge of ELT pipeline design.

Q17. What are the key differences between Snowflake, BigQuery, and Databricks? ▼

Snowflake: virtual warehouses (compute clusters), compute/storage separation, Time Travel (90 days default), Data Sharing, supports semi-structured (VARIANT type). SQL-first. BigQuery: serverless (no clusters to manage), pay per query, columnar storage (Capacitor), built-in ML (BQML), streaming inserts, BI Engine for sub-second BI. Databricks: unified analytics (SQL+Python+Scala+R), Delta Lake, MLflow, photon engine, Unity Catalog. SQL + ML + engineering in one platform. Choose based on: existing cloud, team skills, and whether you need unified ML+data engineering.

Q18. What is a data mesh and how does it differ from traditional DWH? ▼

Data mesh is a decentralised data architecture where individual business domains own their data products — not a central data team. Four principles: (1) Domain ownership: teams publish their own data products; (2) Data as a product: discoverable, trustworthy, documented; (3) Self-serve infrastructure: central platform team provides tooling, not data; (4) Federated computational governance: global standards + local ownership. Traditional DWH: centralised. Data mesh: federated. Solves bottlenecks at the central data team but adds coordination complexity.

Q19. What are the key metrics you should monitor in a DWH pipeline? ▼

Data quality: null rates per column, duplicate key counts, referential integrity violations, schema drift alerts. Pipeline health: job runtime trends (degradation alert), records processed per run, failure rate, SLA compliance. Storage: table growth rate, partition staleness (last loaded timestamp per table). Freshness: lag between source event time and DWH availability. Query performance: slow query log, most frequent long-running queries. Implement with: Great Expectations, dbt tests, Monte Carlo, or custom SQL checks in Airflow.

Q20. What is a data catalog and why is it important in a modern DWH? ▼

A data catalog is a centralised inventory of data assets — tables, columns, dashboards, pipelines — with metadata: descriptions, owners, lineage, quality metrics, access policies, usage stats. Importance: (1) discoverability — analysts find the right table without asking around; (2) trust — consumers see data quality scores and lineage; (3) governance — data stewards manage definitions and access; (4) onboarding — new team members self-serve. Tools: dbt docs (transformations only), Apache Atlas, DataHub, Collibra, Alation, Google Data Catalog. dbt + DataHub is a popular open-source combo.

🔴 Practice

Q&A — Data Warehousing Advanced (20 Questions)

Advanced Topics

Q1. What are the trade-offs between a Data Lake and a Data Warehouse? ▼

Data Lake: stores any format, cheap object storage, schema-on-read, great for raw data and ML. Risk: governance issues, slow query performance without tuning, becomes a "swamp". Data Warehouse: structured/semi-structured only, schema-on-write, enforces quality, fast analytical queries. Higher cost, less flexible. Lakehouse (Delta Lake, Iceberg, Hudi) bridges both: DW's ACID + schema enforcement on lake's cheap storage + open formats. This is the modern default.

Q2. How do you design a slowly changing dimension Type 2 in SQL? ▼

SCD2 adds columns: effective_date (DATE), expiry_date (DATE, default '9999-12-31'), is_current (BOOLEAN). On a change: (1) UPDATE the current row: set is_current=0, expiry_date=today-1. (2) INSERT new row: new values, effective_date=today, expiry_date='9999-12-31', is_current=1. The fact table joins on the surrogate key (specific version), not the business key. Point-in-time query: join where order_date BETWEEN effective_date AND expiry_date.

Q3. What is the difference between a data warehouse and a data mart? ▼

A data warehouse is enterprise-wide — all business domains, single integrated model. A data mart is subject-oriented — scoped to one department (Sales, Finance, Marketing). Data marts can be dependent (sourced from the DWH) or independent (sourced directly from operational systems). In Kimball's approach, the DWH is the integrated collection of data marts sharing conformed dimensions.

Q4. How do you design a SCD Type 6 (hybrid) dimension? ▼

SCD Type 6 = Type 1 + Type 2 + Type 3 combined. Each row has: surrogate_key (unique per version), natural_key, effective_date, expiry_date, is_current flag (Type 2 columns), plus a current_value column that is ALWAYS updated to the latest value (Type 1 behaviour) on ALL historical rows for that natural key. This lets you: (1) query point-in-time history via effective/expiry dates; (2) also ask "what is the current value for each historical row" without joining. Useful for "report customers by their CURRENT segment but using HISTORICAL order data".

Q5. What are dbt materialisation types and when do you use each? ▼

view (default): no storage, query runs every time — for lightweight transformations, staging models. table: CREATE TABLE — full rebuild every run, for models that are expensive to recompute or queried frequently. incremental: MERGE/INSERT new rows since last run — for large fact tables where full rebuild is prohibitively slow; requires unique_key and is_incremental() macro. ephemeral: CTEs injected into referencing models — for intermediate logic, never materialised to disk. Choose: small→view, large+queried→table, huge+append→incremental.

Q6. What is a slowly changing dimension Type 4 and when would you use it? ▼

SCD Type 4 uses a separate history table: the main dimension table always reflects current values (like Type 1), while a separate dim_customer_history table stores all historical versions with timestamps. Benefit: the main dimension stays small and simple for most queries that only need current data; history is available when needed without touching the main table. Use when: high-churn dimensions (e.g. product price changes many times daily), and most queries only need current state.

Q7. How do you implement data lineage tracking in a modern ELT stack? ▼

dbt: every model's dependencies are declared via ref() — dbt auto-generates a lineage DAG viewable in dbt docs generate. For cross-tool lineage (Kafka → Spark → Snowflake → Tableau): use OpenLineage (an open standard) with Marquez as the metadata store. Airflow 2.4+ emits OpenLineage events. Great Expectations integrates too. DataHub and Apache Atlas consume OpenLineage events to build enterprise-wide lineage graphs. Complete lineage enables: impact analysis (what breaks if source X changes), GDPR deletion propagation, root-cause debugging.

Q8. What is the difference between a star schema and an OBT (one big table)? ▼

A star schema normalises into fact + dimension tables — JOINs required at query time. Benefits: storage efficiency (no repeated dimension data), easier dimension updates (change one row). OBT (One Big Table / flat wide table) pre-JOINs everything into one denormalised table. Benefits: zero JOIN overhead, simple queries, fastest read. Downsides: massive storage (redundant data), updating a dimension attribute requires rewriting the entire table, schema is inflexible. OBT suits: final-mile BI tables where query speed is paramount and data changes rarely.

Q9. How do you handle multi-valued dimensions in a dimensional model? ▼

Options: (1) Repeating groups — separate columns for up to N values (not recommended, inflexible); (2) Multi-valued bridge table — link table between fact and dimension, with an optional weighting factor (e.g. order attributed to multiple salespeople with %-contribution); (3) Tag/category array — store as JSON/array column (semi-structured), query with UNNEST/LATERAL FLATTEN (Snowflake). The bridge table is the Kimball-correct solution for true many-to-many; arrays work well in modern cloud DWHs with array support.

Q10. What is the role of an orchestration tool like Apache Airflow in a DWH pipeline? ▼

Airflow manages the scheduling, dependency management, and monitoring of data pipeline tasks. Key concepts: DAGs (pipeline definitions), Tasks (individual steps), Operators (task types: Python, SQL, Bash, dbt, Spark), Sensors (wait for a file/event), XComs (pass data between tasks). Provides: retry logic, alerting on failure, backfill (run historical periods), visual DAG explorer, task logs. Alternative: Prefect, Dagster (better typed, testable), Mage AI (data-first). Airflow is the most widely deployed but has operational overhead — Dagster is gaining ground in modern stacks.

Q11. What are the key design decisions for a partitioning strategy in Snowflake vs BigQuery? ▼

Snowflake: no explicit partitioning syntax — uses micro-partitions (50-500MB) automatically. Use clustering keys (CLUSTER BY (date, customer_id)) to co-locate related data, enabling micro-partition pruning. Re-clustering is automatic (Enterprise+). BigQuery: explicit partitioning by date/timestamp (PARTITION BY DATE(created_at)) or integer range. Also supports clustering (up to 4 columns). Always partition on the most common filter column. Partition expiration for data retention. Shard tables (orders_20240315) as a legacy alternative — avoid in new designs.

Q12. How do you test data quality in a dbt pipeline? ▼

Built-in dbt tests: not_null, unique, accepted_values, relationships (FK integrity). Generic tests via packages: dbt_expectations (Great Expectations-style), dbt_utils (recency test, equal rowcount). Custom SQL tests: any query returning rows = test failure. Run in CI/CD with dbt test --select tag:critical. Severity: warn vs error — warn for soft violations, error to block pipeline. Test at every layer: source freshness (dbt source freshness), staging, marts. Alert on test failures in Slack via dbt Cloud or Airflow.

Q13. What is the semantic layer and why is it important? ▼

The semantic layer sits between the DWH and BI tools — it defines business metrics, dimensions, and their relationships in a centralised, reusable way. Without it: every BI tool/analyst defines "revenue" differently → inconsistent numbers. With it: one definition, many consumers. Examples: dbt Metrics (YAML metric definitions), Looker LookML, AtScale, Cube.js. Benefits: single source of truth for KPIs, reduced duplicated logic, governance. Trend: metric stores (dbt Semantic Layer, Cube) are becoming first-class infrastructure in modern data stacks.

Q14. How would you handle a full historical load of a 5-year transaction table into a DWH? ▼

(1) Extract: chunk by year/month to avoid single huge query timeout — use LIMIT+OFFSET or date ranges; (2) Land as Parquet in S3 (Bronze); (3) Transform: run Spark or dbt incremental models processing one month at a time; (4) Load: use COPY INTO (Snowflake) or LOAD DATA (BigQuery) for bulk loads — much faster than row-by-row INSERT; (5) Validate: compare row counts and sum of amounts per month against source; (6) Switch: update watermark to switch to incremental going forward. Full load should be a one-time operation.

Q15. What is query optimisation in Snowflake and how does the query profile help? ▼

Snowflake's Query Profile (in the web UI) shows the execution plan as a node tree with per-node stats: rows processed, bytes scanned, time spent. Key things to check: (1) TableScan bytes: large? → add clustering or partition better; (2) CartesianJoin: means a cross join happened — usually a bug; (3) Explode nodes (10×+ row expansion): from a bad join condition; (4) Spillage to disk: means warehouse is too small for sort/join — scale up or split query; (5) Partition pruning: check "partitions scanned" vs "partitions total" — want a low ratio.

Q16. How does Snowflake's Zero-Copy Cloning work? ▼

CREATE TABLE orders_dev CLONE orders_prod creates an instant copy that shares the underlying micro-partitions with the original — no data is physically copied. The clone starts empty of its own partitions; as data is modified, copy-on-write creates new micro-partitions for the clone. Result: instant clone, zero storage cost until you modify data. Use cases: dev/test environments (clone prod in seconds), before-migration backups, A/B testing transformations without risk. Clones can be of tables, schemas, or entire databases.

Q17. What are the common performance anti-patterns in DWH SQL? ▼

(1) SELECT * on columnar stores — scans all columns; always specify needed columns; (2) Functions on indexed/clustered columns in WHERE (WHERE YEAR(date) = 2024) — prevents pruning; use WHERE date BETWEEN '2024-01-01' AND '2024-12-31'; (3) Implicit type casts in JOINs (string vs int key) — forces full scan; (4) OR conditions — prevent index use; use UNION ALL instead; (5) Deeply nested subqueries instead of CTEs — not wrong but harder to optimise; (6) Missing WHERE on large table lookups; (7) DISTINCT as a substitute for fixing bad JOINs.

Q18. What is the difference between OLAP cubes and columnar DWH? ▼

OLAP cubes (Microsoft SSAS, SAP BW): pre-aggregated multidimensional structures. Blazing fast for predefined queries. Rigid schema. Must re-process cube when data changes. Storage explosion for high-cardinality dimensions. Columnar DWH (Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift): raw data stored in columns, aggregated at query time. Flexible ad-hoc queries. No pre-aggregation needed (though materialised views help). Scales to any dimension cardinality. Modern consensus: columnar DWH + BI aggregation layer (Cube.js, dbt metrics) has replaced OLAP cubes for most use cases.

Q19. How do you enforce data governance and access control in a cloud DWH? ▼

Snowflake: Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) with object-level and column-level security. Dynamic data masking for PII (mask credit card except last 4 for analysts). Row access policies (filter rows based on user role). BigQuery: IAM at project/dataset/table/column level. Column-level security with policy tags + taxonomy. Row-level security via VPD-equivalent authorized views. Unity Catalog (Databricks): centralised governance across cloud and formats — attribute-based access control. General: tag PII columns, implement least-privilege, audit query logs.

Q20. What is the role of dbt in a modern ELT stack and what are its limitations? ▼

dbt handles the T in ELT — SQL-based transformations in the DWH with software engineering practices (version control, testing, documentation, lineage). Strengths: declarative models, ref() dependency management, incremental models, source freshness checks, auto-generated docs, Jinja templating for DRY code. Limitations: (1) SQL-only — complex Python transformations need dbt Python models (newer, limited support) or external tools; (2) no orchestration — needs Airflow/Prefect/dbt Cloud; (3) no ingestion — needs Airbyte/Fivetran upstream; (4) incremental models can be complex to maintain; (5) debugging compiled SQL can be painful. dbt is best as the transformation layer in a modular stack.
