📌 Chapter 1

What is Big Data?

Big Data refers to datasets too large, fast, or complex for traditional data processing tools. The definition is relative — today's big data is tomorrow's normal data.

The 5 Vs of Big Data

📦

Volume

TBs to PBs of data. Traditional DBs struggle. Requires distributed storage (HDFS, S3) and distributed compute (Spark, Hadoop).

⚡

Velocity

Data arriving in real-time streams (millions of events/second). Requires streaming systems like Kafka, Flink, Spark Streaming.

🗂️

Variety

Structured (DB rows), semi-structured (JSON, XML, logs), unstructured (images, video, text). One pipeline must handle all types.

✅

Veracity

Data quality and trustworthiness. Big Data pipelines must handle noise, duplicates, late arrivals, and schema drift.

💡

Value

The ultimate goal — extracting actionable insights. Big Data is only worthwhile if it drives better decisions or products.

When Do You Need Big Data Tools?

  • Single machine Pandas: data fits in RAM (≤ a few GBs) — use Pandas, DuckDB
  • Single machine + chunking: data is a few GBs–100GB — Polars, DuckDB, SQLite
  • Cluster needed: hundreds of GBs to TBs — PySpark, Dask, Ray
  • Cloud DWH: TBs–PBs with analytical queries — Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift
  • Real-time streaming: millisecond latency — Kafka + Flink or Spark Streaming
🐘 Chapter 2

Hadoop Ecosystem

Hadoop is the original open-source Big Data platform. While Spark has largely replaced MapReduce for compute, HDFS and the broader ecosystem remain foundational knowledge.

Core Components

ComponentRoleModern Equivalent
HDFSDistributed file system (128MB blocks, 3× replication)Amazon S3, Azure ADLS, GCS
YARNCluster resource manager — allocates CPU/RAM to jobsKubernetes, Mesos
MapReduceBatch compute — Map (transform) + Reduce (aggregate)Apache Spark
HiveSQL on Hadoop — compiles HiveQL to MapReduce/TezSpark SQL, Presto, Trino
HBaseNoSQL key-value store on HDFS — random read/writeApache Cassandra, DynamoDB
PigData flow scripting language for MapReducePySpark DataFrames
SqoopImport/export data between RDBMS and HDFSAirbyte, Fivetran, Glue
OozieWorkflow scheduler for Hadoop jobsApache Airflow, Prefect

HDFS Architecture

👑

NameNode

The master — stores the filesystem metadata (which blocks belong to which file, which DataNodes hold each block). Single point of failure — use High Availability (HA) with standby NameNode.

💾

DataNode

Worker nodes — store the actual data blocks (default 128MB). Each block is replicated 3× across different nodes/racks for fault tolerance. Heartbeat sent to NameNode every 3 seconds.

⚡ Chapter 3

Apache Spark Architecture

Execution Model

🎛️

Driver Program

Runs the main() function. Creates SparkContext/SparkSession. Builds the DAG. Coordinates executors. Collects results. One per application.

📋

Cluster Manager

Allocates resources: YARN (Hadoop), Kubernetes, Mesos, or Spark Standalone. Driver requests resources; cluster manager provides executors.

⚙️

Executors

JVM processes on worker nodes. Run tasks. Cache data. Multiple tasks run concurrently per executor (one per core). Communicate results back to driver.

📊

DAG Scheduler

Breaks the logical plan into stages separated by shuffle boundaries. Each stage becomes a set of parallel tasks (one per partition). Handles failures by recomputing lost partitions.

📨 Chapter 4

Apache Kafka

Kafka is a distributed event streaming platform — a durable, high-throughput, fault-tolerant message queue that decouples producers and consumers.

Core Concepts

ConceptDescription
TopicNamed category for messages. Producers publish to topics. Consumers subscribe to topics. Append-only log.
PartitionTopics are split into partitions for parallelism. Each partition is an ordered, immutable sequence. Assigned to a broker.
OffsetEach message in a partition has a sequential ID (offset). Consumers track their offset — this enables replay and exactly-once semantics.
BrokerA Kafka server. A cluster has multiple brokers. Partitions are distributed across brokers for load balancing and replication.
Consumer GroupMultiple consumers sharing work — each partition is consumed by exactly one consumer in the group. Enables horizontal scaling.
RetentionKafka keeps messages for a configured time (default 7 days) regardless of consumption. Consumers can rewind to any offset.
Replication FactorEach partition is replicated across N brokers. If the leader broker fails, a follower becomes leader automatically.

At-most-once: messages may be lost, never duplicated. At-least-once: no loss, possible duplicates — most common. Exactly-once: no loss, no duplicates — requires idempotent producers + transactions (Kafka 0.11+). Exactly-once is hardest but necessary for financial transactions.

📁 Chapter 5

File Formats — Parquet, ORC, Avro

Choosing the Right Format

FormatTypeCompressionSchemaBest For
ParquetColumnarExcellent (Snappy/ZSTD)EmbeddedAnalytics, BI, Spark, Presto — SELECT few columns from large tables
ORCColumnarBetter than Parquet (ZLIB)EmbeddedHive workloads, Hive ACID, slightly better for Hive than Parquet
AvroRow-basedGood (Snappy/Deflate)Separate .avscKafka messages, row serialisation, schema evolution, writes
JSONRow-basedPoor (no compression built-in)NoneAPIs, configs, small data — NOT for analytics at scale
CSVRow-basedPoorNoneHuman-readable exchange — NOT for Big Data storage
Delta/IcebergColumnar + metadataExcellentVersionedLakehouse — ACID, time travel, schema evolution, upserts

Columnar (Parquet, ORC): stores all values of one column together. Analytics reading 3 out of 100 columns reads only 3% of data — massive I/O saving. Also enables superior compression (same-type values compress much better). Row-based (Avro, CSV): stores entire rows together. Better for writing whole records and full-row reads (ETL ingestion, Kafka).

🗄️ Chapter 6

Storage Systems

HDFS vs Object Storage vs Table Formats

🐘

HDFS

Hadoop Distributed File System. Block storage (128MB). Strong consistency. Co-location of compute and storage (data locality). Requires on-prem cluster. Being replaced by cloud object storage.

☁️

Object Storage (S3/GCS/ADLS)

Infinitely scalable, cheap, cloud-native. Decouples storage from compute. Eventual consistency (S3 now strongly consistent). No data locality — network becomes the bottleneck. Standard for modern data lakes.

△

Delta Lake

Open-source storage layer on Parquet + transaction log (JSON). ACID transactions, time travel, schema enforcement, upserts/deletes. Developed by Databricks. Default in Databricks, also runs on Spark/Trino.

🧊

Apache Iceberg

Open table format (Netflix). Metadata layer on top of Parquet/ORC/Avro. Hidden partitioning, schema evolution, time travel, ACID. Supported by Snowflake, BigQuery, Spark, Flink, Trino — true open standard.

📦 Chapter 7

Batch vs Stream Processing

Processing Models Compared

AspectBatch ProcessingStream Processing
DataBounded — fixed datasetUnbounded — infinite stream
LatencyMinutes to hoursMilliseconds to seconds
ThroughputVery high (optimised for bulk)Lower (per-event overhead)
ComplexitySimpler — no state managementHigher — windowing, watermarks, late data
ToolsSpark (batch), Hive, dbt, SQLKafka Streams, Flink, Spark Streaming, Beam
Use caseDaily reports, ML training, ETLFraud detection, alerting, real-time dashboards
CostLower (off-peak clusters)Higher (always-on infrastructure)
🔀 Chapter 8

Lambda vs Kappa Architecture

Big Data Architecture Patterns

λ

Lambda Architecture

Two parallel pipelines: Batch layer (recomputes all historical data periodically, slow but accurate) + Speed layer (processes recent events in real-time, fast but approximate). A serving layer merges both. Problem: two codebases, two bugs to fix.

κ

Kappa Architecture

Single streaming pipeline for everything. Reprocessing is done by replaying from Kafka with a new consumer group. Simpler — one codebase. Requires a replayable message queue (Kafka). Modern default when streaming infrastructure is mature.

Most new architectures lean Kappa or use a Lakehouse approach: stream into a Delta/Iceberg table (batch + stream unified), then query with Spark or a cloud DWH. Flink + Iceberg is a popular modern pattern for exactly this.

🟢 Practice

Q&A — Big Data Beginner (20 Questions)

Core Concepts

Q1. What are the 5 Vs of Big Data? ▼

Volume: size of data (TBs–PBs). Velocity: speed of data generation (real-time streams). Variety: types of data (structured, semi, unstructured). Veracity: data quality, accuracy, trustworthiness. Value: the business outcome — insights and decisions. Some add a 6th V: Variability (inconsistent data formats) or Visualisation.

Q2. What is HDFS and how does it achieve fault tolerance? ▼

HDFS (Hadoop Distributed File System) splits files into blocks (default 128MB) and distributes them across DataNodes. Each block is replicated 3× (default) across different DataNodes, ideally on different racks. If a DataNode fails, the NameNode detects the missing heartbeat (after 10 minutes) and instructs other DataNodes to re-replicate the affected blocks to maintain the replication factor. The NameNode is the single master — use HA mode with an active/standby NameNode pair.

Q3. What is Apache Kafka and why is it widely used? ▼

Kafka is a distributed event streaming platform — a high-throughput, durable, fault-tolerant message queue. Producers write events to topics; consumers read at their own pace. Messages are retained on disk (default 7 days) making replay possible. Used for: decoupling microservices, real-time analytics pipelines, event sourcing, change data capture (CDC), log aggregation. Kafka handles millions of events per second per broker. Consumer groups enable horizontal scaling — multiple consumers split partitions between them.

Q4. Why is Parquet preferred over CSV for Big Data analytics? ▼

Parquet is columnar — stores column values together, not row values. For a query reading 3 out of 100 columns, Parquet reads only 3% of the data vs 100% for CSV. Parquet also: (1) embeds schema, so no type inference errors; (2) compresses much better (same-type data compresses efficiently — 5–10× vs CSV); (3) supports predicate pushdown — filter rows without reading them; (4) supports nested data types. CSV: human-readable, good for small data exchange, terrible for analytics at scale.

Q5. What is the difference between batch and stream processing? ▼

Batch processing: processes a bounded dataset (collected over time) in one job. Latency: minutes to hours. High throughput. Tools: Spark, Hive, dbt. Example: nightly ETL job processing all of yesterday's orders. Stream processing: processes events as they arrive, one at a time or in micro-batches. Latency: milliseconds to seconds. Tools: Kafka Streams, Flink, Spark Structured Streaming. Example: fraud detection on each credit card transaction as it happens.

Q6. What is the difference between vertical and horizontal scaling? ▼

Vertical scaling (scale up): add more CPU/RAM to a single machine. Simple, no code changes, but limited by hardware ceiling and creates a single point of failure. Horizontal scaling (scale out): add more machines to a cluster. Virtually unlimited scale, fault-tolerant, but requires distributed system design (partitioning, coordination). Big Data systems (HDFS, Kafka, Spark) are designed for horizontal scaling — adding a node increases throughput linearly.

Q7. What is the difference between structured, semi-structured, and unstructured data? ▼

Structured: fixed schema, rows and columns — SQL databases, CSV, Excel. Easy to query. Semi-structured: flexible schema, self-describing — JSON, XML, Avro, Parquet with nested types, log files. Can be queried with schema-on-read tools. Unstructured: no schema — images, video, audio, free text, PDFs. Requires ML/NLP/CV to extract meaning. Big Data systems handle all three: HDFS stores blobs, Spark processes JSON, ML models process images. Traditional DWHs primarily handled structured data only.

Q8. What is MapReduce and how does it work? ▼

MapReduce is a programming model for processing large datasets in parallel across a cluster. Two phases: Map: each mapper processes one input split independently, emitting key-value pairs. Reduce: all values for the same key are grouped and sent to one reducer which aggregates them. Between map and reduce, data is sorted and shuffled across the network by key. Example: word count — Map emits (word,1) per word; Reduce sums all 1s per word. Spark's RDD API is a generalisation of MapReduce with more flexibility and in-memory processing.

Q9. What are the main components of the Hadoop ecosystem you should know? ▼

Core: HDFS (distributed storage), YARN (resource management), MapReduce (batch compute — largely replaced by Spark). Query: Hive (SQL on Hadoop), Presto/Trino (fast interactive SQL). Processing: Spark (unified analytics), Flink (streaming). Ingestion: Kafka (streaming), Sqoop (RDBMS↔HDFS), Flume (log ingestion). Coordination: Zookeeper (distributed configuration), Oozie (workflow scheduler). Storage: HBase (NoSQL on HDFS), Cassandra (separate but often co-deployed).

Q10. What is a data pipeline and what are the main types? ▼

A data pipeline is a series of steps that move and transform data from source to destination. Types: (1) Batch pipeline: processes accumulated data periodically (hourly, daily) — simpler, higher latency; (2) Streaming pipeline: processes events as they arrive — lower latency, more complex; (3) Lambda pipeline: batch + stream in parallel; (4) ETL pipeline: extract from source, transform in middleware, load to DWH; (5) ELT pipeline: load raw first, transform in DWH. Components: source connectors, message queues, compute engines, storage, orchestrator.

Q11. What is Apache Zookeeper and what role does it play in Big Data systems? ▼

Zookeeper is a centralised coordination service for distributed systems. It provides: distributed locking (mutex across machines), service discovery (find which broker is leader), configuration management (store shared config with change notifications), leader election (which Kafka broker is partition leader). Used by: Kafka (broker coordination, topic metadata — though newer versions use KRaft to replace Zookeeper), Hadoop (NameNode HA), HBase (region server coordination). Zookeeper itself uses a quorum of odd-numbered nodes (3 or 5) for fault tolerance.

Q12. What is data replication in distributed systems and what are the trade-offs? ▼

Replication stores copies of data on multiple nodes. Benefits: (1) Fault tolerance — node failure doesn't lose data; (2) Read scaling — reads can be served from replicas. Trade-offs: (1) Write latency — must write to N nodes; (2) Consistency — replicas may lag (eventual consistency) or require synchronous acks (strong consistency, higher latency). Kafka: replication factor 3, leader handles all reads/writes, followers replicate. HDFS: 3× replication by default, across racks. Trade-off: storage cost × fault tolerance × write speed.

Q13. What is a message queue and how is it different from a database? ▼

A message queue (Kafka, RabbitMQ, SQS) is designed for event streaming — producers write events, consumers read and acknowledge. Key properties: ordered delivery (within partition), retention (events persist for a configurable period), consumer-controlled offset (replay possible), high throughput (millions/sec). A database stores current state — random read/write, persistent indefinitely, supports complex queries. Use queues for: decoupling producers and consumers, buffering traffic spikes, event sourcing, CDC. Don't use queues as a primary data store.

Q14. What is the difference between a hot path and a cold path in Big Data architectures? ▼

Hot path (speed layer): processes data in real-time, seconds or sub-second latency. Optimised for speed over completeness. Results may be approximate (e.g. approx distinct counts with HyperLogLog). Tools: Kafka Streams, Flink, Spark Streaming. Cold path (batch layer): processes the complete historical dataset periodically. Slower but accurate. Tools: Spark batch, Hive, dbt. Lambda architecture combines both — cold path corrects hot path approximations. Kappa architecture uses only a hot path with replay capability.

Q15. What are the typical SLAs for batch vs streaming pipelines? ▼

Batch pipelines: SLA typically defined as "table refreshed by 8am" or "data available within 4 hours of source". Measured by: job completion time, data freshness (lag from source event to availability), row count vs expected. Streaming pipelines: SLA on end-to-end latency (e.g. "<30 seconds from event to dashboard"), throughput (events/sec sustained), availability (99.9% = <8.7 hours downtime/year). Monitor with: alerting on job failures, freshness checks in dbt, custom Prometheus metrics, Datadog dashboards.

Q16. What is eventual consistency vs strong consistency? ▼

Strong consistency: after a write completes, all subsequent reads see that write — regardless of which node serves the read. Requires synchronous replication or consensus protocol (Raft, Paxos). Higher latency. Used by: RDBMS with synchronous replication, Google Spanner, CockroachDB. Eventual consistency: after a write, replicas will eventually converge — but reads may temporarily return stale data. Much lower latency. Used by: Cassandra (tunable), DynamoDB (default), Kafka consumer lag. Most Big Data systems choose eventual consistency for throughput; financial systems require strong consistency.

Q17. What is Apache HBase and when would you use it? ▼

HBase is a distributed, column-family NoSQL database built on HDFS. Data model: tables have rows (by row key) and column families. Strong consistency. Random read/write access (unlike HDFS which is append-only). Use when: you need random access to large datasets stored on HDFS (HDFS alone only supports sequential read), time-series data keyed by timestamp+entity, high write throughput with random reads (telecom call records, IoT sensor readings). Not a relational DB — no SQL JOINs, no secondary indexes by default. Usually superseded by Cassandra for greenfield projects.

Q18. What is a data lakehouse and which open table formats power it? ▼

A lakehouse combines data lake economics (cheap object storage, open formats) with data warehouse capabilities (ACID, schema enforcement, fast analytics). The key is an open table format layer on top of Parquet: Delta Lake (Databricks — transaction log in JSON/_delta_log/), Apache Iceberg (Netflix — metadata files + manifest lists, truly engine-agnostic), Apache Hudi (Uber — optimised for CDC upserts, record-level indexing). All three provide: ACID transactions, time travel, schema evolution, partition evolution. Iceberg is gaining the most multi-engine adoption in 2024-2025.

Q19. How do you design a data pipeline for high availability? ▼

Key principles: (1) Idempotent processing — re-running a failed job produces the same result, no duplicates; (2) Checkpointing — save progress so restarts don't reprocess from the beginning; (3) Dead letter queues — route failed messages for manual inspection rather than blocking the pipeline; (4) Circuit breakers — stop sending traffic to a failing downstream system; (5) Monitoring + alerting — detect failures immediately; (6) Backpressure — slow producers when consumers are overwhelmed. Tools: Kafka (durability), Airflow (retry + alerting), Delta Lake (ACID), structured streaming (checkpoints).

Q20. What is the difference between a push-based and pull-based data pipeline? ▼

Push-based: the source system sends data when it changes — webhooks, CDC events, Kafka producer. Lower latency, real-time. Source must be aware of the pipeline. Risk: source overwhelms downstream if not rate-limited. Pull-based: the pipeline polls the source on a schedule — batch ETL, SQL queries, Airbyte connectors. Source agnostic, easier to implement. Higher latency (bounded by poll frequency). Most enterprise data integration is pull-based (Fivetran, Airbyte pull every hour). Event-driven architectures prefer push. Many modern tools support both.

🔴 Practice

Q&A — Big Data Advanced (20 Questions)

Advanced Topics

Q1. Explain the CAP theorem and its implications for distributed systems. ▼

CAP theorem: a distributed system can guarantee at most 2 of 3: Consistency (every read returns the latest write), Availability (every request gets a response), Partition tolerance (system works despite network splits). Since network partitions are unavoidable in real distributed systems, you always need P — so the real choice is CP vs AP. CP systems (HBase, Zookeeper, Spanner): sacrifice availability for consistency. AP systems (Cassandra, DynamoDB, Couchbase): sacrifice consistency for availability. Most modern distributed DBs use tunable consistency.

Q2. What is exactly-once processing in Kafka and how is it achieved? ▼

Exactly-once means each message is processed exactly once — no loss, no duplicates. Achieved via: (1) Idempotent producer: Kafka deduplicates retries using a producer ID + sequence number; (2) Transactions: atomic write across multiple partitions and topics — either all writes commit or none; (3) Consumer offset committed atomically with processing result. Kafka Streams has native exactly-once. For Spark Structured Streaming: use idempotent sinks + Kafka's exactly-once. Requires careful coordination between read offset and output commit.

Q3. What is data locality in Hadoop and why does it matter? ▼

Data locality means running compute tasks on the same node where the data block resides — avoiding network transfer. In Hadoop, the ResourceManager (YARN) tries to schedule tasks on DataNodes that hold the required blocks. Three levels: (1) Node-local: task runs on same node as data (ideal); (2) Rack-local: task is on same rack (1 switch hop); (3) Off-rack: data crosses racks (slower). With cloud object storage (S3), data locality disappears — all data is remote, making network bandwidth the new bottleneck. Modern cloud-native systems use high-bandwidth networking to compensate.

Q4. What is Apache Iceberg and why is it considered the open lakehouse standard? ▼

Iceberg is an open table format for large analytic datasets. It adds a metadata layer on top of Parquet/ORC/Avro files, providing: (1) ACID transactions — concurrent reads/writes; (2) Time travel — query any historical snapshot; (3) Hidden partitioning — no partition path in queries, automatic partition pruning; (4) Schema evolution — add/rename/reorder columns safely; (5) Multi-engine support — Spark, Flink, Trino, Presto, Snowflake, BigQuery all read/write Iceberg natively. This vendor-neutrality makes it the emerging standard vs Delta Lake (Databricks-led) or Hudi (Uber-led).

Q5. Explain Lambda vs Kappa architecture — when would you choose each? ▼

Lambda: two separate pipelines — batch (accurate, reprocesses all history) + speed (real-time, approximate). Serving layer merges both. Choose when: batch reprocessing is needed with tools that don't do streaming well, or when the stream layer is approximate and batch corrects it. Downside: two codebases to maintain, potential inconsistencies. Kappa: single streaming pipeline. Reprocessing by replaying Kafka with a new consumer. Choose when: your streaming tool (Flink, Spark Streaming) can handle batch too, Kafka retains data long enough, and you want operational simplicity. Modern lakehouse (stream → Delta/Iceberg → batch queries) is effectively Kappa.

Q6. How does Kafka's consumer group rebalancing work and what is its impact on latency? ▼

When a consumer joins or leaves a group, Kafka triggers a group rebalance: the Group Coordinator stops all consumers in the group, revokes all partition assignments, redistributes partitions to remaining consumers, then resumes consumption. During rebalance, consumption pauses — causing latency spikes. Mitigation: Incremental cooperative rebalancing (Kafka 2.4+) — consumers only release partitions being moved, others continue; Static group membership (group.instance.id) — a consumer that restarts within session.timeout.ms reclaims its partitions without a rebalance.

Q7. How do you implement exactly-once semantics across Kafka and a database? ▼

Pattern: (1) Enable idempotent Kafka producer (enable.idempotence=true); (2) Use Kafka transactions to atomically write to multiple topics; (3) Consume from Kafka with manual offset commit; (4) Write to DB and commit Kafka offset in the same DB transaction (transactional outbox pattern); if the DB commit fails, Kafka offset is not committed, so the message is reprocessed — and because your write is idempotent (use INSERT ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING or MERGE), re-processing doesn't cause duplicates. This pattern requires the sink to support idempotent writes.

Q8. What is Kafka Streams and how does it compare to Flink? ▼

Kafka Streams is a client library (embedded in your Java/Scala app) for building stateful stream processing applications directly on Kafka — no separate cluster needed. State stored in RocksDB locally, backed by Kafka changelog topics. Simple deployment, ideal for microservices. vs Flink: Flink is a full-blown distributed processing framework with its own cluster (or Kubernetes). Flink has richer windowing (session windows, custom triggers), lower latency, better throughput for complex jobs, true event-time semantics. Kafka Streams: simple, embedded, good for 80% of streaming use cases. Flink: when you need full power.

Q9. Explain the difference between event time and processing time in stream processing. ▼

Event time: the timestamp when the event actually occurred (embedded in the event data). Correct for business logic — "how many orders were placed between 10am and 11am" should use event time. Problem: events arrive late due to network delays, mobile clients coming online, etc. Requires watermarks to handle late data. Processing time: the timestamp when the stream processor receives and processes the event. Simple (no watermarks), but can be wrong — a 5-minute delay in Kafka means a 10am event processed at 10:05. Use processing time only when approximate results are acceptable or latency is consistent.

Q10. What is compaction in Kafka and when should you enable it? ▼

Log compaction is a Kafka retention policy that keeps only the latest value for each key, discarding older versions. Set cleanup.policy=compact on the topic. Use cases: (1) Changelog topics for Kafka Streams state stores (need last value per key); (2) Change data capture (CDC) — compact changelog tables; (3) Configuration/lookup topics where consumers need the latest state after restart. Compaction runs in the background — does not guarantee immediate deletion. Combine with time-based retention (cleanup.policy=compact,delete) to also expire old keys.

Q11. How does Spark handle lazy evaluation and what are the implications for debugging? ▼

Spark builds a logical plan of transformations without executing them. Execution only starts when an action is called. Implication for debugging: exceptions from lazy operations only surface when an action is triggered — not at the line where the transformation was written. This makes stack traces point to the action, not the buggy transformation. Solutions: (1) call df.show() after each major transformation during development; (2) use spark.sparkContext.setCheckpointDir() to materialise intermediate results; (3) enable spark.sql.debug.maxToStringFields for better error messages; (4) wrap in try/except around each transformation stage.

Q12. What is the columnar execution advantage in vectorised query engines? ▼

Modern columnar engines (BigQuery, Snowflake, Spark with Photon, DuckDB) process data in columnar batches rather than row-by-row. Benefits: (1) CPU SIMD: operate on a vector of 256/512 values simultaneously with AVX-512 instructions; (2) CPU cache efficiency: columnar layout keeps related values together in L1/L2 cache; (3) Late materialisation: apply filters before reconstructing full rows; (4) Better compression: homogeneous data compresses better with run-length encoding, bit-packing. Result: 5-30× faster than row-oriented engines for analytical aggregations. Fundamental to why Snowflake/BigQuery beat traditional RDBMS at analytics.

Q13. How do you design a real-time fraud detection pipeline? ▼

(1) Ingest: Kafka topic for transaction events; (2) Feature extraction: Flink stateful job computing per-user features (avg spend last 30min, geolocation velocity, merchant category frequency) using keyed state; (3) Model scoring: call ML model (scikit-learn/XGBoost served via REST, or embedded TensorFlow Lite) to get fraud probability; (4) Decision: threshold or rule-engine applies hold/allow; (5) Write back: decision to Kafka, then to operational DB; (6) Latency: target <100ms end-to-end. Challenges: feature freshness, model staleness, handling high-velocity card testing attacks.

Q14. What is consistent hashing and how is it used in distributed systems? ▼

Consistent hashing maps both data keys and nodes to positions on a circular ring (0 to 2³²). A key is assigned to the first node clockwise from its hash position. When a node is added/removed, only keys in the adjacent segment are remapped — O(K/N) keys move vs O(K) in modular hashing (where K=keys, N=nodes). Used by: Cassandra (token ring), DynamoDB, Redis Cluster (hash slots), Memcached. Enables: seamless node addition/removal, load balancing, minimal data movement during scaling. Virtual nodes (vnodes) further distribute load evenly when nodes have different capacities.

Q15. What is the difference between synchronous and asynchronous processing in data pipelines? ▼

Synchronous: the caller waits for the operation to complete before proceeding. Simple to reason about, easy error handling, introduces latency. Suitable for: small data transformations, validation steps, transactional operations requiring immediate confirmation. Asynchronous: the caller submits a task and continues without waiting — result delivered later via callback, event, or polling. Enables higher throughput, decouples components, handles variable load. Used in: Kafka producers (async send), Airflow task submission, async HTTP clients. Risk: harder debugging, need to handle partial failures and out-of-order completions.

Q16. How does HDFS handle block placement and why does rack awareness matter? ▼

HDFS default 3-replica strategy: (1) first replica on the writer's node; (2) second replica on a different rack; (3) third replica on the same rack as the second. This balances: write performance (first replica is local) with fault tolerance (2 racks involved, so one full rack failure doesn't lose data). Rack awareness requires configuring a topology script (net.topology.script.file.name) that maps IP addresses to rack identifiers. Modern cloud environments typically skip rack awareness in favour of availability zone awareness.

Q17. What is the role of a service mesh in Big Data microservices architectures? ▼

A service mesh (Istio, Linkerd) manages service-to-service communication in microservices clusters. Provides: (1) Traffic management: load balancing, circuit breaking, retries; (2) Security: mTLS between services; (3) Observability: distributed tracing, per-service metrics, access logs — without code changes (sidecar proxy). In data pipelines: relevant for ML inference services, REST-based feature stores, API gateways in front of real-time scoring services. Less relevant for batch Spark/Hadoop (which use cluster managers rather than service meshes).

Q18. What are the key differences between Apache Iceberg, Delta Lake, and Apache Hudi? ▼

All three are lakehouse table formats providing ACID + time travel on object storage. Delta Lake: strongest Spark/Databricks integration, JSON transaction log, mature MERGE support, Z-ordering. Iceberg: most engine-agnostic (Spark, Flink, Trino, Snowflake, BigQuery all support natively), hidden partitioning, partition evolution without rewriting data, standardised REST catalog. Hudi: optimised for CDC upserts, record-level indexing (fastest individual row updates), two table types (CoW for read-heavy, MoR for write-heavy). Industry trend: Iceberg is winning as the open standard; Delta is dominant in Databricks shops; Hudi used at Uber-scale upsert workloads.

Q19. How would you design a petabyte-scale data architecture from scratch? ▼

(1) Storage: cloud object storage (S3/ADLS) as the foundation — cheap, infinite, durable; (2) Table format: Apache Iceberg for open, multi-engine access with ACID; (3) Ingestion: Kafka for streaming, Airbyte/Fivetran for batch; (4) Processing: Spark (batch) + Flink (streaming), compute on Kubernetes or Databricks; (5) Transformation: dbt for SQL-based ELT transformations; (6) Serving: query engine (Trino/Athena) for ad-hoc + cloud DWH (Snowflake/BigQuery) for BI; (7) Orchestration: Airflow or Dagster; (8) Governance: Unity Catalog or DataHub. Keep compute and storage separate throughout.

Q20. How do you troubleshoot a Kafka consumer lag problem? ▼

Step 1: measure lag — kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe --group my_group shows per-partition lag. Step 2: identify cause: (a) Slow consumer — processing bottleneck; solution: increase consumer parallelism (add more consumer instances to the group, up to partition count), optimise processing logic; (b) Producer burst — temporary spike; solution: increase consumer throughput or wait for it to drain; (c) Consumer crash — not consuming at all; solution: fix the crash, restart; (d) Rebalancing loop — consumer keeps joining/leaving; solution: increase session.timeout.ms, fix stability. Monitor with Burrow, Kafka Manager, or Grafana + kafka-consumer-offsets metrics.

More Advanced Questions (Q41–Q60)

Q41. Write a query to find customers in the top 10% by lifetime value. ▼
SQL
WITH customer_ltv AS (
  SELECT
    c.id, c.name, c.email,
    SUM(o.total) AS ltv,
    PERCENT_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY SUM(o.total)) AS pct_rank
  FROM customers c
  JOIN orders    o ON c.id = o.customer_id
  GROUP BY c.id, c.name, c.email
)
SELECT id, name, ltv,
  ROUND(pct_rank*100,1) AS percentile
FROM  customer_ltv
WHERE pct_rank >= 0.90   -- top 10%
ORDER BY ltv DESC;
Q42. What is query plan caching? How does it affect stored procedures? ▼

When a query is first executed, the optimizer parses it, creates an execution plan, and caches it. Subsequent calls with the same parameterized shape reuse the cached plan without re-optimization. Stored procedures benefit the most — their queries are compiled and cached when first called, making repeated calls very fast. However, plan caching can cause problems: if statistics change dramatically (e.g., a table grows from 1,000 to 100M rows), the cached plan might no longer be optimal. Solutions: CALL sp_recompile('procedure_name') to force re-compilation, or restructure queries to avoid parameter sniffing.

Q43. Explain the difference between UNION, INTERSECT, and EXCEPT. ▼

These are set operators that combine results of two queries with matching column structures:

SQL
-- UNION: rows in A OR B (deduplicates)
SELECT email FROM customers
UNION
SELECT email FROM suppliers;

-- INTERSECT: rows in BOTH A AND B (PostgreSQL/SQL Server)
SELECT email FROM customers
INTERSECT
SELECT email FROM suppliers;

-- EXCEPT: rows in A but NOT in B (PostgreSQL/SQL Server)
SELECT email FROM customers
EXCEPT
SELECT email FROM suppliers;

-- MySQL workarounds (no INTERSECT/EXCEPT)
-- INTERSECT via JOIN
SELECT a.email FROM customers a
INNER JOIN suppliers b USING(email);
-- EXCEPT via LEFT JOIN anti-join
SELECT a.email FROM customers a
LEFT JOIN suppliers b USING(email)
WHERE b.email IS NULL;
Q44. Write a query to pivot data from rows to columns dynamically. ▼
SQL — Dynamic Pivot via Prepared Statement
-- Step 1: Generate CASE WHEN columns dynamically
SELECT
  GROUP_CONCAT(
    DISTINCT CONCAT(
      "SUM(CASE WHEN product='", product_name, "' THEN qty ELSE 0 END) AS `",
      product_name, "`"
    )
  ) INTO @cols
FROM sales;

-- Step 2: Build and execute the pivot query
SET @sql = CONCAT(
  'SELECT sale_month, ', @cols,
  ' FROM sales GROUP BY sale_month ORDER BY sale_month'
);
PREPARE stmt FROM @sql;
EXECUTE stmt;
DEALLOCATE PREPARE stmt;
Q45. Write a stored function that computes compound interest. ▼
SQL — Stored Function
DELIMITER $$
CREATE FUNCTION CompoundInterest(
  principal  DECIMAL(15,2),
  rate_pct   DECIMAL(6,4),   -- annual rate e.g. 5.25 for 5.25%
  years      INT,
  n_per_year INT              -- compounding freq (12=monthly)
)
RETURNS DECIMAL(15,2)
DETERMINISTIC NO SQL
BEGIN
  -- A = P(1 + r/n)^(n*t)
  RETURN ROUND(
    principal * POW(
      (1 + (rate_pct/100) / n_per_year),
      n_per_year * years
    ), 2
  );
END$$
DELIMITER ;

-- Use in a query
SELECT
  account_id,
  balance AS principal,
  CompoundInterest(balance, 5.25, 10, 12) AS value_after_10_years
FROM savings_accounts;
Q46. Write a query to find all permutations of a customer's product purchases. ▼
SQL — Market Basket Analysis
-- Which product pairs are bought together most often?
SELECT
  p1.product_name                AS product_a,
  p2.product_name                AS product_b,
  COUNT(DISTINCT oi1.order_id) AS times_bought_together
FROM  order_items  oi1
JOIN  order_items  oi2  ON  oi1.order_id   = oi2.order_id
                       AND oi1.product_id < oi2.product_id
JOIN  products     p1  ON  oi1.product_id = p1.id
JOIN  products     p2  ON  oi2.product_id = p2.id
GROUP BY p1.product_name, p2.product_name
HAVING  COUNT(DISTINCT oi1.order_id) > 5
ORDER BY times_bought_together DESC
LIMIT 20;
Q47. What is write-ahead logging (WAL) and how does it relate to durability? ▼

Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) is the mechanism that makes the D in ACID possible. Before any data change is written to the actual data file, it is first written to a sequential log file (the redo log / WAL). The log write is very fast (sequential I/O). If the system crashes, the database can recover by replaying the WAL log from the last checkpoint. In MySQL InnoDB, this is the redo log. Because the log is always written first, no committed transaction can ever be lost — even if the main data pages are in the buffer pool and not yet flushed to disk. The tradeoff is that all writes require at least a WAL write, adding some overhead.

Q48. Write a query to calculate a user retention cohort table. ▼
SQL — Cohort Retention
WITH
cohorts AS (
  SELECT
    user_id,
    DATE_FORMAT(MIN(login_date),'%Y-%m') AS cohort_month
  FROM user_sessions
  GROUP BY user_id
),
activity AS (
  SELECT
    s.user_id,
    c.cohort_month,
    TIMESTAMPDIFF(MONTH,
      STR_TO_DATE(CONCAT(c.cohort_month,'-01'),'%Y-%m-%d'),
      STR_TO_DATE(CONCAT(DATE_FORMAT(s.login_date,'%Y-%m'),'-01'),'%Y-%m-%d')
    ) AS month_num
  FROM user_sessions s
  JOIN cohorts       c USING(user_id)
)
SELECT
  cohort_month,
  COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN month_num=0  THEN user_id END) AS m0,
  COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN month_num=1  THEN user_id END) AS m1,
  COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN month_num=2  THEN user_id END) AS m2,
  COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN month_num=3  THEN user_id END) AS m3
FROM  activity
GROUP BY cohort_month
ORDER BY cohort_month;
Q49. Explain table partitioning — types and a real MySQL example. ▼

Partitioning splits a logically single table into multiple physical storage segments (partitions), invisible to queries. The optimizer prunes partitions — queries only scan relevant ones, skipping others entirely (partition pruning). Types:

  • RANGE: Rows assigned based on a range of values (commonly dates). Best for time-series data.
  • LIST: Rows assigned based on explicit value lists (country = 'India', country = 'USA').
  • HASH: Rows evenly distributed across N partitions by hash of a column. Spreads load evenly.
  • KEY: Similar to HASH but uses MySQL's own hash function on any column type.
SQL — RANGE Partitioning on order_date
CREATE TABLE orders_partitioned (
  id          INT           NOT NULL,
  customer_id INT           NOT NULL,
  order_date  DATE          NOT NULL,
  total       DECIMAL(10,2),
  PRIMARY KEY (id, order_date)  -- partition col must be in PK
)
PARTITION BY RANGE (YEAR(order_date)) (
  PARTITION p2022 VALUES LESS THAN (2023),
  PARTITION p2023 VALUES LESS THAN (2024),
  PARTITION p2024 VALUES LESS THAN (2025),
  PARTITION p_future VALUES LESS THAN MAXVALUE
);

-- This query only scans p2024 partition (partition pruning)
SELECT * FROM orders_partitioned
WHERE order_date BETWEEN '2024-01-01' AND '2024-12-31';

-- Drop old partition (instant! vs DELETE which is slow)
ALTER TABLE orders_partitioned DROP PARTITION p2022;
Q50. Write a query to identify data anomalies — values that are statistical outliers. ▼
SQL — Outlier Detection using Z-Score
WITH stats AS (
  SELECT
    AVG(order_value)    AS mean_val,
    STDDEV(order_value) AS std_val
  FROM orders
),
z_scores AS (
  SELECT
    o.id,
    o.customer_id,
    o.order_value,
    s.mean_val,
    s.std_val,
    ABS((o.order_value - s.mean_val) / NULLIF(s.std_val,0)) AS z_score
  FROM  orders o
  CROSS JOIN stats s
)
SELECT id, customer_id, order_value, ROUND(z_score,2) AS z_score
FROM  z_scores
WHERE z_score > 3   -- >3 standard deviations = statistical outlier
ORDER BY z_score DESC;
Q51. What is a covering index and how do you verify it is being used? ▼

A covering index includes all columns needed by a query — the DB answers it entirely from the index without touching actual table rows, eliminating one disk I/O per row. To verify it is used: run EXPLAIN and look for "Using index" in the Extra column (not "Using index condition" or "Using where"). "Using index condition" still means the DB must fetch some rows from the table. Only "Using index" means a true covering index is in play.

SQL
-- Query needs: customer_id (WHERE), order_date (WHERE), total (SELECT)
CREATE INDEX idx_covering
  ON orders(customer_id, order_date, total);

EXPLAIN SELECT order_date, total
FROM  orders
WHERE customer_id = 42
  AND order_date >= '2024-01-01';
-- Extra: 'Using index' ← confirmed covering index
Q52. Write a complete SCD Type 2 implementation procedure. ▼
SQL — SCD Type 2 Load Procedure
DELIMITER $$
CREATE PROCEDURE LoadCustomerDimSCD2(
  IN p_source_id   INT,
  IN p_name        VARCHAR(100),
  IN p_city        VARCHAR(50),
  IN p_email       VARCHAR(150),
  IN p_effective_dt DATE
)
BEGIN
  DECLARE v_existing_sk  INT           DEFAULT NULL;
  DECLARE v_curr_city    VARCHAR(50);
  DECLARE v_curr_email   VARCHAR(150);

  -- Find current active record
  SELECT  customer_sk, city, email
  INTO    v_existing_sk, v_curr_city, v_curr_email
  FROM    dim_customer
  WHERE   source_customer_id = p_source_id
    AND   is_current        = 1
  LIMIT 1;

  IF v_existing_sk IS NULL THEN
    -- New customer — insert first record
    INSERT INTO dim_customer
      (source_customer_id, name, city, email,
       effective_date, expiry_date, is_current)
    VALUES
      (p_source_id, p_name, p_city, p_email,
       p_effective_dt, '9999-12-31', 1);

  ELSEIF v_curr_city <> p_city OR v_curr_email <> p_email THEN
    -- Attribute changed — close old record
    UPDATE dim_customer
    SET    expiry_date = DATE_SUB(p_effective_dt, INTERVAL 1 DAY),
           is_current  = 0
    WHERE  customer_sk = v_existing_sk;

    -- Insert new version
    INSERT INTO dim_customer
      (source_customer_id, name, city, email,
       effective_date, expiry_date, is_current)
    VALUES
      (p_source_id, p_name, p_city, p_email,
       p_effective_dt, '9999-12-31', 1);
  -- ELSE: no change → do nothing (Type 1 would UPDATE here)
  END IF;
END$$
DELIMITER ;

-- Use it
CALL LoadCustomerDimSCD2(1001, 'Pranav Sharma', 'Indore', '[email protected]', CURDATE());
Q53. What are phantom reads? Which isolation level prevents them? ▼

A phantom read occurs when a transaction reads a set of rows twice, and rows that match the WHERE clause appear or disappear between reads — because another transaction inserted or deleted them in between. Example: Transaction A counts rows WHERE status='active' (gets 100). Transaction B inserts 5 new active rows and commits. Transaction A counts again — gets 105. The new 5 rows are "phantoms." SERIALIZABLE isolation level prevents phantom reads by using range locks that block inserts into the queried range until the transaction completes. REPEATABLE READ prevents non-repeatable reads but not phantoms (though InnoDB's MVCC mitigates this in practice).

Q54. Write a query to implement a session activity timeline (session stitching). ▼
SQL — Session Stitching with LAG
-- Group page views into sessions (new session = 30+ min gap)
WITH gaps AS (
  SELECT
    user_id,
    page_url,
    viewed_at,
    LAG(viewed_at) OVER (
      PARTITION BY user_id
      ORDER BY     viewed_at
    ) AS prev_view
  FROM page_views
),
session_flags AS (
  SELECT
    user_id, page_url, viewed_at,
    CASE
      WHEN prev_view IS NULL
        OR TIMESTAMPDIFF(MINUTE, prev_view, viewed_at) > 30
      THEN 1 ELSE 0
    END AS new_session
  FROM gaps
)
SELECT
  user_id, page_url, viewed_at,
  SUM(new_session) OVER (
    PARTITION BY user_id
    ORDER BY     viewed_at
  ) AS session_id
FROM  session_flags
ORDER BY user_id, viewed_at;
Q55. What is the difference between a natural key, surrogate key, and business key? ▼

A natural key is a unique identifier that exists in the real world — SSN, email, ISBN. Pros: meaningful, no extra column needed. Cons: can change (people change emails), may not be truly unique across systems. A surrogate key is a system-generated meaningless identifier (AUTO_INCREMENT id, UUID). Pros: stable, never changes, joins are fast on integers. Cons: meaningless — you can't derive any information from it. A business key (also called alternate key) is the natural key stored alongside the surrogate key — used by ETL and applications to identify records without relying on internal IDs. Best practice in data warehouses: surrogate key as PK, business key stored as a unique indexed column for lookups.

Q56. Write a query for a full SCD Type 6 implementation in a dimension table. ▼
SQL — SCD Type 6 Dimension Table
-- SCD6 = SCD1 + SCD2 + SCD3 combined
-- Keeps full history (Type 2) + previous value column (Type 3)
-- + current value always updated in every row (Type 1)
CREATE TABLE dim_customer_scd6 (
  customer_sk        INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  source_customer_id INT NOT NULL,            -- business key
  name               VARCHAR(100),

  -- SCD2 columns: historical tracking
  city               VARCHAR(50),             -- value at this version
  effective_date     DATE         NOT NULL,
  expiry_date        DATE         DEFAULT '9999-12-31',
  is_current         TINYINT      DEFAULT 1,

  -- SCD3 column: one prior value
  prev_city          VARCHAR(50),             -- previous city

  -- SCD1 column: always-current value stamped on every row
  current_city       VARCHAR(50),             -- denormalized current state

  INDEX idx_bk  (source_customer_id),
  INDEX idx_curr(source_customer_id, is_current)
);

-- On a city change for customer 1001:
-- 1. Update current row: set expiry, is_current=0, prev_city=old city, current_city=new city
-- 2. Update ALL old rows: current_city = new city (SCD1 propagation)
-- 3. Insert new row: new city, effective_date=today, expiry=9999, is_current=1

-- Query: as-of-today view (just filter is_current=1)
SELECT name, city, prev_city, current_city
FROM   dim_customer_scd6
WHERE  source_customer_id = 1001
ORDER BY effective_date;
Q57. How would you identify and fix a slow query in production? Step-by-step process. ▼
  1. Identify: Enable slow query log (slow_query_log=ON, long_query_time=1). Use pt-query-digest or MySQL Workbench to find the top offenders.
  2. Understand: Run EXPLAIN on the slow query. Look for type=ALL (full scans), high rows estimates, Using filesort, Using temporary.
  3. Check indexes: Are the WHERE and JOIN columns indexed? Run SHOW INDEX FROM table_name.
  4. Rewrite if needed: Replace subqueries with JOINs or CTEs. Avoid functions on indexed columns. Eliminate SELECT *. Rewrite NOT IN as NOT EXISTS.
  5. Add indexes: Create indexes on high-cardinality filtered/joined columns. Consider composite/covering indexes.
  6. Update statistics: Run ANALYZE TABLE table_name to refresh optimizer statistics.
  7. Test and measure: Re-run EXPLAIN to confirm plan changed. Benchmark actual execution time. Monitor impact on write performance.
  8. Deploy carefully: On large tables, new indexes should be created during low-traffic windows. Use pt-online-schema-change or gh-ost for zero-downtime index additions.
Q58. Write a query to unpivot (normalize) a wide table with monthly columns into rows. ▼
SQL — Unpivot via UNION ALL
-- Wide table: product | jan_sales | feb_sales | mar_sales ...
-- Convert to: product | month | sales
SELECT product_name, 'January'  AS month, jan_sales  AS sales FROM monthly_sales
UNION ALL
SELECT product_name, 'February' AS month, feb_sales  AS sales FROM monthly_sales
UNION ALL
SELECT product_name, 'March'    AS month, mar_sales  AS sales FROM monthly_sales
ORDER BY product_name, FIELD(month, 'January','February','March');
-- This pattern is MySQL's way of unpivoting wide tables
Q59. Write a query to find the longest sequence of consecutive daily orders for any customer. ▼
SQL — Longest Consecutive Streak
WITH
daily_orders AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT
    customer_id,
    DATE(order_date) AS ord_day
  FROM orders
),
ranked AS (
  SELECT
    customer_id, ord_day,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
      PARTITION BY customer_id
      ORDER BY     ord_day
    ) AS rn
  FROM daily_orders
),
groups AS (
  SELECT
    customer_id, ord_day,
    DATE_SUB(ord_day, INTERVAL rn DAY) AS grp
  FROM ranked
)
SELECT
  g.customer_id,
  c.name,
  MIN(ord_day) AS streak_start,
  MAX(ord_day) AS streak_end,
  COUNT(*) AS   streak_days
FROM  groups     g
JOIN  customers  c ON c.id = g.customer_id
GROUP BY g.customer_id, c.name, grp
ORDER BY streak_days DESC
LIMIT 10;
